passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Protein kinases transfer the terminal phosphate of ATP to the hydroxyl group of serine, threonine or tyrosine residues. Kinase activity is often measured with a short synthetic peptide that the enzyme recognizes. Kemptide (Leu-Arg-Arg-Ala-Ser-Leu-Gly) is a standard substrate for protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates its single serine. A useful assay must separate the phosphorylated product from the unreacted peptide so that each can be measured.

Researchers used capillary electrophoresis for this purpose. A sample is drawn into a thin capillary filled with buffer, and a voltage is applied so that charged molecules move toward the electrode of opposite charge. The capillary wall was chemically coated to stop the bulk flow of buffer that normally occurs in uncoated glass, so a molecule moved only if it carried a net charge. Positively charged peptides moved toward the negative electrode, where the detector was placed, and a larger net charge for a given size gave a shorter migration time. Charges at each pH were calculated from these pKₐ values: N-terminus 8.0, C-terminus 3.1, arginine side chain 12.5, phosphate group 1.5 and 5.8.
The researchers ran three peptides in buffer at pH 7.4 and in buffer at pH 2.5 (Table 1). The third peptide was a variant in which the serine was replaced by alanine (Ser→Ala).

The method has advantages over older assays that use radioactive ATP, because no radioactive waste is produced and both substrate and product are measured directly in the same run. It requires only a few nanoliters of sample, so many time points can be taken from one small reaction.

To follow the reaction, kemptide (0.2 mM) was mixed with PKA and ATP at pH 7.4 and 30 °C. At each time point a sample was removed and added to an equal volume of cold pH 2.5 buffer, which stopped the reaction, and the sample was then run at pH 2.5. A parallel mixture contained PKA that had been heated to 95 °C for 10 minutes, and a third contained the Ser→Ala peptide with active PKA (Table 2).

qs.q: Why was phospho-kemptide not detected in the run at pH 7.4?
o: It was too large to enter the capillary
Adding one phosphate barely changes size.
It moved toward the positive electrode too fast
A net charge of 0 means no movement either way.
PKA removed the phosphate during the run
No enzyme was active in the run buffer.
Its net charge was zero, so it did not move
Correct: no charge, no migration in a coated capillary.
qs.x: Correct: At pH 7.4 the phosphate group carries about −2, which cancels the +2 of the unphosphorylated peptide. With no net charge and no bulk buffer flow in the coated capillary, the peptide stayed near where it was loaded. Why the others are wrong: One phosphate adds little size; a neutral molecule does not move toward either electrode; the reaction was stopped before the run. Trap: Forgetting that the coating removed the buffer flow that would otherwise carry neutral molecules to the detector.

qs.q: Why did the researchers analyze the reaction samples at pH 2.5 rather than at pH 7.4?
o: PKA works faster at pH 2.5
Low pH was used to stop the reaction.
Kemptide carries no charge at pH 7.4
It carries +2 at pH 7.4.
Both forms are positive and give separate peaks
Correct: both can be measured in one run.
Phosphate groups lose their negative charge entirely at pH 2.5
It still carries about −0.9.
qs.x: Correct: At pH 2.5 the substrate (+2.8) and product (+1.9) are both positive, so both reach the detector, and their different charges give different migration times. Measuring both peaks lets the researchers calculate the percent converted. At pH 7.4 the product would never be seen. Why the others are wrong: Kemptide is charged at pH 7.4; at pH 2.5 the phosphate is only partly neutralized, which is why the two forms still differ; the acid buffer was used to stop the enzyme, not to speed it up. Trap: Assuming the run conditions must match the reaction conditions.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the heated-PKA mixture?
o: To show that PKA stays stable at high temperatures
Heating destroyed its activity.
To show that the conversion needs active enzyme
Correct: ATP and peptide alone gave no product.
To show that heat phosphorylates kemptide
No product formed.
To measure the rate of the reaction at 95 °C
The reaction was still run at 30 °C.
qs.x: Correct: Heated PKA is denatured, so this mixture contains everything except a working enzyme. The lack of product (1% at most) shows that the phosphorylation seen with active PKA is caused by the enzyme and not by ATP reacting with the peptide on its own. Why the others are wrong: Heating inactivated PKA; the heated enzyme was used at 30 °C; no phosphorylation occurred. Trap: Misreading a negative control as a separate experiment about temperature.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the Ser→Ala results?
o: PKA phosphorylates the serine and no other site
Correct: removing serine removed all product.
PKA requires arginine to bind its substrate
The arginines were not changed.
The Ser→Ala peptide inhibits PKA
Inhibition was not tested.
Alanine is phosphorylated more slowly than serine
Alanine has no hydroxyl to phosphorylate.
qs.x: Correct: The Ser→Ala peptide has the same charge and migration time as kemptide, so it was measured just as easily, yet no phosphorylated form appeared. The serine hydroxyl is therefore the only site PKA modified. Why the others are wrong: The arginines are present in both peptides, so the data say nothing about their role; alanine's side chain is a methyl group that cannot accept a phosphate; the experiment did not test whether this peptide blocks PKA from acting on another substrate. Trap: Drawing a conclusion about a residue that the experiment did not change.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the slower rise in product between 20 and 40 minutes?
o: PKA was denatured by the pH 2.5 buffer
The acid only contacted samples already removed.
Less unreacted kemptide was left
Correct: the substrate was being used up.
Heating the enzyme slowed the reaction
The active mixture was not heated.
The phospho-peptide migrated too fast to detect
It was detected at 6.8 min.
qs.x: Correct: In the first 10 minutes about 4% of the peptide was converted per minute; from 20 to 40 minutes only about 1% per minute was converted. As substrate is consumed, its concentration falls below saturation and the rate drops. Why the others are wrong: Only removed samples were mixed with acid; the product peak was measured at pH 2.5; the active-enzyme mixture was never heated. Trap: Blaming the analysis method for a change that happens in the reaction itself.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: During a prolonged fast, the liver oxidizes fatty acids released from adipose tissue faster than it can use the resulting acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle. Much of the extra acetyl-CoA is converted in the mitochondrial matrix to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate (β-HB), the ketone bodies. These leave the liver and are taken up by heart, skeletal muscle and, after several days of fasting, the brain, which convert them back to acetyl-CoA. The liver itself cannot use ketone bodies because it lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase, the enzyme that activates acetoacetate.

Long-chain fatty acids cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly. In the cytosol, a fatty acid is first activated to its acyl-CoA. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1), on the outer membrane, then transfers the acyl group to carnitine, and the acyl-carnitine enters the matrix, where the acyl group is returned to CoA. CPT1 is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, which is abundant in the cytosol after a meal.

Researchers isolated liver mitochondria from rats that had been fed or fasted for 24 hours. The mitochondria were incubated with ATP, CoA, the enzyme that activates fatty acids, and the substrates listed in Table 1. Ketone body output (acetoacetate plus β-HB) was measured after 10 minutes. Each value is the mean of four preparations, and the standard deviation was less than 10% of the mean in every condition.

In a pilot experiment, the researchers confirmed that the mitochondria were intact by showing that they consumed oxygen rapidly when ADP was added and slowly when it was absent. Damaged mitochondria lose this coupling between electron transport and ATP synthesis. Preparations that failed this test were discarded before the ketone measurements.

The researchers noted that malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol and is lost when mitochondria are isolated, so any difference between fed and fasted mitochondria must come from the mitochondria themselves.

qs.q: Why did malonyl-CoA block ketone production from palmitate but not from palmitoyl-carnitine?
o: It converts palmitoyl-carnitine back to palmitate
Malonyl-CoA does not do this.
It competes with palmitate for β-oxidation enzymes
Then palmitoyl-carnitine would also be slowed.
It inhibits HMG-CoA synthase in the matrix
Then both substrates would be blocked.
It inhibits the step that forms acyl-carnitine
Correct: palmitoyl-carnitine skips CPT1.
qs.x: Correct: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT1, the enzyme that joins the fatty acyl group to carnitine. Palmitoyl-carnitine is already the product of that step, so it enters the matrix and is oxidized normally (9.8 versus 10.2). The block must therefore lie at CPT1. Why the others are wrong: Any block inside the matrix would also reduce output from palmitoyl-carnitine; malonyl-CoA does not compete for β-oxidation enzymes or reverse the CPT1 reaction. Trap: Placing the inhibitor downstream when the bypass result shows it acts upstream.

qs.q: What does the condition without added carnitine show?
o: Carnitine inhibits ketone body formation
Output was higher with carnitine.
Palmitate is toxic without carnitine
Toxicity was not measured.
Palmitate needs carnitine to enter
Correct: output fell to near baseline.
Carnitine is oxidized to ketone bodies
Carnitine alone gave only 0.5.
qs.x: Correct: Without carnitine, 1.0 mM palmitate produced only 0.9 nmol/min per mg, close to the 0.5 seen with no substrate. Fatty acids can be oxidized only after the carnitine shuttle carries them into the matrix. Why the others are wrong: Carnitine alone did not raise output; nothing in the data measures toxicity; adding carnitine increased production. Trap: Treating a required cofactor as if it were a substrate.

qs.q: Why did mitochondria from fasted rats produce more ketone bodies from the same substrate?
o: Fasting raised their ketogenic enzyme levels
Correct: the difference is within the mitochondria.
Fasted mitochondria received more palmitate
All received 1.0 mM.
Fasted mitochondria contained more malonyl-CoA
Malonyl-CoA would lower output, and it is lost on isolation.
Fasted mitochondria lacked CPT1
Then output would be near zero.
qs.x: Correct: The passage states that cytosolic malonyl-CoA is lost during isolation, so the higher output (18.5 versus 10.2) must reflect a property of the mitochondria themselves, such as more CPT1 or more mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase. During fasting, low insulin and high glucagon increase the synthesis of these enzymes. Why the others are wrong: Malonyl-CoA would decrease output and was removed anyway; substrate levels were the same; without CPT1, palmitate could not enter. Trap: Using a whole-body explanation that the isolation step rules out.

qs.q: Between 0.5 and 1.0 mM palmitate, ketone output rose by much less than twofold. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The enzymes involved were nearing saturation
Correct: rate levels off at high substrate.
Palmitate was converted into glucose instead
Fatty acids cannot make net glucose.
Ketone bodies were used by the liver mitochondria
The liver lacks the activating enzyme.
The mitochondria ran out of carnitine
Then output would drop, not keep rising.
qs.x: Correct: Output rose from 4.1 to 7.6 to 10.2 as palmitate doubled each time, a pattern of an enzyme-mediated process approaching its maximum rate. Why the others are wrong: Acetyl-CoA from fatty acids cannot be used for net glucose synthesis; the passage states that the liver cannot activate acetoacetate; carnitine was supplied, and output was still rising. Trap: Expecting rate to stay proportional to substrate concentration at every level.

qs.q: A patient has an inherited deficiency of CPT1 in the liver. After an overnight fast, which finding is most likely?
o: High blood ketone bodies with normal glucose
CPT1 is needed to make ketones.
Normal ketone levels because the brain makes them
The brain does not make ketones.
High blood glucose from extra glycogen breakdown
Glycogen runs low overnight.
Low blood glucose with low ketone bodies
Correct: fat cannot be burned or turned into ketones.
qs.x: Correct: Without CPT1, the liver cannot bring long-chain fatty acids into its mitochondria. It cannot make ketone bodies, and it lacks the ATP and NADH from β-oxidation that support glucose synthesis, so fasting causes low glucose without the expected rise in ketones. Why the others are wrong: Ketone production depends on CPT1; overnight fasting depletes liver glycogen rather than raising glucose; the liver, not the brain, makes ketone bodies. Trap: Assuming that low glucose always comes with high ketones.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: In Escherichia coli, the lac operon contains the lacZ, lacY and lacA genes, which are transcribed together from one promoter. The lacI gene, located just upstream, encodes a repressor protein that binds the operator (lacO), a DNA sequence that overlaps the promoter, and blocks RNA polymerase. When lactose is present, some of it is converted to allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. A second level of control acts through the catabolite activator protein (CAP). When glucose is scarce, cyclic AMP rises and binds CAP, and the CAP–cAMP complex helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter.

Researchers measured β-galactosidase (the lacZ product) in several strains grown in a medium with glycerol as the carbon source. Some cultures received isopropyl β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG), a compound that binds the repressor like allolactose but cannot be broken down by the cell. Some also received glucose. The strains carried these mutations: lacI⁻, which makes no functional repressor; lacOᶜ, an operator that the repressor cannot bind; and lacIˢ, which makes a repressor that binds the operator but cannot bind inducer.

Two strains were partial diploids. Each carried a small F′ plasmid with a second copy of the lac region, so the cell had one copy on the chromosome and one on the plasmid. In these strains, the chromosome copy is written first and the plasmid copy after the slash. Activity is reported in Miller units, a standard measure of β-galactosidase activity.

Mutants like these were used in the original studies of the operon. Researchers could not see the repressor or the operator directly, so they inferred which parts of the system were proteins and which were DNA sites by asking whether a second copy of a gene could correct a defect in the other copy. A gene product that can correct a defect on another DNA molecule is said to act in trans; a site that controls only the genes on its own DNA molecule acts in cis.
Before each assay, cells were grown for at least six generations in the stated medium so that enzyme levels had reached a steady state. Each value is the mean of three cultures.

qs.q: What does the lacI⁻ / F′ lacI⁺ result show about the repressor?
o: It is needed to activate transcription
The lacI⁻ strain had high expression.
It diffuses and can act on either copy
Correct: the plasmid lacI⁺ restored control of the chromosome.
It cannot bind IPTG when made from a plasmid
Induction worked normally.
It acts only on the DNA molecule that encodes it
The plasmid gene controlled the chromosomal operon.
qs.x: Correct: The chromosome lacks a working repressor gene, yet adding lacI⁺ on the plasmid restored low expression without IPTG (3) and normal induction (1,490). The repressor protein made from the plasmid must reach the chromosomal operator, so it acts in trans. Why the others are wrong: Action limited to the encoding DNA would leave the chromosomal operon on; the repressor blocks transcription, so losing it raises expression; induction was normal. Trap: Mixing up trans-acting proteins with cis-acting DNA sites.

qs.q: Why is activity low without IPTG in the lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ / F′ lacOᶜ lacZ⁻ strain?
o: The repressor cannot bind the lacOᶜ operator anywhere
It still binds the normal chromosomal operator.
The lacZ⁻ copy makes a protein that blocks the other copy
Nothing suggests interference.
The faulty operator controls only the lacZ⁻ copy
Correct: operators act in cis.
IPTG is needed for any lacZ gene to be transcribed
lacOᶜ alone gave 900 without IPTG.
qs.x: Correct: The lacOᶜ operator is on the plasmid next to a lacZ⁻ gene. That copy is transcribed all the time but makes no active enzyme. The chromosome's working lacZ is controlled by a normal operator, which the repressor still binds, so activity stays low until IPTG is added. An operator affects only the genes on its own DNA molecule. Why the others are wrong: The normal operator can still bind repressor; no blocking protein is needed to explain the result; the lacOᶜ strain shows that transcription can occur without inducer. Trap: Assuming a constitutive operator turns on every lacZ gene in the cell.

qs.q: What would a lacIˢ / F′ lacI⁺ strain most likely show with 1 mM IPTG?
o: High activity, because the normal repressor responds to IPTG
The mutant repressor stays bound.
High activity, because two lacI copies cancel each other
Repressors do not cancel.
Low, because the mutant repressor stays bound
Correct: lacIˢ is dominant.
Activity of about 750, half of wild type
Both operons are repressed by the mutant protein.
qs.x: Correct: The lacIˢ repressor cannot bind inducer, so it stays on the operator whether or not IPTG is present. Because the repressor diffuses, it will occupy the operator even when normal repressor is also made, keeping expression low. The lacIˢ mutation is dominant. Why the others are wrong: Releasing the normal repressor does not help while the mutant one stays bound; the protein can act on any operator in the cell; the two repressors do not neutralize each other. Trap: Assuming that a normal allele always masks a mutant one.

qs.q: Why did glucose lower activity in the lacI⁻ strain, which has no repressor?
o: Glucose converts IPTG into allolactose
IPTG cannot be broken down.
Glucose restores a working repressor
lacI⁻ makes no functional repressor.
Glucose binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Sugars do not bind DNA sites.
Glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is inactive
Correct: catabolite repression is separate from the repressor.
qs.x: Correct: In every strain glucose cut activity about tenfold (for example, 1,510 to 150 in lacI⁻). Because this happened even without a repressor, it must act through a separate system, the CAP–cAMP activator, which is inactive when glucose keeps cAMP low. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not bind the operator; IPTG is not metabolized; glucose cannot repair a mutant gene. Trap: Explaining all lac control through the repressor.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use IPTG instead of lactose as the inducer?
o: Cells cannot break it down
Correct: steady inducer concentration.
It is a stronger carbon source than glucose
It is not used as food.
It binds the operator directly
It binds the repressor.
It activates CAP in place of cAMP
IPTG does not bind CAP.
qs.x: Correct: Lactose is consumed as it induces the operon, and it must first be converted to allolactose by β-galactosidase, so its effect would change over time and would differ in strains with less enzyme. IPTG is not metabolized, so every culture is exposed to the same inducer concentration throughout. Why the others are wrong: IPTG is not a nutrient; it acts on the repressor, not on DNA; CAP responds to cAMP. Trap: Assuming the natural inducer is always the best choice in an experiment.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Methanol poisoning is dangerous because the body oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde and then to formic acid, which causes metabolic acidosis and damages the optic nerve. The first step is catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), the same liver enzyme that oxidizes ethanol. Two treatments are used. One is fomepizole, a drug that binds the ADH active site. The other, used when fomepizole is unavailable, is ethanol itself. Both slow the conversion of methanol to its toxic products while the kidneys and dialysis remove the unchanged methanol.

Researchers studied purified human liver ADH to compare fomepizole with two experimental compounds. They measured the initial rate of NADH formation at 340 nm with ethanol as the substrate at several concentrations, with each inhibitor at a fixed concentration, and fit the data to the Michaelis–Menten equation. Compound N was known from crystal structures to bind a pocket far from the active site. Compound U had been found in a screen and had no known binding site. The fitted constants are shown in Table 1.

To check the fits, the researchers also drew double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) plots of 1/rate against 1/[ethanol] for each condition. In a second experiment, they measured the rate with methanol as the substrate. ADH oxidized methanol with a Kₘ of about 7 mM and a Vₘₐₓ about one-tenth of that for ethanol. When ethanol (5 mM) was added to a reaction containing methanol (5 mM), the rate of formaldehyde formation fell by about 90%.

Because the three inhibitors were tested at different concentrations, the researchers cautioned that the table should not be used to rank their potency. A fair comparison would require the inhibition constant (Ki) of each compound, measured from several inhibitor concentrations.

The researchers concluded that fomepizole is well suited to treatment because it acts at low concentration and does not itself produce a toxic product, whereas ethanol must be kept at a high blood level for many hours and causes intoxication.

qs.q: Which type of inhibition does fomepizole show?
o: Irreversible
Full Vₘₐₓ was still reached.
Competitive
Correct: Kₘ rose and Vₘₐₓ was unchanged.
Noncompetitive
That would lower Vₘₐₓ.
Uncompetitive
That would lower both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ.
qs.x: Correct: Fomepizole raised the apparent Kₘ fourfold but left Vₘₐₓ at 100, the signature of an inhibitor that competes with substrate for the active site. Enough ethanol can still outcompete it. Why the others are wrong: Noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ without changing Kₘ, as compound N does; uncompetitive inhibition lowers both, as compound U does; an irreversible inhibitor would remove active enzyme and lower Vₘₐₓ. Trap: Assuming a drug that works at low concentration must bind irreversibly.

qs.q: At 1 mM ethanol, what is the expected rate with fomepizole present, in µmol/min per mg?
o: This uses compound N's values.
This is the uninhibited rate at Kₘ.
This subtracts the Kₘ from 100.
qs.x: Correct: By the Michaelis–Menten equation, rate = Vₘₐₓ[S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]) = 100 × 1 ÷ (4.0 + 1) = 20. Why the others are wrong: 25 is the rate with compound N (50 × 1 ÷ 2); 50 is the uninhibited rate when [S] equals Kₘ; 80 has no basis in the equation. Trap: Using the uninhibited Kₘ after an inhibitor has changed it.

qs.q: How would the Lineweaver–Burk line for compound N compare with the line for no inhibitor?
o: Identical, because Kₘ is unchanged
Vₘₐₓ changed.
Same y-intercept, x-intercept closer to zero
That is the competitive pattern.
Same x-intercept, higher y-intercept
Correct: Kₘ unchanged, Vₘₐₓ halved.
Parallel to it, shifted upward
That is the uncompetitive pattern.
qs.x: Correct: On a double-reciprocal plot, the y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ and the x-intercept is −1/Kₘ. Compound N halves Vₘₐₓ, so the y-intercept doubles, while Kₘ stays at 1.0 mM, so both lines cross the x-axis at the same point. Why the others are wrong: Moving only the x-intercept describes fomepizole; parallel lines describe compound U; the lines differ because Vₘₐₓ fell. Trap: Mixing up which intercept reports which constant.

qs.q: What do the data suggest about where compound U binds?
o: Only to the enzyme–substrate complex
Correct: Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ fell by the same factor.
Only to the free enzyme's active site
That would raise Kₘ.
To the ethanol molecule before it reaches ADH
That would act like lowering [S].
Equally to free enzyme and the complex
That would leave Kₘ unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: Compound U halved both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ. An inhibitor that binds only after substrate is bound pulls the reaction toward the enzyme–substrate complex, which lowers Kₘ, while also trapping that complex, which lowers Vₘₐₓ. This uncompetitive pattern means its binding site forms only when ethanol is in place. Why the others are wrong: Binding free enzyme at the active site gives competitive inhibition; binding both forms equally gives the noncompetitive pattern of compound N; tying up ethanol would raise the apparent Kₘ, not lower it. Trap: Reading a lower Kₘ as a sign that the inhibitor helps the enzyme.

qs.q: Why does adding 5 mM ethanol sharply reduce formaldehyde formation from 5 mM methanol?
o: Ethanol converts methanol to a harmless product
Ethanol does not react with methanol.
Ethanol lowers the Vₘₐₓ of ADH for all substrates
Ethanol is a substrate, not a noncompetitive inhibitor.
Ethanol destroys formaldehyde as it forms
Formation itself fell.
ADH binds ethanol better and turns it over faster
Correct: ethanol occupies the active site.
qs.x: Correct: Ethanol and methanol compete for the same active site. Because ADH has a much lower Kₘ for ethanol (1.0 mM versus about 7 mM) and turns it over faster, ethanol occupies most of the enzyme, leaving little for methanol. Methanol is then cleared unchanged. Why the others are wrong: The measurement was the rate of formation; ethanol does not change the enzyme's maximum rate; the two alcohols do not react with each other. Trap: Thinking that the treatment neutralizes the toxin instead of slowing its activation.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A protein's amino acid sequence contains the information needed for it to fold. In a classic set of experiments, ribonuclease was fully unfolded in concentrated urea with a reducing agent that breaks its four disulfide bonds. When both were removed, the enzyme refolded and regained nearly all of its activity. Folding is driven mainly by burying hydrophobic side chains away from water, while hydrogen bonds, ion pairs and disulfide bonds add further stability.

Researchers studied a 128-residue enzyme with one disulfide bond, between Cys30 and Cys115, and a single tryptophan buried in its hydrophobic core. When the protein unfolds, the tryptophan becomes exposed to water, and its fluorescence emission peak shifts from 334 nm to 352 nm. The researchers used this shift to measure the fraction of protein unfolded at each urea concentration. From these curves they calculated the urea concentration at which half the protein is unfolded (the midpoint) and the free energy of unfolding in the absence of urea (ΔG). A larger ΔG means a more stable protein. They tested the wild type and three mutants: C30A/C115A, which lacks the disulfide; L58A, in which a core leucine is replaced by alanine; and K12A, in which a lysine on the surface is replaced by alanine. All four had the same activity at 25 °C without urea.

In a second experiment, wild-type enzyme was unfolded in 8 M urea with 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), a reducing agent. In procedure 1, the urea was removed first by dialysis and the DTT was removed afterward, in air. In procedure 2, the DTT was removed first while the protein was still in 8 M urea, and then the urea was removed. Procedure 1 restored 92% of the original activity; procedure 2 restored 3%. Mass spectrometry showed that after procedure 2, most molecules had a disulfide bond, but often between Cys30 and one of the protein's two other cysteines, which are normally free.

qs.q: Why does the tryptophan emission shift when the protein unfolds?
o: The peptide bonds near tryptophan are cut
Unfolding does not break peptide bonds.
The tryptophan becomes exposed to water
Correct: its surroundings become polar.
Urea forms a covalent bond with tryptophan
Urea acts noncovalently.
Tryptophan is converted to a different amino acid
The residue is unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: In the folded protein, the tryptophan side chain sits in the nonpolar core. Unfolding exposes it to water, and this change in environment shifts its fluorescence to longer wavelength. Why the others are wrong: Urea disrupts noncovalent interactions and does not react with side chains; unfolding leaves the primary structure intact; the amino acid itself does not change. Trap: Treating a change in conformation as a chemical change in the residue.

qs.q: Why did L58A lower stability much more than K12A?
o: L58A removes the disulfide bond
The disulfide involves Cys30 and Cys115.
Lysine is hydrophobic, so its loss stabilizes the protein
Lysine is charged and polar.
Alanine cannot be part of an α-helix
Alanine is a strong helix former.
Leu58 is buried in the hydrophobic core
Correct: surface residues add little.
qs.x: Correct: Replacing a large buried leucine with alanine leaves a cavity in the hydrophobic core and weakens the main driving force for folding, lowering ΔG from 6.8 to 3.4 kcal/mol. Lys12 is on the surface, exposed to water, so removing its side chain barely changed stability (6.6 kcal/mol). Why the others are wrong: Lysine is charged; alanine favors helices; the disulfide is unaffected by L58A. Trap: Assuming every mutation affects stability equally.

qs.q: What best explains the low activity after procedure 2?
o: The amino acid sequence was changed by urea
Urea does not alter sequence.
Disulfides formed before the chain folded
Correct: wrong cysteine pairs were locked in.
Removing urea first is harmful to the protein
Procedure 2 removed urea last.
DTT permanently denatured the enzyme
Procedure 1 also used DTT and worked.
qs.x: Correct: In procedure 2, the reducing agent was removed while the chain was still unfolded in urea, so cysteines that happened to be close together formed bonds at random, including wrong pairs. When the urea was removed, these incorrect bonds held the chain in non-native shapes. In procedure 1, the chain folded first, bringing Cys30 and Cys115 together before oxidation. Why the others are wrong: Urea does not change the sequence; procedure 1 shows DTT does no lasting harm; procedure 2 removed urea second. Trap: Concluding that the sequence lacks folding information when the order of steps caused the problem.

qs.q: Which interactions does urea mainly disrupt?
o: Covalent bonds within the amino acid side chains
Side chains are not altered.
Peptide bonds of the backbone
Hydrolysis needs a protease or acid.
Hydrogen bonds and other noncovalent forces
Correct: unfolding without breaking covalent bonds.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines
That requires a reducing agent such as DTT.
qs.x: Correct: Urea forms hydrogen bonds with the protein and makes it easier for water to surround nonpolar groups, weakening the noncovalent forces that hold the folded state together. That is why DTT was needed in addition to break the disulfide. Why the others are wrong: Peptide bonds stay intact; disulfides require reduction; side chains are chemically unchanged. Trap: Assuming a denaturant breaks every kind of bond.

qs.q: At 3 M urea, which proteins would be mostly unfolded?
o: L58A and C30A/C115A
Correct: their midpoints are below 3 M.
Wild type and K12A only
Their midpoints are above 4 M.
All four proteins
Wild type and K12A stay mostly folded.
Only L58A
C30A/C115A's midpoint is 2.6 M.
qs.x: Correct: The midpoint is the urea concentration at which half the protein is unfolded, so at a higher concentration more than half is unfolded. The midpoints of C30A/C115A (2.6 M) and L58A (2.1 M) are below 3 M, while wild type (4.2 M) and K12A (4.1 M) remain mostly folded. Why the others are wrong: Those choices ignore one of the two low-midpoint mutants or include proteins whose midpoints are above 3 M. Trap: Forgetting that the disulfide mutant is also destabilized.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the acid–base properties of five common amino acids—lysine, glutamic acid, histidine, tyrosine, and serine—by performing pH titrations across a pH range of 1–12. The experiment involved preparing 0.1 M solutions of each amino acid in 10 mM phosphate buffer, measuring ¹H NMR chemical shifts at 1‑unit pH intervals, and fitting the data to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to extract pKₐ values for the side‑chain functional groups. The resulting pKₐ values were compared to literature values to assess experimental accuracy. Additionally, the researchers calculated the isoelectric point (pI) for each amino acid by averaging the pKₐ values of the ionizable groups that change charge across the pH range. The study also examined how the presence of a high‑ionic‑strength buffer (150 mM NaCl) affected the apparent pKₐ shifts. The data are summarized in Table 1 below.

qs.q: Among lysine, glutamic acid, histidine, and tyrosine, which has the highest side‑chain pKₐ in Table 1?
o: Lysine
Correct
Glutamic acid
Not the best answer
Histidine
Not the best answer
Tyrosine
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: A) Lysine, 10.5, is the highest of the four listed. Why the others are wrong: B) Glutamic acid is 4.25. C) Histidine is 6.00. D) Tyrosine is 10.07, close to but below lysine. Trap: Choosing tyrosine (10.07) because it is close to lysine, or serine (13.6) from the table even though it is not among the options; only the four listed options count.

qs.q: If a 150 mM NaCl buffer at pH 8.5 is added, which side chain will carry a positive charge?
o: Lysine
Correct
Glutamic acid
Not the best answer
Histidine
Not the best answer
Tyrosine
Not the best answer
qs.x: At pH 8.5 the Lys side chain (pKₐ 10.5) is >99 % protonated (–NH₃⁺, charged). Tyr (pKₐ 10.07) is also mostly protonated, but protonated Tyr is a neutral phenol; Glu is deprotonated and His is mostly neutral. Trap: Choosing tyrosine because its pKₐ (10.07) is near lysine; at pH 8.5 the phenol is still protonated but a protonated Tyr is neutral, so it carries no positive charge.

qs.q: Calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of a dipeptide composed of lysine and glutamic acid, using the side‑chain pKₐ values provided and an α‑NH₃⁺ pKₐ of ≈9.0 for the free N‑terminus.
o: Correct
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
qs.x: The net charge is zero between deprotonation of the Glu side chain (pKₐ 4.25) and the free α‑NH₃⁺ (pKₐ ≈ 9.0), while the Lys side chain (10.5) is still protonated: pI = (4.25 + 9.0)/2 ≈ 6.6. Trap: Averaging the wrong pair of pKₐ values (for example including the Lys side chain at 10.5) instead of the two values that bracket the neutral species, Glu side chain and free amino terminus.

qs.q: Which statement about pKₐ values is NOT correct?
o: A group is half‑ionized when the pH equals its pKₐ.
Not the best answer
The pKₐ of a group is completely unaffected by ionic strength and temperature.
Correct
At a pH two units below its pKₐ, a group is about 99% protonated.
Not the best answer
The apparent pKₐ of a side chain can shift in a different environment, such as high‑salt buffer.
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: B) is false: apparent pKₐ values shift with ionic strength and temperature (extended Debye–Hückel: pKₐ′ = pKₐ + A(2z − 1)√I/(1 + √I)), as the 150 mM NaCl experiment examines. Why the others are wrong: A) At pH = pKₐ the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is 1, so the group is half‑ionized; this is correct. C) pH − pKₐ = −2 gives a 100:1 ratio of protonated to deprotonated form, about 99% protonated; this is correct. D) Environment, including salt, can shift apparent pKₐ; this is correct. Trap: Treating pKₐ as a fixed constant that never changes, even though the passage tests apparent pKₐ shifts in 150 mM NaCl buffer.

qs.q: Which amino acid side chain most commonly acts as a proton shuttle in enzyme active sites near physiological pH?
o: Histidine (imidazole pKₐ ≈ 6)
Correct
Lysine (pKₐ ≈ 10.5)
Not the best answer
Aspartate (pKₐ ≈ 3.7)
Not the best answer
Leucine (no ionizable side chain)
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: Histidine's imidazole pKₐ (about 6–7) lets it act as both proton donor and acceptor near pH 7, which is why it is common in general acid–base catalysis such as serine proteases. Why the others are wrong: B) Lysine pKₐ of 10.5 means it is almost always protonated near pH 7, so it is a poor shuttle. C) Aspartate pKₐ of about 3.7 means it is almost always deprotonated near pH 7. D) Leucine has no ionizable side chain, so it cannot transfer protons. Trap: Choosing lysine or aspartate because they are charged; a shuttle needs a pKₐ near the working pH so that it is both protonated and deprotonated.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: At high altitude, the barometric pressure is lower, so each breath delivers oxygen at a lower partial pressure. At 4,300 m, inspired PO₂ is about 60% of its sea-level value. The body responds in stages. Within minutes, breathing increases. Over several days, the kidneys adjust the acid–base balance of the blood. Over weeks, red blood cell production rises in response to erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone released by the kidney when its oxygen supply falls.

To study these stages, investigators enrolled 64 healthy adults who lived near sea level and were about to spend three weeks at a research station at 4,300 m. No participant had been above 2,000 m in the previous year, and none took acetazolamide or any other drug to prevent altitude sickness. Measurements were taken at sea level the day before departure (day 0) and on days 1, 3 and 21 at altitude. Arterial blood was sampled from the radial artery at rest, and minute ventilation was measured with a mouthpiece while participants sat quietly. Plasma volume was estimated with a dye-dilution method.

Each participant also completed a symptom questionnaire every morning, and the investigators recorded sleep quality, because breathing during sleep at altitude often becomes irregular, with pauses followed by rapid breaths. This periodic breathing is thought to result from the push and pull between the drive from low oxygen and the brake from low carbon dioxide.

New red blood cells take about five to seven days to mature in the bone marrow and enter the circulation after EPO rises. Six participants developed headache and nausea on day 1, consistent with acute mountain sickness; their symptoms resolved by day 4 and their data were kept in the analysis. The investigators noted that the study had no comparison group remaining at sea level, but argued that the large changes seen were unlikely to occur in healthy adults over three weeks without a change in altitude.

qs.q: Which receptors are most directly responsible for the rise in ventilation on day 1?
o: Carotid body chemoreceptors
Correct: they sense the fall in arterial PO₂.
Pulmonary stretch receptors
These limit, rather than drive, breathing.
Central chemoreceptors in the medulla
They respond to CO₂ and H⁺, which fell.
Aortic baroreceptors
These sense blood pressure, not oxygen.
qs.x: Correct: Arterial PO₂ fell from 95 to 45 mmHg, which strongly stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies. These are the only receptors that respond directly to low arterial oxygen. Why the others are wrong: The central chemoreceptors respond to rising CO₂ and acidity, and both PCO₂ and H⁺ fell, which would reduce their drive; stretch receptors inhibit inspiration; baroreceptors respond to pressure. Trap: Choosing the central chemoreceptors because they normally set the pace of breathing.

qs.q: What best explains why arterial pH returned close to 7.40 by day 21 even though PCO₂ kept falling?
o: Breathing slowed and CO₂ was retained
Ventilation kept rising.
The kidneys excreted more bicarbonate
Correct: HCO₃⁻ fell from 24 to 17 mEq/L.
The lungs began to excrete bicarbonate
The lungs remove CO₂, not HCO₃⁻.
Red blood cells produced more lactic acid
No lactate data are given.
qs.x: Correct: Hyperventilation lowered PCO₂, producing a respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.47 on day 1). Over the following days, the kidneys compensated by excreting bicarbonate, which fell steadily, bringing pH back toward normal despite the low PCO₂. Why the others are wrong: Ventilation rose and PCO₂ fell throughout; the lungs do not excrete bicarbonate; the data say nothing about lactic acid. Trap: Expecting the respiratory system to correct a disturbance it caused.

qs.q: What most likely explains the rise in hemoglobin between day 0 and day 3?
o: EPO caused a burst of new red cells within hours
New cells take five to seven days to appear.
Low PO₂ increased the hemoglobin in each red cell
Red cells do not make new hemoglobin.
The spleen destroyed fewer red cells at altitude
No data on red cell breakdown are given.
Less plasma water concentrated the red cells
Correct: plasma volume fell 11%.
qs.x: Correct: Plasma volume fell to 89% of its starting value by day 3, so the same red cells were suspended in less fluid and hemoglobin concentration rose. New red cells produced in response to EPO do not reach the blood for about a week, so they explain the later rise to day 21. Why the others are wrong: The passage states the maturation time; mature red cells lack nuclei and cannot make new protein; no data address red cell destruction. Trap: Attributing every hemoglobin rise to new red cell production.

qs.q: Which description best fits this study's design?
o: A case-control study
Participants were not chosen by outcome.
A randomized controlled trial
No one was randomly assigned to a condition.
A prospective repeated-measures study
Correct: one group followed over time.
A cross-sectional survey of travelers
Each person was measured four times.
qs.x: Correct: The same 64 people were measured before and at three times during exposure, with each person serving as his or her own baseline. There was no randomization and no separate comparison group. Why the others are wrong: A randomized trial would assign people to altitude or sea level; a case-control study starts from people who already have an outcome; a cross-sectional study measures each person once. Trap: Calling any study with planned measurements an experiment.

qs.q: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the kidney and speeds acclimatization. Which mechanism best explains this?
o: It raises the oxygen affinity of hemoglobin in the lungs
It does not act on hemoglobin.
It blocks the carotid body response to low oxygen
That would reduce ventilation.
It stops the kidneys from releasing EPO
That would slow acclimatization.
Bicarbonate loss in urine drives breathing further
Correct: a mild acidosis stimulates ventilation.
qs.x: Correct: By blocking carbonic anhydrase in the renal tubule, acetazolamide causes bicarbonate to be lost in the urine. The resulting metabolic acidosis does quickly what the kidneys did slowly from day 1 to day 21, offsetting the alkalosis that otherwise limits the rise in breathing. Why the others are wrong: The drug does not act on hemoglobin; blocking EPO or the carotid bodies would worsen adaptation. Trap: Overlooking that the respiratory alkalosis itself restrains ventilation early at altitude.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Human skeletal muscle contains a mixture of fiber types. Type I (slow-twitch) fibers have a slow form of myosin ATPase, many mitochondria, abundant myoglobin and a dense capillary supply; they resist fatigue and rely on oxidative phosphorylation. Type II (fast-twitch) fibers have a fast myosin ATPase and generate high force and power, but many of them rely heavily on glycolysis and fatigue quickly. Each motor neuron innervates fibers of only one type, and the proportion of each type in a muscle varies widely among people.

Investigators took needle biopsies from the vastus lateralis (a thigh muscle) of 12 elite sprinters, 12 elite distance runners and 12 untrained adults of similar age. Fibers were typed by staining for myosin ATPase activity. Mitochondrial volume was measured by electron microscopy, and capillaries were counted in cross sections. Each participant also performed a cycling test to measure maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max) and a 6-second sprint to measure peak power (Table 1).

To see how much of these differences could be produced by training, the untrained participants then completed 12 weeks of supervised endurance cycling, five sessions a week. Their biopsies were repeated at the end (Table 2).

All participants were men aged 21 to 30, and none had used anabolic steroids, which were screened for in urine. Training sessions lasted 45 minutes at about 70% of each person's VO₂max, and attendance averaged 94%. Diet was not controlled, but body mass changed by less than 1 kg on average over the 12 weeks.

The investigators noted that studies of twins suggest that fiber type proportion is strongly inherited, while mitochondrial content and capillary density respond to training in people of any genetic background. They also noted that a biopsy samples only a few hundred fibers from one site, and that fiber proportions can vary somewhat between the surface and the deeper parts of the same muscle.

qs.q: Why would distance runners benefit from their high mitochondrial volume and capillary density?
o: They store creatine phosphate for sprints
That is a short-term energy store.
They support aerobic ATP production
Correct: sustained work needs oxidative ATP.
They allow faster glycolysis without lactate
Glycolysis does not require mitochondria.
They increase the force of each contraction
Force depends on fiber size and myosin type.
qs.x: Correct: Long-distance running depends on oxidative phosphorylation, which needs a steady oxygen supply from capillaries and many mitochondria to use it. These features also match the highest VO₂max in the table (74 mL/kg/min). Why the others are wrong: Force comes from contractile proteins, not mitochondria; glycolysis occurs in the cytosol; creatine phosphate buffers ATP for a few seconds and is not stored in capillaries or mitochondria. Trap: Linking mitochondria to strength instead of endurance.

qs.q: What do the training results suggest?
o: Training made the untrained group equal to distance runners
Their values remained far lower.
Training converted most type II fibers to type I
Type I rose only from 52% to 54%.
Training improved the fibers already present
Correct: type I % barely changed.
Training had no effect on oxidative capacity
Mitochondria rose by almost half.
qs.x: Correct: Twelve weeks of endurance training raised mitochondrial volume (4.5% to 6.6%), capillaries (1.8 to 2.3 per fiber) and VO₂max (42 to 49), but the proportion of type I fibers barely changed. The adaptation occurred within the fibers that were already present. Why the others are wrong: Fiber proportion changed by only two percentage points; oxidative capacity clearly increased; the trained group stayed well below the distance runners on every measure. Trap: Assuming endurance training transforms fiber types.

qs.q: What limits the conclusion that sprint training caused the low type I percentage seen in sprinters?
o: Fast-fibered people may choose sprinting
Correct: selection could explain it.
Sprinters were biopsied from the wrong muscle
All groups used the same muscle.
Type I fibers cannot be identified by staining
Myosin ATPase staining identifies them.
Sprinters had a lower VO₂max than distance runners
That is a result, not a limitation.
qs.x: Correct: The athlete comparison is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether training changed the fibers or whether people born with many fast fibers became sprinters because they were fast. The training data and the twin studies both suggest that fiber proportion changes little with training, which favors selection. Why the others are wrong: The same muscle was sampled in every group; a lower VO₂max is a finding; myosin ATPase staining is a standard way to type fibers. Trap: Reading cause and effect into a comparison of existing groups.

qs.q: Which feature best explains the sprinters' high peak power?
o: A larger mitochondrial volume in each fiber
Sprinters had the lowest.
A higher VO₂max than the other groups
Distance runners had the highest.
Their high density of capillaries
Sprinters had the fewest.
Fast myosin ATPase in type II fibers
Correct: faster cross-bridge cycling.
qs.x: Correct: Power is force times velocity. Type II fibers cycle cross-bridges faster because their myosin hydrolyzes ATP more quickly, so a muscle rich in them shortens rapidly with high force. Sprinters had 76% type II fibers and the highest power (22 W/kg). Why the others are wrong: Sprinters had the lowest capillary density, mitochondrial volume and VO₂max of the athletes. Trap: Attributing power to aerobic features that support endurance.

qs.q: During a 30-second all-out sprint, sprinters' type II fibers produce lactate. Why?
o: Pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺
Correct: this lets glycolysis continue.
Lactate is made to store glucose for later
Glucose is stored as glycogen.
Mitochondria convert pyruvate directly into lactate
Lactate dehydrogenase is cytosolic.
Lactate is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain
Oxygen is the final acceptor.
qs.x: Correct: Rapid glycolysis produces NADH faster than mitochondria can reoxidize it. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and regenerates NAD⁺, which glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs to keep glycolysis running. Why the others are wrong: Oxygen is the terminal acceptor of the electron transport chain; glucose is stored as glycogen; lactate is made in the cytosol. Trap: Thinking lactate is a waste product with no purpose.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, can obtain ATP from glucose in two ways. In aerobic respiration, glucose is fully oxidized to CO₂, and the NADH formed is reoxidized by the electron transport chain, with O₂ as the final electron acceptor. In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde and CO₂, and acetaldehyde is then reduced to ethanol by NADH, regenerating NAD⁺. Fermentation yields 2 ATP per glucose, while respiration yields about 30.

In the nineteenth century, Louis Pasteur observed that yeast consumes much less sugar when air is present, a finding now called the Pasteur effect. Later work showed a second effect: at high glucose concentrations, many yeast strains ferment even when oxygen is plentiful. This is called the Crabtree effect, and it is the reason yeast in sugary dough or grape juice produces ethanol even when it is well aerated.

Researchers grew yeast in liquid medium and measured, per gram of cells per hour, the glucose consumed, the oxygen consumed, and the ethanol and CO₂ released. In some flasks they added sodium cyanide, which binds cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). Table 1 shows the results. All flasks were held at 30 °C and pH 5.0, and each value is the mean of three flasks.

Before the measurements, cells were taken from a starter culture, washed to remove any ethanol, and suspended at the same density in every flask. Dissolved oxygen was monitored with an electrode; in the aerobic flasks it stayed above 50% of air saturation throughout, and in the no-oxygen flasks, which were flushed with nitrogen, it stayed below the limit of detection.

The researchers also measured cell growth. Over 8 hours, cells in the aerobic, low-glucose flasks gained about four times as much mass per mole of glucose consumed as cells without oxygen. They proposed that respiration supplies more ATP per glucose and therefore supports more growth for the same amount of sugar.

qs.q: Why did yeast use about six times more glucose without oxygen?
o: Ethanol speeds up glycolysis directly
No evidence supports this.
Each glucose yields far less ATP by fermentation
Correct: cells use more sugar to meet ATP demand.
Oxygen inhibits the transport of glucose into cells
Cyanide cells with oxygen also used more.
Fermentation produces more ATP per glucose
It produces 2 versus about 30.
qs.x: Correct: Without oxygen, yeast obtains only 2 ATP per glucose by fermentation instead of about 30 by respiration. To meet its ATP needs, it must run glycolysis much faster, so glucose consumption rises from 1.0 to 6.0 mmol. Why the others are wrong: Cyanide-treated cells had oxygen and still used 5.8 mmol, so oxygen does not block uptake; fermentation yields less ATP; ethanol is a product, not an activator. Trap: Thinking that cells need less fuel when they cannot respire.

qs.q: Why do the cyanide results closely match the no-oxygen results?
o: Cyanide removes oxygen from the medium
Oxygen was still present.
Cyanide inhibits pyruvate decarboxylase
Ethanol was still made.
Cyanide stops O₂ from being used
Correct: respiration is blocked even with O₂ present.
Cyanide breaks down ethanol
Ethanol output was high.
qs.x: Correct: Cyanide binds complex IV, the enzyme that passes electrons to O₂. The electron transport chain stops, O₂ use falls to nearly zero (0.1 mmol), and the cells must ferment, giving the same pattern as cells with no oxygen. Why the others are wrong: Oxygen remained in the flask but could not be used; the fermentation pathway, including pyruvate decarboxylase, kept working; ethanol was produced in large amounts. Trap: Confusing a lack of oxygen with a lack of oxygen use.

qs.q: Why must yeast make ethanol when oxygen cannot be used?
o: To produce additional ATP from pyruvate
Ethanol formation makes no ATP.
To regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis
Correct: NADH is reoxidized as acetaldehyde is reduced.
To provide carbon for the citric acid cycle
The cycle needs respiration to run.
To store energy for later aerobic use
Ethanol formation serves NAD⁺ recycling.
qs.x: Correct: Glycolysis reduces NAD⁺ to NADH at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step. Without a working electron transport chain, the only way to restore NAD⁺ is to pass the electrons to acetaldehyde, making ethanol. Without this step glycolysis would stop. Why the others are wrong: The fermentation steps after pyruvate make no ATP; ethanol formation recycles NAD⁺ and is not done to store energy; the citric acid cycle needs NAD⁺ regenerated by respiration. Trap: Assuming that every step of a pathway produces ATP.

qs.q: What does the aerobic, 5% glucose result show?
o: Yeast cannot use oxygen at high glucose levels
Some oxygen (1.2 mmol) was still used.
The flask ran out of oxygen
The flask was aerated.
Cyanide was present in that flask
Cyanide was added only to the cyanide flask.
High glucose suppresses respiration
Correct: the Crabtree effect.
qs.x: Correct: In the presence of oxygen, high glucose cut O₂ use from 5.4 to 1.2 mmol and raised ethanol output from 0.2 to 7.0 mmol. The cells fermented even though they could respire, which is the Crabtree effect. Why the others are wrong: Oxygen use was reduced but not zero; the flask was aerated; no cyanide was added. Trap: Assuming that ethanol production always means oxygen is absent.

qs.q: About how much ATP per gram per hour do cells without oxygen make from glucose?
o: 2 mmol
This is ATP per glucose, not per hour.
6 mmol
This is glucose used, not ATP.
12 mmol
Correct: 6.0 mmol glucose × 2 ATP.
180 mmol
This uses the aerobic yield.
qs.x: Correct: Without oxygen all ATP comes from glycolysis at 2 ATP per glucose, so 6.0 mmol of glucose gives about 12 mmol of ATP per gram per hour. Why the others are wrong: 2 mmol is the yield per glucose; 6 mmol is the amount of glucose; 180 mmol would assume 30 ATP per glucose, which requires respiration. Trap: Applying the respiration yield to fermenting cells.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cells respond to low oxygen (hypoxia) by turning on genes such as EPO, which encodes erythropoietin, and VEGF, which promotes blood vessel growth. These responses depend on the transcription factor HIF-1, a dimer of HIF-1α and HIF-1β. HIF-1β is always present, but HIF-1α is destroyed within minutes in normal oxygen. Prolyl hydroxylase enzymes use O₂ to add hydroxyl groups to two prolines in HIF-1α. The von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) protein, part of a ubiquitin ligase, recognizes the hydroxylated prolines and tags HIF-1α for destruction by the proteasome. In hypoxia, the hydroxylases are inactive, HIF-1α accumulates, and HIF-1 binds hypoxia response elements (HREs) containing the core sequence 5′-RCGTG-3′.

Researchers tested whether a 50-base-pair sequence from the 3′ end of the EPO gene acts as an HRE. They inserted it into a plasmid in which a minimal promoter drives firefly luciferase, an enzyme whose light output can be measured. Cells were transfected with each plasmid along with a second plasmid in which a constant promoter drives Renilla luciferase, a different enzyme measured separately. Firefly light was divided by Renilla light in each well. Cells were then held for 16 hours at 21% O₂ or 1% O₂. Some cells received a small interfering RNA (siRNA) against HIF-1α, and some received cobalt chloride (CoCl₂), which inhibits the prolyl hydroxylases.

Before the main experiment, the researchers confirmed by western blot that HIF-1α protein was nearly undetectable at 21% O₂, rose sharply within 4 hours at 1% O₂, and was reduced by about 85% in cells given the siRNA. HIF-1β protein was present at similar levels under all conditions, as expected for a subunit that is not regulated by oxygen.
Values are relative to the minimal promoter at 21% O₂. Each is the mean of four wells, and the standard deviation was under 15% of the mean in every case.

qs.q: What do the results for the reversed and downstream constructs show?
o: The sequence must sit right next to the promoter
It worked 2 kb downstream.
The sequence works only in its natural orientation
The reversed copy gave 13.6.
The sequence is an enhancer
Correct: it works in either orientation and at a distance.
The sequence is the gene's promoter
The minimal promoter was supplied separately.
qs.x: Correct: An enhancer raises transcription regardless of its orientation and can work thousands of base pairs from the promoter, upstream or downstream. The EPO sequence gave strong induction in reverse (13.6) and from 2 kb downstream (11.9), so it behaves as an enhancer. Why the others are wrong: The sequence worked far from the promoter; the plasmid already had a promoter; orientation did not matter. Trap: Confusing an enhancer with a promoter.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the HIF-1α siRNA condition?
o: To show that induction requires HIF-1α
Correct: knocking it down removed most of the response.
To raise HIF-1α levels at 1% O₂
siRNA lowers the level of its target.
To show that the CGTG core is needed
The mutant construct tests that.
To correct for differences in transfection
That is the role of Renilla luciferase.
qs.x: Correct: siRNA directs the destruction of HIF-1α mRNA, so less HIF-1α protein is made. Hypoxic induction then fell from 14.2 to 2.0, showing that the response depends on HIF-1α rather than on another oxygen-sensitive factor. Why the others are wrong: siRNA reduces expression of its target; normalization is done with Renilla; the mutant sequence, not the siRNA, tests the CGTG core. Trap: Mixing up which control answers which question.

qs.q: Why did CoCl₂ raise luciferase in normal oxygen?
o: CoCl₂ binds the HRE in place of HIF-1
The mutant HRE did not respond.
CoCl₂ lowered the oxygen level in the medium
The cells were held at 21% O₂.
CoCl₂ activates luciferase directly
The promoter-only construct did not respond.
HIF-1α escaped hydroxylation
Correct: CoCl₂ mimics hypoxia.
qs.x: Correct: The prolyl hydroxylases must modify HIF-1α before VHL can tag it. With these enzymes blocked by cobalt, HIF-1α escaped destruction even in 21% O₂ and activated the HRE (12.8). Why the others are wrong: Oxygen was normal; cobalt's effect required an intact CGTG core, which points to HIF-1; the promoter-only construct did not change, so the enzyme was not activated directly. Trap: Assuming a drug that mimics hypoxia must remove oxygen.

qs.q: Why was firefly light divided by Renilla light in each well?
o: To measure the effect of oxygen on Renilla
Renilla is driven by a constant promoter.
To correct for uneven transfection
Correct: Renilla is a constant reference.
To remove the effect of the HRE sequence
The HRE is on the firefly plasmid.
To convert light units into mRNA amounts
Light measures enzyme activity.
qs.x: Correct: Some wells take up more plasmid or contain more cells than others. Because Renilla luciferase is made from a constant promoter, it reports how much DNA entered the cells in each well, and dividing by it lets wells be compared fairly. Why the others are wrong: Renilla is the reference, not the variable being studied; luciferase light reflects protein activity rather than mRNA; the HRE affects only the firefly reporter. Trap: Forgetting why a second reporter is needed.

qs.q: Cells lacking functional VHL would most likely show which result with the EPO sequence construct at 21% O₂?
o: Low luciferase, because hydroxylation would stop
VHL acts after hydroxylation.
Low luciferase, because HIF-1α could not be made
VHL does not make HIF-1α.
High, because HIF-1α would escape destruction
Correct: no tagging, no degradation.
No change, because VHL acts only in hypoxia
VHL acts in normal oxygen.
qs.x: Correct: VHL is needed to recognize hydroxylated HIF-1α and target it to the proteasome. Without VHL, HIF-1α accumulates even in normal oxygen and activates the HRE. This is why people with inherited VHL mutations develop tumors with abundant blood vessels. Why the others are wrong: VHL controls destruction, not synthesis; hydroxylation would continue but have no effect; VHL's role is in normal oxygen. Trap: Thinking that losing a protein in a pathway always reduces the output.

r: Promoter + EPO sequence, CGTG changed to AAAG
EPO sequence placed 2 kb downstream of gene

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: β-thalassemia results from reduced or absent production of β-globin, one of the two chain types in adult hemoglobin (HbA, α₂β₂). In red cell precursors, the unpaired α chains that are left over precipitate and damage the cells, so many precursors die in the bone marrow. More than 200 variants of the β-globin gene, HBB, are known. Many alter splicing of the HBB pre-mRNA, which contains three exons and two introns.

Spliceosomes recognize a 5′ splice site that begins each intron with GU and a 3′ splice site that ends each intron with AG. A variant can destroy one of these sites or create a new one. A variant that introduces a premature stop codon can also lower mRNA levels, because the cell detects stop codons that lie upstream of the last exon junction and degrades the mRNA by nonsense-mediated decay.

A hematology clinic studied four patients and a healthy control. In reticulocytes (young red cells), they measured the amount of correctly spliced HBB mRNA relative to the control and the ratio of newly made β chains to α chains. Patient 1 is homozygous for a G→A change at the first nucleotide of intron 1. Patient 2 is homozygous for a G→A change 21 nucleotides before the end of intron 1, which creates a new AG within the intron. Patient 3 is homozygous for a C→T change in codon 39 of exon 2, which changes CAG (glutamine) to TAG. Patient 4 carries the patient 1 variant on one chromosome and a normal HBB gene on the other.

Patients 1 and 3 needed regular blood transfusions. Patient 2 needed occasional transfusions. Patient 4 had small red cells but no symptoms. In patient 2, most HBB transcripts were spliced at the new AG, which kept 19 intron nucleotides in the mature mRNA. In patient 3, the mRNA that remained was spliced correctly. All patients had a fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α₂γ₂) level above normal.

qs.q: Why does patient 1 make no correctly spliced HBB mRNA?
o: The intron's 5′ GU signal is destroyed
Correct: the spliceosome cannot use the normal site.
The variant creates a stop codon in exon 1
It lies in the intron.
The variant blocks transcription of HBB
Splicing, not transcription, is affected.
The variant makes a new AG that is preferred
That describes patient 2.
qs.x: Correct: Changing the first G of intron 1 to A turns GU into AU, so the spliceosome cannot recognize the normal 5′ splice site. No transcript is spliced correctly, and no β chains are made. Why the others are wrong: The variant lies in the intron, not in a codon; pre-mRNA is still made, so transcription is intact; creating a new AG is the change in patient 2. Trap: Treating every splicing variant as if it worked the same way.

qs.q: Why does patient 2 still make about 10% of the normal amount of correctly spliced mRNA?
o: Half of the patient's cells lack the variant
The patient is homozygous.
The extra 19 nucleotides are removed later
They remain in the mature mRNA.
Nonsense-mediated decay repairs the transcript
It degrades transcripts, not repairs them.
Some transcripts still use the normal site
Correct: the new AG competes but does not always win.
qs.x: Correct: The variant creates a competing AG upstream of the normal 3′ splice site, which remains intact. Most transcripts are spliced at the new site, keeping 19 intron nucleotides and shifting the reading frame, but a minority still use the normal site and give correct mRNA. Why the others are wrong: A homozygous patient has the variant on both copies; the extra nucleotides stay in the mRNA; nonsense-mediated decay destroys transcripts rather than fixing them. Trap: Assuming a new splice site replaces the old one completely.

qs.q: Why is patient 3's HBB mRNA so low even though it is spliced correctly?
o: Exon 2 is skipped during splicing
The mRNA is spliced correctly.
Its premature stop causes mRNA decay
Correct: the mRNA is degraded.
The variant destroys the promoter
It lies in exon 2.
TAG codes for an amino acid that blocks splicing
TAG is a stop codon.
qs.x: Correct: The TAG at codon 39 lies upstream of the last exon junction, so the cell recognizes it as a premature stop and degrades the mRNA. Only about 4% remains, and the protein that could be made from it would be truncated, so no β chains are made. Why the others are wrong: TAG is a stop codon, not an amino acid; the promoter is unaffected; the passage says splicing is normal. Trap: Thinking that a coding variant affects only the protein and not the amount of mRNA.

qs.q: Why does a low β/α ratio damage red cell precursors?
o: The cells make too much β chain
The β/α ratio is low.
α chains bind oxygen too tightly to release it
The problem arises before oxygen transport.
Excess α chains precipitate inside the cells
Correct: unpaired α chains are toxic.
β chains are needed to make the cell membrane
Globins are not membrane proteins.
qs.x: Correct: α and β chains normally pair one to one. When β production falls, extra α chains have no partner and form insoluble precipitates that damage the precursor cell membrane, causing many cells to die in the marrow. Why the others are wrong: Globins are cytoplasmic proteins; the damage occurs in the marrow, before cells carry oxygen; a ratio below 1 means too little β. Trap: Focusing only on too little hemoglobin and missing the harm caused by the surplus chain.

qs.q: A drug that raises γ-globin production in adults helps patients like these. What is the best explanation?
o: γ chains pair with the extra α chains
Correct: fewer free α chains and more hemoglobin.
γ chains replace α chains in HbA
γ replaces β, not α.
γ chains repair the HBB splicing defect
γ-globin is a separate protein.
γ chains block nonsense-mediated decay
γ-globin is not involved in mRNA decay.
qs.x: Correct: Fetal hemoglobin is made of two α and two γ chains. Raising γ production gives the surplus α chains a partner, which reduces precipitation and increases the total amount of working hemoglobin. The above-normal HbF in these patients already shows a partial version of this. Why the others are wrong: γ-globin cannot fix a splicing defect in another gene; γ substitutes for β, not α; it plays no role in mRNA decay. Trap: Assuming a treatment must correct the original variant to help.

h: Correctly spliced HBB mRNA (% of control)

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) combines two kinds of damage. In chronic bronchitis, the small airways become inflamed and narrowed by mucus and thickened walls. In emphysema, the walls between alveoli are destroyed, which reduces the surface area for gas exchange and removes the elastic tissue that normally pulls the small airways open. During a forced exhalation, pressure outside the airways rises, and airways that have lost this support collapse early, trapping air in the lungs.

Spirometry measures the volume a person can exhale in the first second of a forced breath (FEV₁) and the total volume exhaled (forced vital capacity, FVC). An FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70 after a bronchodilator indicates airflow obstruction. The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) measures how readily gas crosses from the alveoli into the blood, and residual volume (RV) is the air left in the lungs after a full exhalation.

Researchers tested 1,200 adults aged 40 to 75 from one city who answered a mailed invitation. Each person was tested once. Participants were grouped as never smokers, former smokers who had quit at least five years earlier, and current smokers (Table 1). Among current smokers, the prevalence of obstruction was 17% in those with fewer than 20 pack-years, 30% in those with 20 to 40 pack-years, and 49% in those with more than 40 pack-years. One pack-year equals one pack a day for one year.

The researchers also asked about symptoms. Chronic cough with sputum on most days for at least three months in each of two years was reported by 4% of never smokers, 11% of former smokers and 27% of current smokers. Some participants with obstruction on spirometry reported no symptoms at all, which is common in early disease.

Former smokers had smoked for an average of 19 years before quitting, while current smokers had smoked for an average of 31 years. The researchers cautioned that the study could not show when the lung changes began relative to smoking, and that people who agree to take part in a lung study may differ from those who do not.

qs.q: Why does airflow obstruction lower FEV₁ more than it lowers FVC?
o: The lungs hold less total air in people with COPD
Total lung volume is often increased.
Narrowed airways slow how fast air leaves
Correct: the first second is most affected.
Less oxygen reaches the blood
Gas exchange does not set airflow.
Inspiratory muscles are weakened in COPD
FEV₁ measures exhalation.
qs.x: Correct: Narrow and collapsible airways limit the speed of exhalation, so less air leaves in the first second. Given enough time, much of the air can still be exhaled, so FVC falls less and the FEV₁/FVC ratio drops. Why the others are wrong: Lung volumes are often larger, not smaller, in COPD; FEV₁ depends on expiratory flow; oxygen transfer is a separate measure (DLCO). Trap: Thinking obstruction mainly reduces how much air the lungs can hold.

qs.q: What best explains the higher residual volume in current smokers?
o: Smokers inhale more deeply than people who never smoked
RV is measured after full exhalation.
Alveoli fill with fluid in COPD
Fluid would lower air volume.
Smoking strengthens the chest wall
No evidence supports this.
Airways collapse before the lungs can empty
Correct: air is trapped.
qs.x: Correct: When alveolar walls and their elastic tissue are lost, the small airways have less support and close early during exhalation. Air behind the closed airways cannot leave, so residual volume rises (128% of predicted). Why the others are wrong: RV is the volume left after maximal exhalation, not a measure of how deeply someone inhales; fluid would displace air; nothing suggests a stronger chest wall. Trap: Assuming a larger lung volume means healthier lungs.

qs.q: Why is DLCO lowest in current smokers?
o: Alveolar walls are lost, reducing exchange area
Correct: diffusion depends on surface area.
Carbon monoxide is already bound to their hemoglobin
The test corrects for this.
Their airways are too narrow for CO to enter
Gas still reaches the alveoli.
Smoking thickens red blood cell membranes
This is not a recognized effect.
qs.x: Correct: The rate of diffusion across a membrane is proportional to its surface area. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and the capillaries in them, so the area available for gas exchange shrinks and DLCO falls (74% of predicted). Why the others are wrong: Standard DLCO testing adjusts for carbon monoxide already in the blood; narrowing slows airflow but gas still reaches the alveoli during a slow breath hold; no such effect on red cell membranes is known. Trap: Blaming the airway narrowing for a problem in the alveoli.

qs.q: Which finding most strengthens the argument that smoking causes the obstruction?
o: Never smokers had a mean ratio of 0.78
That is the reference value.
Each person was tested only once
That is a limitation.
Obstruction rises with pack-years
Correct: a dose–response gradient.
Participants answered a mailed invitation
That raises a selection concern.
qs.x: Correct: Obstruction rose from 17% to 30% to 49% as cumulative smoking increased. A dose–response pattern is hard to explain by chance and supports a causal link, even though a cross-sectional study cannot show timing. Why the others are wrong: The never-smoker value is a baseline, not evidence of cause; testing once and recruiting by mail weaken, rather than strengthen, the argument. Trap: Mistaking a description of the study for evidence of causation.

qs.q: Which is a plausible alternative explanation for why former smokers had better values than current smokers?
o: Former smokers were tested with a different machine
All were tested the same way.
Former smokers had smoked fewer years in total
Correct: less exposure, not only quitting.
Current smokers were younger on average
Age was not reported.
Quitting fully reverses emphysema
Lost alveolar walls do not regrow.
qs.x: Correct: Former smokers averaged 19 years of smoking, compared with 31 years for current smokers. Their better lung function could reflect less total exposure rather than any benefit from quitting, so the two groups are not directly comparable. Why the others are wrong: No difference in testing is described; destroyed alveolar walls do not regenerate; the passage gives no age difference. Trap: Attributing a group difference to the label that defines the group while ignoring other differences.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Sleep supports attention and memory in different ways. Even one night of short sleep slows reaction time and increases lapses, moments when a person fails to respond at all. Sleep also helps consolidate newly learned material; slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, is linked in particular to strengthening memories for facts and word lists. Adolescents are at special risk of short sleep. At puberty, the evening release of melatonin shifts later, so teenagers tend to feel alert late at night, yet school often begins early in the morning.

Researchers asked 150 students aged 14 to 17 to wear wrist actigraphs, devices that estimate sleep from movement, for the two weeks before final exams. Students were grouped by their average nightly sleep. During the second week, each student completed a 10-minute psychomotor vigilance task (PVT), pressing a button whenever a counter appeared on a screen at random intervals. A response slower than 500 ms was scored as a lapse. On the same evening, students studied a list of 30 unrelated words for five minutes and were asked to recall as many as they could the next morning. Each also rated sleepiness on a 9-point scale.

The actigraph data also showed that, on average, students slept about 90 minutes longer on weekend nights than on school nights, a pattern sometimes called social jet lag. Students in the shortest-sleep group had the largest weekend difference, about two and a half hours.

Twenty students in the shortest-sleep group reported drinking a caffeinated energy drink before the PVT. Their mean reaction time (286 ms) was close to that of the middle group, but their next-morning recall (14.0 words) did not differ from the rest of their group. The researchers also found that students in the shortest-sleep group reported more evening screen time and higher exam anxiety than the other students.

qs.q: Which description best fits the design of this study?
o: Case-control, because students were grouped by their sleep
Grouping was not by outcome.
Longitudinal, because performance was followed for years
It lasted two weeks.
Experimental, because sleep was the independent variable
Sleep was not manipulated.
Correlational; sleep was measured, not assigned
Correct: students chose their own sleep.
qs.x: Correct: The researchers recorded how much students slept but did not control it. Comparing groups formed by a behavior the participants chose is a correlational design, even when the groups are given names. Why the others are wrong: An experiment would assign sleep amounts; a case-control study selects people by an outcome and looks back for exposures; the study lasted two weeks. Trap: Calling a study experimental because the groups are labeled like conditions.

qs.q: Which alternative explanation could account for the poorer recall in the shortest-sleep group?
o: The word lists were different in each group
The same task was used.
Actigraphs measure sleep perfectly
Perfect measurement would not create a confound.
Anxiety could cut sleep and hurt memory
Correct: a possible third variable.
The PVT took longer for some students
Every PVT lasted 10 minutes.
qs.x: Correct: The shortest-sleep group also reported more anxiety and more screen time. Anxiety could both reduce sleep and impair learning, so it could produce the link between sleep and recall without sleep itself being the cause. Why the others are wrong: The PVT had a fixed length; nothing suggests the word lists differed; accurate measurement of sleep would not explain the pattern. Trap: Forgetting that the study's own data reveal possible confounds.

qs.q: What does the caffeine subgroup suggest?
o: Caffeine aids alertness, not memory
Correct: reaction time improved, recall did not.
Caffeine prevents slow-wave sleep entirely
Sleep stages were not measured.
Caffeine improves both attention and memory
Recall stayed at 14 words.
Short sleep does not affect reaction time
Without caffeine it was 342 ms.
