qs.x: Correct: The energy drink brought reaction time down to near the middle group's value, but next-morning recall stayed at the short-sleep level. A stimulant can mask sleepiness in the moment but cannot replace the consolidation that happens during sleep. Why the others are wrong: Recall did not improve; the group without caffeine had slow reactions; actigraphs cannot measure sleep stages. Trap: Assuming that feeling alert means the effects of lost sleep are gone.

qs.q: Why do many adolescents struggle to fall asleep early on school nights?
o: Melatonin is released later
Correct: their circadian timing is delayed.
Adolescents have no circadian rhythm
The rhythm is shifted, not lost.
Melatonin levels stop rising at night
Release is delayed, not absent.
Adolescents need less sleep than adults
Teenagers need about 8–10 hours.
qs.x: Correct: Around puberty, the evening rise in melatonin occurs later, delaying the time when sleep comes easily. Early school start times then cut sleep short. Why the others are wrong: Adolescents need more sleep than adults; melatonin still rises, just later; the rhythm persists. Trap: Blaming late bedtimes only on choice.

qs.q: Which sleep stage is most closely linked to consolidating word lists?
o: Stage N1 sleep
This is light, transitional sleep.
REM sleep only
REM is more linked to procedural and emotional memory.
Slow-wave (N3) sleep
Correct: linked to memory for facts and words.
Wakefulness after waking
Consolidation occurs mainly during sleep.
qs.x: Correct: Slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, is associated with the replay and strengthening of declarative memories such as word lists. The passage notes this link directly. Why the others are wrong: N1 is a brief transition stage; REM sleep is more strongly linked to skills and emotional memory; consolidation of this kind depends on sleep. Trap: Assuming all memory consolidation happens during REM sleep.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Attachment theory describes the emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. In the strange situation procedure, a 12-month-old infant and caregiver enter a playroom; a stranger joins them, the caregiver leaves twice, and the infant's behavior at each reunion is observed. Securely attached infants explore freely, may be upset when the caregiver leaves, and are quickly comforted when the caregiver returns. Insecure-avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver at reunion. Insecure-resistant infants are very distressed and are hard to comfort, often seeking and resisting contact at once. Disorganized infants show contradictory or confused behavior, such as freezing or approaching the caregiver with their head turned away.

Researchers followed 180 infants from a community sample. Each was classified in the strange situation at 12 months and again at 24 months by coders who did not see the earlier result. When the children were 6 years old, their first-grade teachers rated each child's competence with peers on a 1–5 scale. The teachers did not know about the study's attachment results. Parents reported major family stress, such as job loss, serious illness or divorce, at each visit.

Classifications at both ages were made from video recordings by trained coders. A second coder independently rated a random 20% of the recordings, and the two coders agreed on 88% of cases. Twelve families moved away before the age-6 assessment; their children's 12-month classifications did not differ from those of the families who stayed.

Of the 19 children who changed from secure at 12 months to insecure at 24 months, 13 (68%) had families that reported a major stress between the two visits, compared with 22% of children whose secure classification was stable. The researchers also noted that infant temperament, measured by parent questionnaire at 6 months, was modestly related both to attachment classification and to later peer ratings.

qs.q: What behavior at reunion best identifies a securely attached infant?
o: Ignores the caregiver and keeps playing
That is the avoidant pattern.
Seeks the caregiver and is soon comforted
Correct: the caregiver works as a secure base.
Clings but also pushes the caregiver away
That is the resistant pattern.
Freezes or approaches with head turned away
That is the disorganized pattern.
qs.x: Correct: A secure infant may be upset by separation but seeks contact on reunion, is quickly soothed and returns to play. Why the others are wrong: Ignoring the caregiver marks avoidance; mixed seeking and resisting marks resistance; freezing or contradictory approach marks disorganization. Trap: Treating a lack of distress as a sign of security.

qs.q: What do the stress data suggest about why attachment classification can change?
o: Attachment is fixed at birth by genes
Many classifications changed.
Secure infants become insecure as they age
Most secure infants stayed secure.
Coders made more errors at 24 months
Coders were blind and nothing suggests error.
Family stress can disrupt attachment
Correct: stress was linked to shifts.
qs.x: Correct: Children who moved from secure to insecure were three times as likely to have had a major family stress (68% versus 22%). Stress can disrupt the sensitivity of caregiving, and attachment reflects the ongoing relationship rather than a fixed trait. Why the others are wrong: Classification changed in many children; blind coding protects against bias; 82% of secure infants stayed secure. Trap: Treating attachment as a permanent label.

qs.q: What most limits the conclusion that secure attachment causes better peer competence?
o: The sample was drawn from a community
That helps generalization.
Temperament may influence both measures
Correct: a possible confound.
Teachers did not know the attachment results
That is a strength.
Attachment was assessed twice
That improves measurement.
qs.x: Correct: The design is correlational. Temperament was related to both attachment and later peer ratings, so it could account for part of the link. A child's easy temperament might both make secure attachment more likely and help with peers. Why the others are wrong: Blind teacher ratings, repeated assessment and a community sample all strengthen the study. Trap: Choosing a strength of the study when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use teacher ratings rather than parent ratings of peer competence?
o: Teachers saw the strange situation sessions
Teachers did not attend them.
Parents cannot rate social behavior
Parents often do.
Teachers were unaware of attachment status
Correct: their ratings are less likely to be biased.
Teachers know the children better than parents
Parents usually know their children best.
qs.x: Correct: Parents took part in the strange situation and might rate their children in ways related to their own relationship with them. Teachers who did not know the attachment results provide an independent measure, reducing the chance of a shared bias between the predictor and the outcome. Why the others are wrong: Parents typically know their children well; parents can rate social behavior; teachers were not present at the sessions. Trap: Assuming the closest observer always gives the best measure.

qs.q: About how many of the 180 children had the same classification at 12 and 24 months?
o: About 90
This counts secure children only.
About 108
This is the number of secure infants at 12 months.
About 130
About 150
This overestimates stability.
qs.x: Correct: Multiply each group by its stability: 108 × 0.82 ≈ 89, 36 × 0.61 ≈ 22, 18 × 0.56 ≈ 10 and 18 × 0.50 = 9, for a total of about 130 children, or 72%. Why the others are wrong: About 90 counts only the stable secure children; 108 is the total number of secure infants; 150 assumes more stability than the table shows. Trap: Averaging the percentages without weighting by group size.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are RNAs about 22 nucleotides long that are processed from hairpin precursors and loaded into Argonaute proteins. A loaded miRNA pairs with sites in the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR) of target mRNAs. In animals, pairing is usually imperfect; a match between the target and nucleotides 2 to 8 of the miRNA, called the seed, is often enough. Bound Argonaute recruits proteins that block translation and shorten the poly(A) tail, which can lead to mRNA decay. Because a match of only seven nucleotides is required, one miRNA can regulate hundreds of different genes.

miR-122 makes up about 70% of all miRNA in human liver cells but is nearly absent from most other cell types. One of its targets is the mRNA for CAT-1, a membrane transporter for the amino acid arginine, which has seed-matching sites in its 3′ UTR. Researchers used two cell lines: Huh7 liver cancer cells, which make miR-122, and HeLa cervical cancer cells, which do not. In Huh7 cells, they added either a control oligonucleotide or an antisense oligonucleotide that binds and blocks miR-122. In HeLa cells, they added either a control RNA or a synthetic miR-122 mimic. In one HeLa condition, the cells' own CAT-1 gene was silenced and replaced by a CAT-1 gene whose 3′ UTR seed sites had been changed. CAT-1 mRNA was measured by quantitative PCR and CAT-1 protein by western blot, both relative to the matching control.

To make sure the oligonucleotides did not harm the cells, the researchers measured total protein and the level of a housekeeping protein, β-actin, in every sample. Neither changed with any treatment, and the CAT-1 western blot signals were divided by β-actin before comparison.

miR-122 has another, unusual role. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) has an RNA genome, and miR-122 binds two sites near its 5′ end, where it protects the viral RNA from degradation. In HCV-infected Huh7 cells, the anti-miR-122 oligonucleotide reduced viral RNA by about 90% within three days.

qs.q: What does the difference between the mRNA and protein changes suggest?
o: miR-122 mainly blocks translation
Correct: protein changed far more than mRNA.
miR-122 acts on the CAT-1 gene's promoter
miRNAs act on mRNA.
miR-122 increases CAT-1 translation
Blocking miR-122 raised protein.
miR-122 mainly destroys CAT-1 mRNA
mRNA changed only modestly.
qs.x: Correct: Blocking miR-122 raised CAT-1 protein 3.5-fold but mRNA only 1.4-fold, and adding miR-122 cut protein to 0.3 while mRNA fell only to 0.8. Most of the effect is on how much protein is made from each mRNA, with a smaller effect on mRNA stability. Why the others are wrong: Mainly destroying the mRNA would change mRNA and protein about equally; removing miR-122 increased protein, so it normally represses it; miRNAs act on mRNA in the cytoplasm, not on promoters. Trap: Assuming gene silencing always means loss of mRNA.

qs.q: What does the mutant seed-site condition show?
o: HeLa cells cannot take up the mimic
The mimic worked on normal CAT-1.
miR-122 lowers CAT-1 by acting on another gene
The mutant sites would not block that.
CAT-1 protein cannot be measured in HeLa cells
It was measured in every condition.
Repression needs pairing at the seed sites
Correct: changing them removed the effect.
qs.x: Correct: With the mimic present, normal CAT-1 protein fell to 0.3, but CAT-1 with altered seed sites stayed at 0.95. Repression therefore depends on miR-122 pairing directly with those sites in the CAT-1 3′ UTR. Why the others are wrong: An indirect effect through another gene would not be blocked by changing CAT-1's own sites; the same mimic worked in the other HeLa condition; protein was measured throughout. Trap: Overlooking that the only change was in the target's binding sites.

qs.q: Why did the researchers add the mimic to HeLa cells rather than to Huh7 cells?
o: HeLa cells contain no Argonaute protein
The mimic needs Argonaute to work.
Huh7 cells do not express CAT-1
CAT-1 was measured in Huh7 cells.
HeLa cells already make too much miR-122
HeLa cells make almost none.
HeLa cells lack miR-122
Correct: a gain-of-function test.
qs.x: Correct: Huh7 cells already contain large amounts of miR-122, so adding more might change little. In HeLa cells, which lack it, adding the mimic tests whether miR-122 alone is enough to repress CAT-1. The two cell lines provide complementary loss-of-function and gain-of-function tests. Why the others are wrong: The mimic works through Argonaute, which HeLa cells have; Huh7 cells express CAT-1; HeLa cells make almost no miR-122. Trap: Missing why a second cell line was needed.

qs.q: How can one miRNA regulate hundreds of different mRNAs?
o: Each miRNA is many kilobases long
miRNAs are about 22 nucleotides.
miRNAs bind every mRNA equally
Binding requires a seed match.
Only a short seed match is needed
Correct: seven nucleotides recur in many 3′ UTRs.
miRNAs are translated into regulatory proteins
miRNAs are not translated.
qs.x: Correct: Animal miRNAs usually need to match only nucleotides 2 to 8 of the seed. A seven-nucleotide sequence appears by chance in the 3′ UTRs of many genes, so one miRNA can pair with many targets. Why the others are wrong: Mature miRNAs are about 22 nucleotides long; targeting is selective; miRNAs function as RNA. Trap: Assuming that a regulator must match its target perfectly.

qs.q: What does the HCV result suggest about anti-miR-122 as a treatment?
o: It removes a host factor the virus needs
Correct: viral RNA fell 90%.
It would have no effect on liver proteins
CAT-1 protein rose 3.5-fold.
It would act by blocking a viral enzyme
It targets a host miRNA.
It would increase HCV RNA by freeing it from repression
Viral RNA fell.
qs.x: Correct: HCV depends on miR-122 binding to protect its RNA. Blocking the host miRNA cut viral RNA by about 90%, so the drug works by taking away something the virus needs from the host. Because it also raised CAT-1, it would change the expression of host genes as well. Why the others are wrong: The oligonucleotide targets a host RNA; CAT-1 protein rose; viral RNA fell. Trap: Assuming miRNAs only ever repress their targets.

r: miR-122 mimic, CAT-1 with mutant seed sites

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Sound waves enter the ear canal, move the eardrum and the ossicles, and set up a traveling wave along the basilar membrane of the cochlea. The membrane is narrow and stiff at the base, near the oval window, and wide and flexible at the apex. High frequencies produce their largest vibration near the base and low frequencies near the apex, an arrangement called tonotopy. Hair cells on the membrane convert vibration into neural signals. Loud sound can damage these cells, and in mammals they do not regenerate. The ear canal itself acts as a resonating tube that amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz.

Researchers measured hearing thresholds in three groups of workers at one manufacturing company: office staff with little noise exposure, machine operators with at least 10 years of work in areas averaging 95 dB who seldom wore hearing protection, and machine operators with similar exposure whose earplug use was logged by supervisors at more than 90% of shifts. Workers chose whether to wear earplugs. Each person's hearing threshold at each frequency was measured in a sound booth after at least 16 hours away from work. A higher threshold, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), means worse hearing.

Because hearing tests depend on the listener's responses, the researchers repeated the 4,000 Hz measurement in each ear on a second day. The two measurements differed by no more than 5 dB in 94% of ears, and the average of the two was used. Workers with a history of ear surgery or frequent ear infections were excluded.

In a separate test, 20 operators had their hearing measured at the end of an unprotected shift. Their threshold at 4,000 Hz was on average 15 dB higher than their own baseline, but it returned to baseline after 16 hours of quiet. The researchers noted that the average age of the three groups was similar (44 to 46 years).

qs.q: Why is the loss in seldom-protected operators greatest at 4,000 Hz?
o: Low-frequency hair cells are the most fragile
Losses at 500 Hz were small.
The ear canal boosts sound near this frequency
Correct: those hair cells receive the most energy.
Noise damages the ossicles at 4,000 Hz
Noise mainly damages hair cells.
The apex of the cochlea receives the most energy
The apex codes low frequencies.
qs.x: Correct: The ear canal's resonance amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz, so the hair cells tuned to that range receive the strongest stimulation and are damaged first, producing a characteristic notch at 4,000 Hz. Why the others are wrong: Low-frequency thresholds changed little; the apex responds to low frequencies; the passage identifies hair cells as the site of injury. Trap: Assuming noise damages every frequency equally.

qs.q: Where along the basilar membrane is the 4,000 Hz damage most likely located?
o: At the apex
The apex codes the lowest frequencies.
In the semicircular canals
Those sense head rotation.
Toward the base
Correct: higher frequencies map nearer the base.
Evenly along the whole membrane
Damage is frequency-specific.
qs.x: Correct: Because high frequencies vibrate the stiff, narrow base most strongly, the hair cells that respond to 4,000 Hz sit in the basal part of the cochlea. Why the others are wrong: The apex responds to low frequencies; the 4,000 Hz notch shows that damage is localized; the semicircular canals belong to the vestibular system. Trap: Reversing the tonotopic map.

qs.q: What is the most important limitation in concluding that earplugs prevented hearing loss?
o: Thresholds were measured after 16 hours of quiet
This avoids temporary shifts.
Office staff were included as a comparison
That is a strength.
Thresholds were measured in a sound booth
That improves accuracy.
Workers chose whether to wear earplugs
Correct: the groups may differ in other ways.
qs.x: Correct: Because workers chose for themselves, those who wore earplugs may differ in other ways, such as noise outside work, attention to health or the specific machines they used. The comparison supports a protective effect but cannot rule out these differences. Why the others are wrong: Testing after 16 hours of quiet removes temporary shifts; a low-exposure comparison group and a sound booth both strengthen the study. Trap: Choosing a design feature that helps the study when asked about a weakness.

qs.q: Why is a temporary threshold shift after a shift an important warning sign?
o: It shows the eardrum has ruptured
Thresholds returned to baseline.
Repeated stress can kill hair cells
Correct: temporary can become permanent.
It means the auditory nerve has been cut
Function recovered.
It shows that hearing loss is always temporary
The seldom-protected group had lasting loss.
qs.x: Correct: The 15 dB shift shows that the hair cells were stressed by the noise. They recovered within 16 hours, but repeated stress over years kills hair cells, which mammals cannot replace, producing permanent loss like that seen in the seldom-protected operators. Why the others are wrong: A ruptured eardrum or cut nerve would not recover in 16 hours; the long-term data show lasting loss. Trap: Treating a recoverable change as harmless.

qs.q: Why do even office staff show their highest threshold at 8,000 Hz?
o: Aging affects high pitches first
Correct: at 44–46 years, some loss is expected.
The ear canal amplifies 8,000 Hz most
It amplifies 2,000–4,000 Hz.
Office noise is concentrated at 8,000 Hz
Office staff had little noise exposure.
Thresholds at 8,000 Hz cannot be measured
They were measured.
qs.x: Correct: Presbycusis, the gradual hearing loss of aging, affects the highest frequencies first because the basal hair cells receive the most stimulation over a lifetime. Workers in their mid-forties often show small losses at 8,000 Hz even without noise exposure. Why the others are wrong: Office staff had little noise exposure; the ear canal resonance is at lower frequencies; thresholds at 8,000 Hz were recorded. Trap: Assuming every high-frequency loss is caused by noise.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is a quick way to follow the progress of a reaction. A small spot of the mixture is placed near the bottom of a glass plate coated with silica gel, a polar stationary phase whose surface is covered with Si–OH groups. The plate is stood in a shallow pool of solvent, the mobile phase, which climbs the plate by capillary action. Compounds that bind the silica strongly, especially through hydrogen bonds, move only a short distance; less polar compounds stay dissolved in the solvent and travel farther. The retardation factor, Rf, is the distance a spot travels divided by the distance the solvent front travels.

A student reduced benzophenone, a ketone, to diphenylmethanol, a secondary alcohol, using sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in methanol at room temperature. To follow the reaction, the student removed a drop of the mixture at 0, 10 and 30 minutes and spotted it on silica plates next to standards of pure starting material and pure product. In one lane, the 10-minute sample was spotted directly on top of a spot of the product standard, a technique called co-spotting. The plates were run in 4:1 hexane:ethyl acetate, and the solvent front traveled 8.0 cm on every plate. Spots were seen under ultraviolet light, where both compounds absorb because of their aromatic rings.

Before choosing the solvent, the student ran both standards in three hexane:ethyl acetate mixtures. Ethyl acetate is more polar than hexane, so mixtures richer in it compete more effectively with the compounds for the silica surface.

A single plate cannot prove what a compound is. Two different substances can happen to have the same Rf in one solvent, so a match is stronger evidence when it holds in more than one solvent system. For a firm identification, chemists confirm the structure by a spectroscopic method such as nuclear magnetic resonance or infrared spectroscopy.

After 30 minutes, the student added dilute acid to destroy the remaining NaBH₄, extracted the product into ethyl acetate and evaporated the solvent, leaving white crystals that gave a single spot at Rf 0.35.

qs.q: What is the Rf of diphenylmethanol on the reaction plates?
o: Correct: 2.8 cm ÷ 8.0 cm.
This divides by the benzophenone distance.
This is the Rf of benzophenone.
This divides the front by the spot distance.
qs.x: Correct: Rf = distance traveled by the spot ÷ distance traveled by the solvent front = 2.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.35, which matches the value in the solvent table. Why the others are wrong: 0.54 uses the wrong denominator; 0.65 belongs to benzophenone; Rf cannot exceed 1. Trap: Inverting the ratio.

qs.q: Why does diphenylmethanol travel a shorter distance than benzophenone?
o: Its O–H group binds the silica
Correct: stronger binding to the stationary phase.
It has a much larger molar mass
The two masses differ by only 2 g/mol.
It does not absorb ultraviolet light
It was seen under UV.
It is less polar than benzophenone
The alcohol is more polar.
qs.x: Correct: Diphenylmethanol has an O–H group that can donate a hydrogen bond to the Si–OH groups of the silica. Benzophenone's carbonyl can only accept hydrogen bonds. The alcohol binds the plate more strongly and moves less. Why the others are wrong: Reduction adds just two hydrogens; the alcohol is the more polar compound; both compounds were visible under UV. Trap: Explaining TLC movement by mass rather than by polarity.

qs.q: Which solvent gives the best separation of the two compounds?
o: 9:1, because both spots stay near the origin
Spots near the origin are poorly resolved.
All three separate the compounds equally well
The Rf gaps differ.
4:1, because the Rf values differ the most
Correct: 0.65 versus 0.35.
1:1, because both spots travel the farthest
They crowd near the solvent front.
qs.x: Correct: The gap in Rf is 0.26 in 9:1, 0.30 in 4:1 and 0.14 in 1:1. The 4:1 mixture also places both spots in the middle of the plate, where they are easiest to see and measure. Why the others are wrong: In 9:1 the product barely leaves the origin; in 1:1 both compounds run close to the front and close to each other; the separations clearly differ. Trap: Choosing the solvent that makes spots travel farthest.

qs.q: What does the 30-minute plate show?
o: Both compounds are present in equal amounts
Only one spot is seen.
The product has broken down
The product spot is present.
No reaction has taken place
The starting material spot is gone.
The benzophenone has been used up
Correct: only the product spot remains.
qs.x: Correct: At 30 minutes, the spot at 5.2 cm (benzophenone) is gone and only the spot at 2.8 cm (diphenylmethanol) remains, so the starting material has been converted. Why the others are wrong: A reaction clearly occurred; the product spot is still there; a single spot means one compound. Trap: Overlooking that a missing spot is as informative as a new one.

qs.q: What does the co-spotted lane add to the analysis?
o: It shows that NaBH₄ has been used up
NaBH₄ is not the spot being tested.
It confirms the new spot is the product
Correct: one round spot means the same Rf.
It measures how much product has formed
TLC spots are not quantitative here.
It shows the product is more polar than the solvent
Co-spotting compares two samples.
qs.x: Correct: If the new spot in the reaction mixture were a different compound with a similar Rf, co-spotting it with the standard would usually give an elongated or double spot. A single round spot at 2.8 cm shows that the two run identically, supporting the conclusion that the new spot is diphenylmethanol. Why the others are wrong: Spot intensity on a simple plate gives only a rough sense of amount; NaBH₄ does not appear on the plate; co-spotting compares the sample with a standard, not with the solvent. Trap: Assuming that matching Rf values in separate lanes always proves identity.

r: Reaction, 10 min co-spotted with product standard

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: In most cells, the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the mitochondrial matrix, and the protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving ATP production. The rate of oxygen use is therefore tied to the demand for ATP: when ADP is scarce, ATP synthase slows, the proton gradient builds up, and electron transport slows. Brown adipose tissue (BAT), found in newborns, hibernating animals and small amounts in adults, breaks this link. Its mitochondria contain uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which lets protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase. The energy of the gradient is released as heat. Purine nucleotides such as GDP bind UCP1 and close it, while fatty acids released during cold exposure open it.

Researchers housed wild-type mice and mice lacking the UCP1 gene (UCP1 knockout) either at 30 °C, where mice do not need to produce extra heat, or at 4 °C for 7 days, after which BAT had grown and become more active. They isolated BAT mitochondria and measured oxygen use with succinate as the fuel, first without ADP, then with ADP, and in a separate sample without ADP but with GDP. They also measured the membrane potential across the inner membrane, a measure of the proton gradient, without ADP.

The researchers checked that the isolated mitochondria were intact before each measurement by confirming that oxygen use rose when ADP was added and fell again once the added ADP had been converted to ATP. Preparations that did not show this response were discarded.

In a separate experiment, mice that had been kept at 30 °C were moved directly to 4 °C. After 6 hours, wild-type mice had a body temperature of 35.5 °C, while UCP1 knockout mice had cooled to 29 °C and were shivering vigorously. Knockout mice that were first moved to 18 °C for a week before the 4 °C test maintained their body temperature, a finding the researchers attributed to slower adaptations such as increased shivering capacity.

qs.q: Why is oxygen use high without ADP in wild-type mitochondria from cold-adapted mice?
o: Protons leak back through UCP1
Correct: the gradient keeps being used up.
Succinate is oxidized without the chain
Oxygen use requires the chain.
GDP opens UCP1
GDP closes it.
ATP synthase keeps working without ADP
It needs ADP to make ATP.
qs.x: Correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase is idle, so in ordinary mitochondria the proton gradient builds and slows electron transport. In cold-adapted BAT, protons leak back through abundant UCP1, so the gradient never builds up and oxygen use stays high (210). Why the others are wrong: ATP synthase requires ADP; oxygen is consumed only by the electron transport chain; GDP inhibits UCP1. Trap: Assuming oxygen use always reflects ATP production.

qs.q: What happens when GDP is added to these mitochondria?
o: Oxygen use rises because GDP is a fuel
GDP is an inhibitor here.
The membrane potential falls further
Closing the leak would raise it.
Oxygen use falls as the leak closes
Correct: from 210 to 70.
ATP synthesis rises without ADP
ATP synthase still lacks ADP.
qs.x: Correct: GDP binds and closes UCP1. Protons can no longer leak back, the gradient builds up, and electron transport slows, cutting oxygen use from 210 to 70. Why the others are wrong: GDP is not oxidized as fuel in this system; ATP synthase still needs ADP; closing the leak would allow the gradient, and the potential, to rise. Trap: Treating every nucleotide as an energy source.

qs.q: Why is the membrane potential lowest in cold-adapted wild-type mitochondria?
o: ADP was present in these samples
The potential was measured without ADP.
Cold mitochondria pump more protons
More pumping would raise it.
The knockout has more UCP1
The knockout has none.
The proton leak discharges it
Correct: UCP1 discharges it.
qs.x: Correct: Each proton that returns through UCP1 lowers the gradient, so mitochondria with the most UCP1 have the lowest potential (120 mV). The knockout, with no UCP1, keeps the highest potential (175 mV). Why the others are wrong: More pumping alone would raise the potential; the knockout lacks UCP1; ADP was absent. Trap: Linking high oxygen use with a high membrane potential.

qs.q: Why did knockout mice moved directly to 4 °C become cold?
o: They could not shiver
They shivered vigorously.
They could not make heat in brown fat
Correct: no UCP1-driven heat.
They had no mitochondria in brown fat
Mitochondria were isolated from them.
Their brown fat used too much oxygen
Knockout BAT used little oxygen.
qs.x: Correct: Without UCP1, brown fat cannot run electron transport freely to release heat, so the mice depended on shivering alone and their body temperature fell to 29 °C. Gradual adaptation allowed other mechanisms to compensate. Why the others are wrong: The mice did shiver; knockout BAT oxygen use was low; their mitochondria were present and functional. Trap: Assuming shivering alone can defend body temperature in sudden cold.

qs.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol carries protons across the inner membrane. Which effect would it most likely have in a person?
o: No effect, because it is not a protein
It acts as a chemical uncoupler.
More oxygen use and a higher temperature
Correct: an uncontrolled leak, like UCP1 everywhere.
Higher ATP production in every cell
The gradient is bypassed.
Lower oxygen use because the chain stops
The chain runs faster.
qs.x: Correct: Dinitrophenol lets protons cross the inner membrane in every cell, not just in brown fat. Electron transport speeds up, ATP synthesis falls, and the energy is released as heat, which can cause dangerous overheating. It was once sold as a weight-loss drug and caused deaths. Why the others are wrong: ATP production falls because protons bypass ATP synthase; electron transport speeds up rather than stopping; an uncoupler does not need to be a protein. Trap: Thinking faster fuel burning means more ATP.

h: O₂ use, no ADP (nmol/min per mg)

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: A cell that has damaged DNA must repair it before replication, or the damage will be copied into both daughter cells. The protein p53 coordinates this response. After damage, p53 escapes its normal rapid destruction and accumulates. It acts as a transcription factor, switching on genes such as CDKN1A, which encodes the protein p21. p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, so the cell cannot pass from G1 into S phase. If the damage is too severe to repair, p53 also switches on genes that trigger apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death in which the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into small fragments, and the remains are cleared by neighboring cells.

Researchers compared two human cell lines: line A, which carries two normal copies of TP53, and line B, which carries a mutation in both copies that prevents the protein from binding DNA. Both lines were exposed to 5 gray of ionizing radiation, which creates double-strand breaks. Twenty-four hours later, the fraction of cells in each phase of the cycle was measured by flow cytometry, which sorts cells by DNA content. Apoptotic cells were counted by a stain that detects cut DNA ends.

Protein levels were also measured. Four hours after radiation, line A showed a sixfold rise in p53 protein and a fivefold rise in p21, while line B showed a fivefold rise in p53 protein but no rise in p21. TP53 mRNA levels changed little in either line.

The researchers noted that flow cytometry measures DNA content rather than the phase directly: a cell with the DNA content of G1 could in principle be an arrested cell or one preparing to divide. To check their reading of the data, they repeated the experiment with a chemical that labels cells actively copying DNA, and found that the fraction of labeled cells matched the S-phase fractions in the table.
When line B was given a plasmid carrying a normal TP53 gene before radiation, the G1 fraction rose to 81% and apoptosis to 15%, close to the values for line A.

qs.q: Why did line A accumulate in G1 after radiation?
o: The cells entered mitosis and were held there
The G2/M fraction fell.
p53 directly copied the damaged DNA
p53 is a transcription factor.
p21 blocked the kinases that start S phase
Correct: the G1 checkpoint held.
Radiation destroyed the cells in S phase
S-phase cells would appear as apoptotic.
qs.x: Correct: Radiation raised p53, which switched on CDKN1A. The p21 protein then inhibited the cyclin-dependent kinases that drive the G1-to-S transition, so cells piled up in G1 (86%) while the S fraction fell to 4%. Why the others are wrong: Selective killing of S-phase cells would not raise the G1 percentage this much and would show in the apoptosis count; p53 regulates transcription rather than replicating DNA; the G2/M fraction decreased. Trap: Assuming any cell cycle arrest happens at mitosis.

qs.q: What does the rise in p53 protein without a rise in TP53 mRNA show?
o: p53 protein is made from p21 mRNA
Each protein has its own gene.
TP53 is transcribed faster after damage
mRNA levels changed little.
Radiation stabilizes all cellular proteins
p21 rose only in line A.
p53 is controlled by its destruction rate
Correct: less degradation, not more transcription.
qs.x: Correct: If more protein appears while its mRNA stays constant, the change must come after transcription. Normally p53 is tagged for destruction within minutes; DNA damage blocks this tagging, so the existing protein accumulates. Why the others are wrong: The mRNA did not increase; p21 is made from its own mRNA; p21 did not rise in line B, so the effect is not a general one. Trap: Assuming more protein always means more transcription.

qs.q: Why did p21 fail to rise in line B?
o: Mutant p53 cannot bind DNA
Correct: it cannot act as a transcription factor.
Line B lacks the CDKN1A gene
Nothing suggests the gene is missing.
Line B does not make p53 protein
Its p53 rose fivefold.
Radiation destroys p21 protein
p21 rose normally in line A.
qs.x: Correct: Line B's p53 accumulates after damage but carries a mutation that prevents it from binding DNA. Without binding, it cannot switch on CDKN1A, so no extra p21 is made and the G1 checkpoint does not engage. Why the others are wrong: Line B makes plenty of p53 protein; the plasmid rescue shows the downstream machinery works; p21 rose in line A under the same radiation. Trap: Equating the amount of a transcription factor with its activity.

qs.q: What is the purpose of giving line B a normal TP53 gene?
o: To repair the radiation damage directly
TP53 encodes a transcription factor.
To increase the amount of p53 protein
Line B already accumulates p53.
To show that plasmids cause G1 arrest
Arrest depended on the gene carried.
To show the defect lies in TP53
Correct: restoring it restored the response.
qs.x: Correct: Line B differs from line A in many ways besides TP53. Putting a working copy of the gene back and seeing the G1 arrest (81%) and apoptosis (15%) return shows that the missing function of p53 explains the difference. Why the others are wrong: The problem is the quality of p53, not its quantity; p53 does not repair DNA itself; an empty plasmid would not produce this effect. Trap: Treating a rescue experiment as just another treatment.

qs.q: Why does losing p53 function contribute to cancer?
o: Cells divide more slowly without p53
Line B cycled normally.
Damaged cells keep dividing
Correct: the checkpoint and apoptosis are lost.
Cells without p53 cannot replicate DNA
Line B had 25% of cells in S phase.
p53 normally promotes entry into S phase
p53 blocks it after damage.
qs.x: Correct: Without working p53, a cell with broken DNA neither pauses to repair nor dies. Line B kept cycling after radiation (52% G1, 25% S) with only 3% apoptosis. Over many divisions, such cells collect mutations that can drive cancer, which is why TP53 is mutated in about half of human tumors. Why the others are wrong: Line B divided normally; p53 restrains the cycle after damage; DNA replication continued. Trap: Assuming a growth-restraining gene must be needed for growth.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: In photosynthesis, the light reactions in the thylakoid membrane use light energy to make ATP and NADPH and release O₂ from water. The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses that ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into sugar, with rubisco catalyzing the first step. Net CO₂ assimilation measured on an intact leaf is the difference between photosynthesis and the CO₂ released by respiration and photorespiration, which continue in the light.

Rubisco can also add O₂ instead of CO₂ to its substrate. This begins photorespiration, which consumes ATP and releases CO₂ without making sugar. The oxygenation reaction becomes more common when the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls or the temperature rises. Stomata, the pores in the leaf surface, open to let CO₂ in but also let water vapor out, so a plant short of water closes them and the internal CO₂ falls.

Researchers measured net CO₂ assimilation in Arabidopsis thaliana in a growth chamber. Leaves were sealed in a cuvette through which air of known CO₂ concentration flowed, and assimilation was calculated from the difference between the CO₂ entering and leaving. Light intensity was varied at ambient CO₂ (400 ppm) and again at high CO₂ (1,000 ppm), which suppresses photorespiration by favoring carboxylation (Table 1).

The researchers also calculated the quantum yield of each curve, the initial slope of assimilation against light intensity, which reports how efficiently absorbed photons are converted into fixed carbon. The slope was about 40% steeper at 1,000 ppm than at 400 ppm over the first two light levels.

In a second experiment at 400 ppm and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, plants whose soil had been allowed to dry for six days had an assimilation rate of 4.2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and a stomatal conductance (a measure of how open the stomata are) one-fifth of that in well-watered plants.

qs.q: Why is net assimilation negative in the dark?
o: The leaf absorbs CO₂ faster than it fixes it
Absorption would give a positive value.
Respiration continues without photosynthesis
Correct: the leaf releases CO₂.
Rubisco runs in reverse without light
Rubisco does not reverse.
The cuvette leaks CO₂ in the dark
A leak would affect every measurement.
qs.x: Correct: A negative value means the leaf released more CO₂ than it took up. With no light there is no photosynthesis, but mitochondrial respiration continues, so the leaf gives off 1.5 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ of CO₂. Why the others are wrong: Taking up CO₂ gives a positive value; rubisco catalyzes carboxylation in one direction; a leak would not depend on the light. Trap: Reading a negative rate as a measurement error.

qs.q: Why does the curve at 400 ppm level off above 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?
o: The leaf has run out of chlorophyll
Chlorophyll is not consumed.
The light reactions stop above this level
They continue to supply ATP and NADPH.
CO₂ supply now limits the rate
Correct: CO₂ supply becomes limiting.
Light damages rubisco at this intensity
The 1,000 ppm curve keeps rising.
qs.x: Correct: At 400 ppm the rate flattens near 13, but at 1,000 ppm the same leaf reaches 28 at the same light. Light is therefore not the limit; the supply of CO₂ to rubisco is. Why the others are wrong: Chlorophyll is not used up; damage would also cap the high-CO₂ curve; the light reactions keep running. Trap: Assuming a plateau always means the machinery is saturated.

qs.q: Why is assimilation higher at 1,000 ppm at every light level above zero?
o: More CO₂ favors carboxylation
Correct: less photorespiration and more fixation.
High CO₂ speeds the light reactions
Those are driven by light.
High CO₂ opens the stomata wider
High CO₂ tends to close stomata.
High CO₂ increases the number of chloroplasts
Not within a single measurement.
qs.x: Correct: Rubisco can use either CO₂ or O₂. Raising CO₂ makes carboxylation more likely, so more carbon is fixed and less is lost to photorespiration, which otherwise consumes energy and releases CO₂. Why the others are wrong: Chloroplast number cannot change during a measurement; high CO₂ usually narrows stomata; the light reactions depend on light, not CO₂. Trap: Explaining a CO₂ effect through the light reactions.

qs.q: What best explains the low rate in the drought-stressed plants?
o: Drought stopped respiration in the leaf
That would raise net assimilation.
Drought destroyed the thylakoid membranes
Nothing suggests structural damage.
The plants received less light
Light was held at 800.
Closed stomata cut the CO₂ supply
Correct: conductance fell to one-fifth.
qs.x: Correct: Stomata close to conserve water. With the pores nearly shut, CO₂ cannot diffuse into the leaf fast enough, so assimilation falls from 13.0 to 4.2 even at full light. Why the others are wrong: No damage is described; less respiration would increase the net value; light was identical. Trap: Blaming the light reactions for a shortage of CO₂.

qs.q: Which measurement would best show that photorespiration was reduced at 1,000 ppm?
o: A higher rate of O₂ release at 1,000 ppm
That reflects the light reactions.
Less CO₂ released in the light
Correct: photorespiration releases CO₂.
More chlorophyll per unit leaf area
Pigment content is a separate measure.
A larger stomatal conductance at 1,000 ppm
Conductance concerns gas entry.
qs.x: Correct: Photorespiration's defining output is CO₂ released in the light without sugar made. Measuring that release directly, for example by following labeled carbon, would show whether it fell. Why the others are wrong: O₂ release tracks the light reactions; conductance describes the pores; chlorophyll content is unrelated. Trap: Choosing a measure of overall photosynthesis instead of one specific to the process in question.

h: Net CO₂ assimilation at 400 ppm (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)
Net CO₂ assimilation at 1,000 ppm (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Human color vision normally depends on three cone types with peak sensitivities near 420 nm (S, short), 530 nm (M, medium) and 560 nm (L, long). The brain compares their outputs, so a color is identified by the pattern of activity across cone types rather than by any one cone alone. The genes for the M and L pigments sit next to each other on the X chromosome and are very similar in sequence, which makes unequal crossing over between them relatively common. The S pigment gene is on chromosome 7.

Because the M and L genes are X-linked, a man with a defective copy has no second copy to compensate, while a woman is affected only if both of her X chromosomes carry a defect. Anomalous trichromacy, in which one pigment's peak is shifted rather than missing, is more common than the complete loss of a cone type.

Researchers tested 600 men and 600 women with two methods. In the Rayleigh match, the observer mixes red and green light to match a yellow reference; people with a shifted M or L pigment need an unusual proportion of red. In the Ishihara plates, numbers are formed by dots that differ in color but not in brightness. Participants also named the colors of 20 standard samples under controlled lighting (Table 1).

Color vision deficiency affects everyday tasks unevenly. Traffic signals are distinguished partly by position, so they cause little trouble, while reading a colored map, judging whether meat is cooked, or noticing a rash can be harder. Some occupations, such as commercial piloting, require a color vision test.

Among the 49 men with an abnormal match, 36 could still distinguish red from green samples under bright light but made errors with pale or dim colors, while 13 made errors under all conditions. The researchers also noted that about 15% of women in the sample had one normal and one anomalous gene by DNA testing but normal color vision on every test.

qs.q: Why is red-green color vision deficiency much more common in men?
o: The S pigment gene is on the X chromosome
It is on chromosome 7.
Men have fewer cones than women
Cone numbers are similar.
The M and L genes lie on the X chromosome
Correct: men have only one copy.
Men's lenses absorb more red light
Lens absorption is not the cause.
qs.x: Correct: A man has one X chromosome, so a single defective M or L gene produces the deficiency. A woman needs a defect on both X chromosomes, which is far less likely, matching the 8.2% and 0.6% rates in the table. Why the others are wrong: Cone density does not differ this way; the S gene is autosomal; lens differences do not explain the pattern. Trap: Attributing an X-linked pattern to a general difference between the sexes.

qs.q: What do the 36 men who erred only with pale or dim colors most likely have?
o: A shifted pigment, not a missing cone
Correct: anomalous trichromacy.
No M cones at all
Then bright red and green would also be confused.
Normal color vision with poor attention
Their Rayleigh matches were abnormal.
A defect in the S pigment
That affects blue-yellow vision.
qs.x: Correct: Anomalous trichromacy shifts one pigment's peak so that the M and L signals become more similar. Colors that differ strongly still produce different patterns, but faint differences are lost. Complete absence of a cone type would cause errors in all conditions, as in the other 13 men. Why the others are wrong: Missing M cones would impair bright colors too; the S pigment serves blue-yellow discrimination; all 36 failed an objective matching test. Trap: Treating color deficiency as all-or-nothing.

qs.q: Why do the Ishihara plates use dots that differ in color but not brightness?
o: So people with normal vision also fail
They pass the plates.
So the test measures visual acuity
Acuity is measured separately.
So the plates can be printed cheaply
Cost is not the reason.
So brightness cannot replace color
Correct: the test isolates hue.
qs.x: Correct: If the numbers also differed in lightness, someone who cannot distinguish the hues could still read them from brightness alone. Matching the brightness forces the observer to rely on color. Why the others are wrong: Printing cost is irrelevant; people with normal vision read the plates correctly; acuity is a different measure. Trap: Missing that a good test removes the alternative cue.

qs.q: What do the 15% of women with one anomalous gene and normal vision illustrate?
o: Color vision genes are not inherited
They are X-linked genes.
One normal copy is enough
Correct: the trait is recessive on the X.
X inactivation removes all anomalous cones
Some cones express the anomalous gene.
The anomalous gene is dominant in women
Those women saw normally.
qs.x: Correct: These women are carriers. Because the normal gene on one X chromosome supports a normal population of cones, their color vision tests normally, which is why the deficiency is described as X-linked recessive. Why the others are wrong: Normal vision shows the anomalous allele is not dominant; the genes are inherited; random X inactivation leaves some cones expressing each allele. Trap: Assuming a carrier must show a partial version of the trait.

qs.q: Why does the brain need more than one cone type to identify a color?
o: Cones cannot respond to dim light
Rods handle dim light, but cones still respond.
One cone type gives an ambiguous signal
Correct: comparison resolves it.
Each cone type sends signals to a different eye
Both eyes contain all cone types.
A single cone type responds to only one wavelength
Each responds over a broad range.
qs.x: Correct: A single cone gives the same response to a dim light at its peak wavelength and a bright light off-peak, so its output alone is ambiguous. Comparing two or more cone types resolves the ambiguity and yields hue. Why the others are wrong: Each cone type responds across a broad band of wavelengths; cones work in moderate light; both eyes have all cone types. Trap: Thinking each cone type reports one specific color.

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Signal detection theory separates two influences on a yes-or-no judgment. Sensitivity (d′) reflects how well a person can tell signal trials from noise trials. The criterion (c) reflects how willing the person is to say "yes." A criterion of 0 is neutral, a negative value is liberal (more "yes" responses), and a positive value is conservative. Both are calculated from the hit rate (the proportion of signal trials called "yes") and the false-alarm rate (the proportion of noise trials called "yes"). Sensitivity is unaffected by shifts in criterion.

Researchers asked 40 radiology residents to judge whether each of 200 chest X-rays showed a lung nodule. Half of the images contained a nodule confirmed by later CT scanning. In the first session, held at the start of a day shift, residents read one block under neutral instructions. They then read one block after being told that missed nodules lead to delayed cancer diagnoses (liberal instructions) and one block after being told that false alarms lead to unnecessary biopsies (conservative instructions). Block order was counterbalanced. In a second session, the same residents read a neutral block at the end of a 12-hour overnight shift. Mean results are shown in Table 1.

The residents also rated their confidence on each image from 1 (certainly no nodule) to 5 (certainly a nodule). By treating each confidence level as a separate cutoff, the researchers plotted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for each block, showing the hit rate against the false-alarm rate at each cutoff. The three start-of-shift curves fell almost on top of one another, while the end-of-shift curve lay closer to the diagonal line that represents guessing. A curve that bends farther toward the upper left corner indicates higher sensitivity at every criterion.
The researchers noted that hospitals often track only the number of nodules a reader finds, and that this figure rose after the liberal instructions.

qs.q: What did the change from neutral to liberal instructions mainly alter?
o: The difficulty of the images
The same kinds of images were used.
The residents' criterion for answering "yes"
Correct: c fell while d′ barely changed.
The number of images that contained a nodule
Half the images had nodules in every block.
The residents' ability to see nodules
d′ stayed near 1.6–1.7.
qs.x: Correct: Under liberal instructions both hits (0.80 to 0.90) and false alarms (0.20 to 0.36) rose, which is the pattern of a lower criterion. Sensitivity was essentially unchanged (1.68 versus 1.64), so the residents became more willing to say "yes" without becoming better at telling the two kinds of images apart. Why the others are wrong: d′ did not improve; the proportion of nodule images was fixed by design; nothing suggests the images changed. Trap: Reading more hits as better detection.

qs.q: What best describes the effect of the overnight shift?
o: The criterion became much more liberal
c moved slightly in the conservative direction.
Sensitivity rose but residents said "yes" less often
d′ fell.
Both sensitivity and criterion were unchanged
d′ dropped substantially.
Sensitivity fell, with little change in criterion
Correct: d′ dropped from 1.68 to 1.05.
qs.x: Correct: At the end of the shift, hits fell and false alarms rose at the same time. Moving in opposite directions like this is the sign of reduced sensitivity, and d′ dropped from 1.68 to 1.05. The criterion moved only from 0.00 to +0.12. Why the others are wrong: c became slightly more conservative, not liberal; d′ clearly changed; sensitivity went down, not up. Trap: Looking only at the hit rate, which also falls with a conservative shift.

qs.q: The hospital wants residents to miss fewer nodules without making more false alarms. Which approach is most likely to work?
o: Rewarding residents for each nodule they report
This lowers the criterion.
Telling residents to report only obvious nodules
This raises misses.
Improving image quality or adding rest breaks
Correct: both act on sensitivity.
Telling residents to report any doubtful shadow
This raises false alarms too.
qs.x: Correct: Raising hits while lowering false alarms requires better sensitivity. Clearer images make signal and noise easier to tell apart, and the end-of-shift data show that fatigue lowers d′, so rest should help. Why the others are wrong: Reporting doubtful shadows and paying per nodule both shift the criterion and trade misses for false alarms, as the liberal block shows; reporting only obvious nodules does the reverse. Trap: Assuming that instructions or incentives can improve both kinds of error at once.

qs.q: A resident has a hit rate of 0.95 and a false-alarm rate of 0.60. Compared with the start-of-shift neutral average, this resident most likely has:
o: a more conservative criterion and higher sensitivity
The false-alarm rate is very high.
a more liberal criterion and lower sensitivity
Correct: many false alarms and a smaller gap.
the same criterion and higher sensitivity
The criterion is clearly liberal.
a more liberal criterion and higher sensitivity
The hit and false-alarm rates are close together.
qs.x: Correct: Saying "yes" to 60% of normal images shows a liberal criterion. Sensitivity depends on the distance between hits and false alarms on a z-scale; z(0.95) ≈ 1.64 and z(0.60) ≈ 0.25, so d′ ≈ 1.39, below the neutral average of 1.68. Why the others are wrong: Very frequent false alarms rule out a conservative or unchanged criterion; despite the high hit rate, sensitivity is lower than average. Trap: Treating a high hit rate as proof of high sensitivity.

qs.q: Why might counting nodules found be a misleading measure of reader quality?
o: It rises with a liberal criterion alone
Correct: more "yes" responses raise the count.
It cannot rise when instructions change
The count rose under liberal instructions.
It ignores the number of images each resident read
Every resident read the same number.
It depends only on sensitivity, not on criterion
Hits depend on both.
qs.x: Correct: A count of nodules found equals the number of hits, and hits rise whenever a reader says "yes" more often. The liberal block raised this count while d′ stayed flat and false alarms nearly doubled, so the count can improve without any gain in skill. Why the others are wrong: All residents read the same images; hits depend on both sensitivity and criterion; the passage states the count rose after liberal instructions. Trap: Accepting a single outcome measure without checking false alarms.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Bipolar I disorder is defined by at least one manic episode: a week or more of elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, rapid speech, racing thoughts and risky behavior. Depressive episodes usually occur as well, and across the course of the illness patients typically spend more days depressed than manic. Lithium reduces the frequency of episodes but has a narrow therapeutic range: levels below about 0.6 mmol/L often fail to prevent episodes, while levels above about 1.2 mmol/L cause tremor, confusion and kidney injury. Lithium is cleared by the kidney, and it is reabsorbed along with sodium, so dehydration or a low-sodium state raises its blood level.

Researchers followed 240 adults with bipolar I disorder for two years at four clinics. All had been stable for at least a month when they entered. Treatment was chosen by each patient and clinician, not assigned by the researchers. Blood lithium was measured every three months in those taking it. An episode was counted when a psychiatrist who did not know the patient's treatment judged that full criteria were met (Table 1).

Adherence was estimated from pharmacy refill records. Patients who filled at least 80% of their prescribed doses were counted as adherent; this was true of 71% of the lithium group and 66% of the valproate group. Episodes were more common among non-adherent patients in both groups.

Among the 42 patients taking no mood stabilizer, 29 had declined one and 13 had stopped because of side effects. Patients in this group had been ill for fewer years on average than those taking lithium. Three patients on lithium developed levels above 1.5 mmol/L; in two of these, the rise followed a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting, and in the third it followed the start of a thiazide diuretic, which increases sodium loss.

qs.q: Why does a thiazide diuretic raise blood lithium?
o: Lost sodium drives reabsorption of lithium
Correct: the kidney handles the two alike.
The diuretic blocks lithium metabolism in the liver
Lithium is not metabolized.
The diuretic binds lithium in the blood
No such binding occurs.
The diuretic increases lithium absorption from food
Absorption is unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: Lithium is handled by the kidney much like sodium. When sodium is lost, the kidney reabsorbs more of both, so lithium leaves the body more slowly and its blood level rises. Why the others are wrong: Lithium is an ion that is excreted unchanged rather than metabolized; it does not bind the drug; intestinal absorption is not affected. Trap: Explaining an ion's handling with liver metabolism.

qs.q: What is the most important limitation of this study's comparison of treatments?
o: Episodes were judged by a blinded psychiatrist
That is a strength.
Patients were not randomly assigned
Correct: groups may differ at the start.
The study lasted two years
Two years is a reasonable period.
Blood levels were measured every three months
That is reasonable monitoring.
qs.x: Correct: Treatment was chosen rather than assigned, and the no-stabilizer group had been ill for fewer years, so the groups differ in ways that could affect episode rates on their own. Blinded outcome judging helps, but it does not make the groups comparable. Why the others are wrong: Blinding, regular monitoring and a two-year follow-up all strengthen the study. Trap: Choosing a strength when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: What do the two lithium groups together suggest?
o: Lithium is less effective than no treatment
Both lithium groups did better.
Higher levels are always safer
Levels above 1.2 cause toxicity.
Lithium works equally at any dose
The episode rates differ sharply.
Benefit depends on the blood level
Correct: 34% versus 61% with episodes.
qs.x: Correct: Patients averaging 0.8 mmol/L had episodes half as often as those averaging 0.5 mmol/L, which is why clinicians monitor blood levels rather than dose alone. Why the others are wrong: The two groups differed; higher levels bring toxicity; both lithium groups fared better than no stabilizer. Trap: Treating a drug as either effective or not without considering its concentration.

qs.q: Which feature distinguishes a manic episode from ordinary high energy?
o: A week of elevated mood with impairment
Correct: duration and impairment.
Speaking quickly when excited about plans
Rapid speech alone is not an episode.
Feeling happy for a day after good news
Mood reacting to events is normal.
Sleeping nine or ten hours each night
Mania reduces the need for sleep.
qs.x: Correct: Diagnosis depends on a syndrome lasting at least a week, with several symptoms together and clear impairment or risk, rather than on any single feature. Why the others are wrong: Normal mood responds to events; mania reduces sleep need; fast speech alone, without duration and impairment, is not enough. Trap: Diagnosing from one symptom in isolation.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the case that lithium itself reduced episodes?
o: Lithium levels stayed stable over two years
Stability is about measurement.
Episodes were counted by a blinded psychiatrist
Blinding was already in place.
Episodes fell in patients after starting it
Correct: each patient serves as a control.
The lithium groups were larger than the others
Group size does not address confounding.
qs.x: Correct: Comparing each patient's episode rate before and after starting lithium removes differences between people, including illness duration, which is the main confound here. A sharp drop within patients would be much harder to explain by selection. Why the others are wrong: Larger groups reduce random error but not bias; blinding was already used; stable levels concern adherence and monitoring. Trap: Confusing precision with freedom from bias.
