passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Insomnia is defined by difficulty falling or staying asleep together with daytime impairment. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) combines several parts. Stimulus control rebuilds the association between the bed and sleep: the person gets out of bed when unable to sleep and uses the bed only for sleep. Sleep restriction limits time in bed to the hours actually slept, which builds the homeostatic sleep drive, the pressure to sleep that grows with time awake. Cognitive work addresses beliefs such as "if I sleep badly I cannot function at all." Sedative-hypnotic drugs act quickly but their effects often fade after they are stopped.

Researchers randomly assigned 180 adults with chronic insomnia to six weeks of CBT-I, a sedative-hypnotic drug, or a waiting list. Allocation was by computer in blocks of six, and the person who prepared the assignments was not involved in the treatment. Participants kept daily sleep diaries, and a subset wore actigraphs. The main outcome was sleep onset latency, the time from lights out to sleep. Sleep efficiency is time asleep divided by time in bed. Measurements were taken after six weeks and again six months later (Table 1).

The researchers noted that a waiting-list group controls for the passage of time and for repeated measurement, but not for the expectation of being treated. A placebo pill group would separate the drug's chemical effect from the belief that one is being treated; it was not included because the funder judged a six-month placebo period unacceptable.

Baseline sleep onset latency was about 48 minutes in all three groups. Participants and therapists knew which treatment was given; the researcher who analyzed the diaries did not. Fourteen people in the drug group and three in the CBT-I group left the study early. Among those who completed treatment, 52% of the drug group reported daytime drowsiness, compared with 11% of the CBT-I group.

qs.q: Which part of CBT-I most directly builds the homeostatic sleep drive?
o: Sleep restriction
Correct: less time in bed means more time awake.
Cognitive restructuring
That targets beliefs about sleep.
Sleep hygiene advice
That concerns habits such as caffeine use.
Stimulus control
That rebuilds the bed–sleep association.
qs.x: Correct: The pressure to sleep builds with time spent awake. Limiting time in bed increases that pressure, so sleep comes faster and is more consolidated. Why the others are wrong: Cognitive work changes beliefs, stimulus control changes learned associations, and hygiene advice changes daily habits; none directly increases time awake. Trap: Picking the component that sounds most like a sleep routine.

qs.q: What is the most important finding at six months?
o: The waiting list improved on its own
It was unchanged at 45 minutes.
Both treatments failed by six months
CBT-I held its gain.
Only CBT-I kept its benefit
Correct: 20 versus 44 minutes.
The drug worked better than CBT-I
Its benefit disappeared.
qs.x: Correct: At six weeks the two treatments looked similar (15 and 18 minutes), but six months later the drug group had returned to 44 minutes, close to the waiting list's 45, while the CBT-I group stayed at 20. The skills learned in CBT-I persist after the sessions end. Why the others are wrong: The drug's advantage did not last; CBT-I maintained its gain; the waiting list did not improve. Trap: Judging a treatment by its short-term result alone.

qs.q: Why does the uneven dropout weaken the comparison?
o: Dropout was caused by randomization
Assignment was random and blind.
Dropout makes the remaining groups larger
It reduces group size.
Dropout affected only the waiting list
Most dropouts were in the drug group.
The remaining drug group may be unusual
Correct: 14 versus 3 left.
qs.x: Correct: If people who tolerated the drug poorly left, the remaining drug group is made up of those who did best with it, which can flatter the drug's results. Random assignment makes groups comparable at the start, but differential dropout can undo that. Why the others are wrong: Dropout shrinks groups; random assignment does not cause people to leave; the drug group lost the most. Trap: Assuming randomization protects a trial against everything that follows.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the person analyzing the diaries did not know the group assignments?
o: It allows participants to be blinded too
They knew their treatment.
It makes the treatment more effective
Analysis does not change the effect.
Expectations cannot shape the scoring
Correct: blind outcome assessment.
It removes the need for a control group
A comparison group is still needed.
qs.x: Correct: Participants and therapists could not be blinded here, so the outcome assessment is the one place blinding can be preserved. An analyst who does not know the groups cannot unconsciously score ambiguous diary entries in the expected direction. Why the others are wrong: Participants still knew their treatment; analysis does not alter the treatment's effect; the waiting list remains essential. Trap: Treating one form of blinding as a substitute for another.

qs.q: What does the waiting-list group's stability over six months show?
o: The waiting list received a placebo
No placebo is described.
Measurement becomes unreliable over time
Stable values suggest the opposite.
The treatments have no real effect
Both treatment groups improved at 6 weeks.
Insomnia did not improve by itself
Correct: 47 to 45 minutes.
qs.x: Correct: Without treatment, latency stayed at about 45 minutes, so the improvements in the treated groups cannot be explained by time passing or by the condition running its course. Why the others are wrong: Both treatments improved sleep at six weeks; a waiting list is not a placebo, which is why the drug group is not fully controlled for expectation; the stable values support reliable measurement. Trap: Mixing up a no-treatment control with a placebo control.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Sound from several sources arrives at the ear as one pressure wave, so hearing a single voice in a crowd requires the auditory system to assign parts of that wave to separate sources. The resulting perceptual objects are called streams, and the cues that build them are regularities that natural sources tend to obey.

Three cues are well established. Frequency separation matters because a single source usually produces sounds in a limited range, so tones far apart in pitch tend to split into two streams. Rate matters because a fast sequence gives less time to integrate successive tones into one line. And common onset matters because components that begin together usually come from one event.

Segregation is not fixed at the start of a sequence. Listening to an alternating sequence for several seconds makes it more likely to split, a build-up that suggests the system accumulates evidence for two sources rather than deciding once.

Listeners heard sequences of alternating high and low tones and reported whether they heard one stream or two. Frequency separation and presentation rate were varied within listeners, and reports were taken in the first second and after ten seconds (Table 1).

Both cues act and build-up acts on top of them. Frequency separation has the larger effect, raising two-stream reports by about 32 points at the slow rate and 57 at the fast rate, while rate contributes 8 to 33 points depending on separation. Every condition shows more splitting after ten seconds than in the first second.

The build-up itself varies with the strength of the cues. It adds 5 points in the weakest condition and 23 points in the 10-semitone slow condition, which is the ambiguous case where accumulated evidence has the most room to change the outcome.

Two cautions apply. The report is a subjective judgment with no objective criterion, so a listener's willingness to say "two" could shift with the sequence rather than their perception changing. And the sequences were isolated tones in quiet, while real segregation operates on speech and music in noise, where additional cues such as harmonicity and spatial location are available.

qs.q: Why does the build-up over ten seconds favor an evidence-accumulation account?
o: Two streams are reported far more at the fast rate
That is the rate cue, not build-up.
The widest separation produces the most splitting
That is the frequency cue.
Listeners heard each sequence more than one time
Each sequence was heard once.
Perception changes while the stimulus is unchanged
Correct: the decision is not made once.
qs.x: Correct: Nothing about the sequence differs between the first second and the tenth, so a rise in two-stream reports over that interval means the system is still gathering evidence and can revise an initial grouping. Why the others are wrong: The rate and frequency effects are separate cues, and repetition across trials is not what the comparison rests on. Trap: Explaining a change over time with one of the stimulus cues.

qs.q: In which condition does build-up contribute most, and why?
o: The ambiguous 10-semitone slow-rate condition
Correct: the outcome is least determined there.
The 10-semitone fast condition, where splitting is highest
It is near ceiling at 94%.
All conditions equally, since time is the same
The gains range from 5 to 23 points.
The 2-semitone slow condition, where cues are weakest
Weak cues leave little to accumulate.
qs.x: Correct: Build-up adds 23 points in the 10-semitone slow condition, where the first-second report of 38% shows the grouping is genuinely undecided and accumulated evidence can tip it. Why the others are wrong: Weak cues give little to accumulate, the fast wide condition is close to ceiling, and the gains are plainly unequal. Trap: Assuming an effect of time must be the same size wherever time passes.

qs.q: What is an auditory stream?
o: The pathway from cochlea to auditory cortex
That is anatomy, not perception.
A continuous tone of one single unchanging frequency
Streams can contain many frequencies.
The pressure wave that arrives at the eardrum
That is the unseparated input.
A perceived sound source built from the signal
Correct: a perceptual object.
qs.x: Correct: A stream is the perceptual grouping that the auditory system assigns to one presumed source, constructed from cues in a signal that arrives already mixed. Why the others are wrong: A stream need not be a single frequency, the arriving wave is what must be separated, and the ascending pathway is a separate matter. Trap: Identifying a perceptual object with the physical signal that gives rise to it.

qs.q: By how many percentage points does the wider separation raise two-stream reports at the fast rate in the first second?
o: That is the rate effect at the narrow separation.
That is the separation effect at the slow rate.
That is the rate effect at the wide separation.
Correct: 71 minus 14.
qs.x: Correct: At the fast rate in the first second, two-stream reports run 14% at 2 semitones and 71% at 10 semitones, a difference of 57 points. Why the others are wrong: 32 points is the same contrast at the slow rate, and 8 and 33 points are rate effects within a separation. Trap: Comparing rows that differ in rate rather than in separation.

qs.q: Why does the subjective report limit the conclusions?
o: Listeners cannot judge their own perception
They are the only source for it here.
The sequences were too short to judge
Ten seconds is ample for the judgment.
Willingness to say "two" may itself shift
Correct: criterion and perception are confounded.
Reports were collected only after ten seconds
They were collected at both times.
qs.x: Correct: With no objective answer against which a report can be scored, a change in the proportion saying "two" could reflect a shift in how readily that word is applied rather than a change in what was heard. Why the others are wrong: Subjective report is the appropriate measure here, the sequences were long enough, and reports were taken at both time points. Trap: Treating a response measure as a direct readout of perception.

h: Two streams reported, after ten seconds

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Max Weber described rationalization as the spread of calculation, efficiency and formal rules into areas of life once governed by tradition or personal judgment. Bureaucracy, with its written rules, specialized roles and hierarchy, is its clearest form. Weber argued that rationalization raises efficiency but can leave people feeling trapped in an impersonal system, and that formal rules sometimes crowd out the goals they were meant to serve, an outcome later called goal displacement. George Ritzer applied these ideas to modern services, arguing that organizations pursue efficiency, calculability, predictability and control, and that these can come at the cost of personal attention.

Researchers studied the introduction of a standardized electronic checklist at 40 primary care clinics in one health system. The checklist prompted the clinician to record a fixed set of items at every visit and would not close until each field was filled. Twenty clinics adopted it in January and the other twenty kept their existing records for that year, with assignment made by the health system according to which clinics had updated computers. The researchers compared the two groups over 12 months using appointment records, chart audits and patient surveys (Table 1).

Patient surveys were sent to a random sample of 50 patients from each clinic, and 61% responded at checklist clinics and 64% at comparison clinics. Burnout was measured with a standard questionnaire given to every clinician at the start and the end of the year; the scores in the table are end-of-year values, and the two groups had started within 0.3 points of each other.

In interviews, clinicians at checklist clinics described spending much of the visit facing the screen and said they sometimes deferred a patient's concern to a later visit in order to complete the required fields. Several said the checklist had caught problems they might otherwise have missed. One clinic in the comparison group began using a shortened checklist of its own in month 9.

qs.q: Which feature of the checklist best illustrates Weber's idea of formal rationality?
o: Clinicians work in the same building
Shared space is not a rule system.
Visits vary in length by patient
Variation is the opposite of standardization.
A fixed set of items at every visit
Correct: rules replace individual judgment.
Patients choose their own clinician
That is personal choice.
qs.x: Correct: Formal rationality means decisions are governed by explicit, uniform rules rather than by tradition or personal discretion. A checklist that must be completed identically at every visit is exactly this kind of rule. Why the others are wrong: Sharing a building is not a rule; patient choice and variable visit length reflect discretion rather than standardization. Trap: Treating any organized activity as bureaucratic.

qs.q: Which pair of findings best illustrates goal displacement?
o: More screenings but less listening
Correct: the measured task crowds out the purpose.
Shorter visits with more visits per day
Both show efficiency.
Higher burnout with longer visits
Visits were shorter at checklist clinics.
Higher follow-up calls with higher screening
Both are intended results.
qs.x: Correct: Goal displacement occurs when attention to the formal rule replaces the underlying purpose. Screenings rose to 92%, but the share of patients who felt listened to fell to 58%, and clinicians described deferring patients' concerns to finish the fields. The measured task displaced the care it was meant to support. Why the others are wrong: Efficiency measures and intended results are not displacement; visits were shorter, not longer. Trap: Reading any unwanted side effect as goal displacement.

qs.q: What most limits a causal interpretation of these results?
o: Patient surveys were used as a measure
Surveys are a reasonable measure.
The study ran for only 12 months
A year is a reasonable period.
Chart audits were used
Audits give objective data.
Clinics were not randomly assigned
Correct: not random assignment.
qs.x: Correct: Clinics received the checklist based on which had updated computers, so the two groups may differ in funding, staffing or patient population. Differences in outcomes could reflect those features rather than the checklist. Why the others are wrong: Surveys, audits and a 12-month period are all reasonable methods. Trap: Confusing a measurement method with a design flaw.

qs.q: How does the comparison clinic that adopted its own checklist in month 9 affect the study?
o: It makes the two groups more alike
Correct: a true difference may be understated.
It makes the checklist look more effective
Shared practice narrows the gap.
It invalidates the patient surveys
Surveys were still collected.
It has no bearing on the results
That clinic's data are included.
qs.x: Correct: If a comparison clinic starts doing what the intervention group does, the measured difference between the groups shrinks. Any real effect of the checklist would be understated rather than exaggerated. Why the others are wrong: Contamination weakens rather than strengthens an apparent effect; the surveys remain valid; the clinic is part of the comparison group. Trap: Assuming any flaw must exaggerate the finding.

qs.q: Which concept best describes clinicians' sense of being controlled by the system they work in?
o: Mechanical solidarity
That describes cohesion through shared beliefs.
The looking-glass self
That concerns self-image from others' views.
The iron cage
Correct: Weber's image of rationalized constraint.
The sick role
That describes expectations for people who are ill.
qs.x: Correct: Weber used the image of an iron cage for the way rationalized systems constrain the people inside them, even those who run them. Clinicians facing the screen and deferring patients' concerns describe this experience. Why the others are wrong: The looking-glass self is Cooley's idea about self-concept; mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's term for cohesion in simple societies; the sick role is Parsons's account of expectations for ill people. Trap: Choosing a familiar sociology term without matching it to the situation.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Size-exclusion chromatography separates molecules by size. The column is packed with porous beads; small molecules enter the pores and take a long path, while molecules too large to enter flow around the beads and leave first. The volume at which a protein emerges, its elution volume, therefore decreases as size increases. Proteins larger than the largest pore all leave together in the void volume. Because the method separates by the size and shape of the molecule as it is in solution, it reports the size of an assembled complex rather than of a single chain.

SDS-PAGE separates proteins differently. Sodium dodecyl sulfate coats each chain with negative charge in proportion to its length and unfolds it, and the reducing agent β-mercaptoethanol breaks disulfide bonds. Migration then depends on the mass of the individual chain.

Researchers purified an enzyme from liver. They first calibrated a size-exclusion column with proteins of known mass, then ran their enzyme. They also ran the enzyme on SDS-PAGE, with and without β-mercaptoethanol, beside a ladder of mass standards (Table 1).

Before the calibration, the researchers checked the column by running a mixture of blue dextran, a very large polymer, and a small dye. Blue dextran emerged at 40 mL, defining the void volume, and the dye at 98 mL, defining the total volume accessible to small molecules. Every protein therefore had to elute between these two values, and a protein that emerged outside that window would indicate that it was binding the beads rather than being separated by size.

The researchers then repeated the size-exclusion run in buffer containing 6 M guanidinium chloride, a denaturant, with a reducing agent. Under those conditions the enzyme emerged at 92 mL, corresponding to about 35 kDa. Enzyme activity was measured in fractions from the original run and appeared only in the fractions around 66 mL.

qs.q: What is the most likely structure of the native enzyme?
o: Four 35 kDa chains, joined in pairs by disulfides
Correct: 140 kDa made of two 70 kDa halves.
A single folded chain of 140 kDa
SDS-PAGE gives a 35 kDa band.
Two 70 kDa chains with no disulfides
Reducing agent splits the 70 kDa band.
Four 35 kDa chains held only by noncovalent forces
A 70 kDa band persists without reduction.
qs.x: Correct: The native mass is 140 kDa. Without reducing agent the chains run as 70 kDa, so pairs are joined by disulfide bonds; with reducing agent each is 35 kDa. Four chains of 35 kDa, linked as two disulfide-bonded pairs that associate noncovalently, account for all three numbers. Why the others are wrong: A single 140 kDa chain would give one 140 kDa band; the other options cannot produce both the 70 kDa and 35 kDa bands. Trap: Reading the native mass as the mass of one chain.

qs.q: Why do larger proteins leave a size-exclusion column first?
o: They are attracted to the column wall
Separation does not depend on wall binding.
They cannot enter the beads' pores
Correct: they take the shorter path.
They carry more negative charge
This method does not separate by charge.
They diffuse faster through the buffer
Larger molecules diffuse more slowly.
qs.x: Correct: The pores add path length. Molecules too large to enter travel only the space between beads and so elute in a smaller volume. Why the others are wrong: Wall interactions are an artifact to be avoided; charge-based separation is ion exchange; larger molecules diffuse more slowly, which is not what sets elution volume here. Trap: Assuming that bigger molecules move more slowly in every method.

qs.q: What does the run in guanidinium chloride with reducing agent show?
o: The 140 kDa form is built from 35 kDa chains
Correct: denatured and reduced, it elutes as 35 kDa.
The enzyme is a single 35 kDa chain in the cell
It elutes at 140 kDa when native.
Guanidinium chloride cuts peptide bonds
It disrupts noncovalent interactions.
The column pores shrink in denaturant
Pore size is a property of the beads.
qs.x: Correct: The denaturant breaks the noncovalent contacts between chains and the reducing agent breaks the disulfides, so the complex falls apart into single 35 kDa chains, which elute later at 92 mL. Why the others are wrong: The native enzyme is a 140 kDa assembly; denaturants do not hydrolyze peptide bonds; pore size does not change. Trap: Taking a denatured result as the protein's normal state.

qs.q: Why is enzyme activity found only near 66 mL?
o: Activity requires the reducing agent
No reducing agent was in that run.
Activity is destroyed by the column beads
It was recovered at 66 mL.
Only the assembled complex is active
Correct: activity follows the native form.
Small fragments elute before large ones
Larger molecules elute first.
qs.x: Correct: Activity co-elutes with the 140 kDa peak, so the complete, folded assembly is the active species. Fractions that contain no complex contain no activity. Why the others are wrong: Activity survived the column; large molecules elute first; the native run contained no reducing agent. Trap: Ignoring that where activity appears identifies which species is functional.

qs.q: Why can SDS-PAGE not report the native mass?
o: SDS-PAGE cannot resolve proteins above 50 kDa
Standards above 50 kDa were used.
SDS unfolds and separates the chains
Correct: it reports chain mass.
SDS adds mass that cannot be corrected
Binding is proportional to length.
SDS-PAGE separates by charge alone
Coating makes charge proportional to size.
qs.x: Correct: SDS denatures proteins and disrupts the noncovalent contacts that hold a complex together, so each chain migrates separately according to its own mass. The native assembly no longer exists on the gel. Why the others are wrong: Large proteins can be resolved with the right gel; the uniform coating is what makes mass estimation possible; migration reflects chain length because charge is proportional to it. Trap: Expecting one method to report both chain mass and assembled mass.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Many chemotherapy drugs act on dividing cells. Some damage DNA directly, some block the enzymes that copy or untangle it, and some interfere with the spindle. A cell that cannot repair the damage may undergo apoptosis, a controlled death in which the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into fragments and its remains are cleared, or it may die by necrosis, in which the membrane breaks and the contents spill out and provoke inflammation.

Researchers tested a new compound, drug X, on three cultures: HCT116 colon cancer cells, which divide about every 20 hours; the same line treated to stop dividing but stay alive; and normal colon epithelial cells, which divide about every 48 hours. Cells were exposed for 48 hours. Viability was measured with a dye reduced only by cells with working mitochondria, and the concentration that reduced viability by half (IC₅₀) was calculated. Apoptosis was measured by a stain that detects cut DNA ends, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release into the medium was measured as a marker of broken membranes (Table 1).

In a second experiment, dividing HCT116 cells were treated with 10 µM drug X for 12 hours and examined by flow cytometry. The fraction of cells with the DNA content of G2/M rose from 18% to 61%. Microscopy showed condensed chromosomes that were not aligned at the metaphase plate, and spindles that appeared short and disorganized.

The researchers also checked that the viability dye was reporting what they intended. They counted cells directly under a microscope after trypan blue staining, which labels cells with broken membranes, and found that the proportion of unstained cells matched the dye result within 5% at every concentration tested.
A caspase inhibitor was added with drug X in a third experiment. Apoptosis at 10 µM fell from 46% to 7%, but viability at 72 hours rose only slightly, from 31% to 38%.

qs.q: What do the three IC₅₀ values suggest about drug X?
o: It is equally toxic to all three cultures
The values differ 28-fold.
It harms cancer cells regardless of division
Nondividing cancer cells resisted it.
It is more toxic to normal cells
Their IC₅₀ is nine times higher.
It mainly harms rapidly dividing cells
Correct: 2.1 µM versus 58 and 19.
qs.x: Correct: The same cancer line needed 28 times more drug when it was not dividing, and the slower-dividing normal cells needed nine times more than the dividing cancer cells. The decisive factor is division rate, not whether the cell is cancerous. Why the others are wrong: Nondividing cancer cells were largely spared; the values are far apart; the normal cells were the less sensitive of the two dividing cultures. Trap: Assuming a drug that kills cancer cells recognizes cancer itself.

qs.q: Which mechanism best fits the second experiment?
o: The drug disrupts spindle assembly
Correct: G2/M arrest with disorganized spindles.
The drug blocks DNA replication in S phase
Cells accumulated in G2/M.
The drug prevents cells from leaving G1
The G1 fraction fell.
The drug stops protein synthesis in all cells
Nondividing cells were spared.
qs.x: Correct: Cells piled up with G2/M DNA content, their chromosomes were condensed but not aligned, and their spindles were short and disorganized. That combination points to the spindle rather than to DNA replication. Why the others are wrong: An S-phase block gives intermediate DNA content; a G1 block does not raise the G2/M fraction; blocking protein synthesis would harm nondividing cells too. Trap: Choosing a DNA-damaging mechanism because chemotherapy usually acts on DNA.

qs.q: What explains the low LDH release alongside high apoptosis?
o: HCT116 cells do not produce any LDH
It is a common cytosolic enzyme.
The dye assay also measures LDH
They are separate measurements.
The drug fails to kill these cells
Viability fell sharply.
Apoptosis keeps membranes intact
Correct: contents are not spilled.
qs.x: Correct: In apoptosis the cell shrinks and is packaged for clearance, so cytosolic enzymes such as LDH stay inside. Necrosis breaks the membrane and releases them. The low LDH (8%) with 46% apoptosis shows the cells died in an orderly way. Why the others are wrong: Viability clearly fell; LDH is present in these cells; the two assays measure different things. Trap: Expecting every form of cell death to release cell contents.

qs.q: What does the caspase-inhibitor result suggest?
o: Caspases are not involved in this death
Apoptosis fell from 46% to 7%.
The inhibitor makes the drug more toxic
Viability rose slightly.
Blocking apoptosis does not save them
Correct: viability barely improved.
Apoptosis is the only route of death here
Cells still died without it.
qs.x: Correct: The inhibitor nearly abolished the apoptotic signal, confirming that caspases carry out that program, yet viability at 72 hours rose only from 31% to 38%. The underlying damage remains, so cells die by other routes or simply fail to recover. Why the others are wrong: The drop in apoptosis shows caspases are involved; viability did not fall; the small rescue shows apoptosis is not the only route. Trap: Assuming that blocking the visible form of death rescues the cell.

qs.q: Why were nondividing HCT116 cells included?
o: To measure the drug's stability in medium
Stability was not assessed.
To separate cancer from division rate
Correct: same cells, different division.
To show the dye works without mitochondria
The dye requires mitochondria.
To provide a dose–response curve
Each culture gave one.
qs.x: Correct: Comparing a cancer line with normal cells confounds two differences: the cells are different, and one divides faster. Using the same cancer line in a nondividing state leaves division rate as the only variable, and the IC₅₀ rose 28-fold. Why the others are wrong: No stability measurement is described; every culture yielded a curve; the dye depends on working mitochondria. Trap: Overlooking why a comparison uses the same cell line twice.

h: LDH released at 10 µM (% of total)

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Bacteria are classified in part by their cell envelope. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer outside the plasma membrane. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and, outside it, an outer membrane whose outer leaflet is made largely of lipopolysaccharide. This extra membrane keeps many compounds out and makes gram-negative bacteria harder to treat.

Antimicrobial peptides are part of innate immunity in many animals. Most are short, carry a positive charge and fold so that nonpolar and charged residues sit on opposite faces. The positive charge draws the peptide to the negatively charged surfaces of bacterial membranes, and the nonpolar face lets it insert into the lipid interior, forming pores. Mammalian plasma membranes have mostly neutral outer leaflets and contain cholesterol, which makes them less attractive targets.

Researchers tested peptide P, a 22-residue peptide with six lysines, against two bacteria and against human red blood cells. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth. Hemolysis was measured as the release of hemoglobin from red blood cells, and membrane permeability was measured with a dye that enters only cells with damaged membranes (Table 1).

The MIC was read after 18 hours of growth in broth, and each measurement was repeated three times on separate days. Wells with no peptide grew to full density every time, and wells with no bacteria stayed clear, confirming that the medium was not contaminated.

Killing was rapid: at four times the MIC, more than 99% of S. aureus cells were killed within 20 minutes, before the cells could divide. In a serial-passage experiment, S. aureus was grown for 25 days in gradually rising concentrations of peptide P or of ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic that inhibits DNA gyrase. The MIC of ciprofloxacin rose 64-fold over this period, while the MIC of peptide P rose twofold. Adding 150 mM NaCl raised peptide P's MIC against S. aureus from 4 to 32 µg/mL.

qs.q: Why is peptide P less active against E. coli than against S. aureus?
o: E. coli divides too quickly to be killed
Killing occurred before division.
E. coli has a thicker peptidoglycan layer
Its peptidoglycan layer is thin.
The outer membrane blocks access
Correct: a second barrier must be crossed.
E. coli membranes carry a positive charge
Bacterial surfaces are negative.
qs.x: Correct: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide that excludes many compounds. Loosening it lowered the MIC from 16 to 2 µg/mL, which identifies that barrier as the obstacle. Why the others are wrong: The thick peptidoglycan belongs to gram-positive cells; bacterial surfaces are negatively charged, which attracts the peptide; killing was faster than division. Trap: Assuming the thicker wall is always the greater barrier.

qs.q: Why does peptide P damage bacterial membranes but spare red blood cells?
o: Bacterial surfaces are more negatively charged
Correct: charge directs the peptide.
Bacterial membranes contain cholesterol
Cholesterol is in animal membranes.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria to damage
The peptide acts on membranes.
Red blood cells have no plasma membrane
They have one.
qs.x: Correct: The peptide's lysines give it a positive charge, and electrostatic attraction concentrates it on the negatively charged bacterial surface. Mammalian outer leaflets are largely neutral and contain cholesterol, which stiffens the bilayer, so only 3% hemolysis occurred at a concentration that permeabilized most bacteria. Why the others are wrong: Red blood cells have a plasma membrane; the mechanism does not involve mitochondria; cholesterol is found in animal rather than bacterial membranes. Trap: Looking for a target inside the cell when the mechanism acts at the surface.

qs.q: What does the salt result suggest about how the peptide works?
o: Salt makes bacterial membranes thicker
No such effect is described.
Ions shield the charge attraction
Correct: binding weakens, so more peptide is needed.
Salt destroys the peptide's amino acids
Salt does not break peptide bonds.
Salt provides an alternative nutrient
MIC measures growth inhibition, not nutrition.
qs.x: Correct: Dissolved ions surround charged groups and weaken the electrostatic attraction between the positively charged peptide and the negatively charged bacterial surface. More peptide is then needed, so the MIC rose from 4 to 32 µg/mL. This is a known obstacle to using such peptides in blood, which contains about 150 mM salt. Why the others are wrong: Salt does not hydrolyze the peptide; no membrane change is described; the assay measures inhibition of growth. Trap: Treating a change in MIC as proof that the drug was destroyed.

qs.q: Why did resistance develop so much more slowly to peptide P than to ciprofloxacin?
o: Peptide P was used at a lower concentration
Both were raised gradually.
Peptide P does not kill the bacteria
It killed over 99% within 20 minutes.
Ciprofloxacin kills bacteria faster
Speed does not determine resistance.
The membrane target has no single mutation
Correct: no single target.
qs.x: Correct: Ciprofloxacin acts on one enzyme, so a single point mutation in DNA gyrase can reduce binding. Peptide P acts on the membrane itself, and a cell would need to remodel the charge of its entire surface, which is costly and requires many changes. Why the others are wrong: Both were tested the same way; killing speed does not by itself set the rate of resistance; the peptide killed effectively. Trap: Assuming resistance arises at the same rate for any effective drug.

qs.q: Why does rapid killing argue against a mechanism that blocks cell wall synthesis?
o: Killing speed is the same for every mechanism
Mechanisms differ in speed.
Wall synthesis occurs only in gram-negative cells
Both types build walls.
Wall-synthesis inhibitors need cells to grow
Correct: killing came before division.
Peptidoglycan is not part of the cell wall
It is the main component.
qs.x: Correct: A drug that blocks wall synthesis kills as the growing cell fails to maintain its wall, which takes at least a division cycle. Peptide P killed more than 99% of cells in 20 minutes, before division, which fits immediate membrane damage. Why the others are wrong: Both gram types synthesize peptidoglycan; peptidoglycan is the wall's main polymer; killing speed varies by mechanism. Trap: Overlooking timing as evidence about mechanism.

r: E. coli plus a compound that loosens the outer membrane

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is defined by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that begin in childhood, exceed what is expected for the child's developmental level, and cause impairment. A central requirement is that the symptoms appear in more than one setting, which is why evaluations collect ratings from parents and from teachers rather than from either source alone.

The reason for that requirement is diagnostic rather than statistical. Difficulty confined to one setting usually has a cause located in that setting: a mismatch between a child and a particular classroom, an unmanageable schedule at home, or a teacher whose tolerance for movement is low. A disorder of attentional control, by contrast, should follow the child across settings, so cross-setting agreement is evidence that the problem is in the child rather than in the environment.

The treatments act on catecholamine signaling. Stimulants block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, raising their availability in prefrontal circuits that support working memory and inhibitory control. Atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is an alternative that is not a stimulant.

A specialty clinic evaluated 200 children referred for attention problems, collecting standardized rating scales from one parent and one teacher for each child, and recorded whether the child ultimately met full diagnostic criteria after a full evaluation (Table 1).

The gradient is steep. Agreement between informants is almost diagnostic on its own, at 96%, while a single elevated informant leaves roughly nine in ten children not meeting criteria, which is what the cross-setting requirement is designed to accomplish.

Two cautions follow. These are referred children, so the proportions in each row describe a clinic population and not the general population, where the share of children with elevated ratings anywhere is much lower. More importantly, the rating pattern was part of the information available when the diagnosis was made, so the association between agreement and diagnosis is partly circular; an independent diagnostic procedure blind to the ratings would be needed to estimate how well informant agreement actually predicts the disorder.

qs.q: Why does the diagnosis require symptoms in more than one setting?
o: The symptoms of this disorder appear only at school
They appear across settings.
Difficulty in only one setting usually has a cause in that setting
Correct: it localizes the problem.
Two settings provide twice as many symptoms to count
The count is not what changes.
Teachers rate children far more accurately than their parents do at home
Neither informant is privileged.
qs.x: Correct: A disorder of attentional control should travel with the child, so problems confined to one setting point instead to something about that setting, and requiring both informants screens those cases out. Why the others are wrong: Neither informant is treated as the more accurate, the requirement is about generality rather than symptom count, and school-only presentation is exactly what the criterion excludes. Trap: Reading a criterion meant to locate the cause as a way of gathering more evidence.

qs.q: What is the strongest reason to doubt that informant agreement predicts the diagnosis as well as Table 1 suggests?
o: Only 200 children were evaluated at the clinic
That affects precision, not circularity.
All of the children had been referred for attention problems
That limits generalization.
The rating scales informed the diagnosis itself
Correct: the predictor entered the outcome.
One parent and one teacher rated each of the children
Two informants is the standard.
qs.x: Correct: Clinicians who made the diagnosis could see the rating scales, so children with agreement across settings were more likely to be diagnosed partly because the agreement counted as evidence, which inflates the association beyond what an independent diagnosis would show. Why the others are wrong: Sample size affects the precision of the estimates, referral status limits how far the proportions generalize, and the two-informant design is appropriate. Trap: Choosing a generalization limit when the flaw is that predictor and outcome are not independent.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitter systems do stimulant medications mainly act on?
o: Acetylcholine and glycine
Not the mechanism here.
Dopamine and norepinephrine
Correct: reuptake is blocked.
Serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid
Those are other drug targets.
Histamine and glutamate
Also not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: Stimulants block the transporters that clear dopamine and norepinephrine from the synapse, raising signaling in prefrontal circuits that support working memory and inhibition. Why the others are wrong: Serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid are targets of antidepressants and anxiolytics, while acetylcholine, glycine, histamine and glutamate are not what these medications act on. Trap: Naming the best-known transmitter rather than the one the drug class targets.

qs.q: Stimulants also improve sustained attention in children without the disorder. Why does that matter for diagnosis?
o: Response to the drug cannot serve as a diagnostic test
Correct: improvement is not specific.
It implies every child meets the criteria for the disorder
Improvement is not diagnosis.
It means that medication is unnecessary for diagnosed children
Effectiveness is not in question.
It shows that stimulant medications do not actually work
They do improve attention.
qs.x: Correct: If a drug improves the measured function in people with and without the condition, then improving on the drug says nothing about whether the condition is present, so a trial of medication cannot be used to confirm a diagnosis. Why the others are wrong: The finding shows the drug works broadly rather than not at all, broad effectiveness is not evidence that everyone is affected, and nothing here bears on whether treatment helps those diagnosed. Trap: Converting a point about specificity into a claim about efficacy.

qs.q: Why do 12% of the children rated elevated at school only still meet full criteria?
o: Those children in fact have no symptoms at all
They met full criteria.
The criteria require elevation in only a single setting
They require more than one.
Ratings from schools are sufficient on their own
The 88% who did not qualify show otherwise.
A parent may underreport symptoms seen at home
Correct: one informant can miss them.
qs.x: Correct: A rating scale is one informant's report, and a parent who sees the child mainly in unstructured time, or who is reluctant to report problems, can produce a low score in a child whose home difficulties emerge on fuller evaluation. Why the others are wrong: The criteria do demand cross-setting symptoms, school ratings alone leave most children not qualifying, and these children did meet criteria. Trap: Treating a rating scale as a direct measurement of symptoms rather than as a report.

r: Elevated at home and at school

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide (AMP) on the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in vitro. Twenty-four bacterial cultures were inoculated in 96-well plates and exposed to AMP concentrations of 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 µg/mL for 24 hours. After incubation, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured to assess bacterial growth. The results, summarized in Table 1, show a dose-dependent decrease in OD600, with complete inhibition observed at 32 µg/mL. In addition, the study measured the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) by serial dilution and determined the MIC to be 32 µg/mL. The researchers also performed time‑kill assays at each concentration; after 6 hours the reduction in colony‑forming units was 2.5 log at 8 µg/mL and 3.5 log at 32 µg/mL. Statistical analysis (ANOVA) indicated significant differences between concentrations (p < 0.01). The authors concluded that the AMP has potent antibacterial activity and could serve as a lead compound for new antibiotics.

qs.q: Which concentration shows the highest % inhibition?
o: 2 µg/mL
Not the best answer
8 µg/mL
Not the best answer
16 µg/mL
Not the best answer
32 µg/mL
Correct
qs.x: The table indicates that 32 µg/mL achieves 100% inhibition, the highest among the tested concentrations. Trap: The answer may be mistakenly chosen as 8 µg/mL because it shows a large inhibition (60%) but does not reach complete inhibition.

qs.q: Which experimental approach best determines the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the AMP?
o: A single OD600 reading at one AMP concentration
Not the best answer
Time‑kill assay at 6 hours
Not the best answer
Serial dilution with growth assessment
Correct
ANOVA
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: C) The MIC is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires a series of (typically twofold) dilutions, each scored for growth. Why the others are wrong: A) one reading at a single concentration cannot locate the lowest inhibitory concentration. B) a time‑kill assay measures the rate and extent of killing (log CFU reduction) over time, not the growth-inhibition threshold. D) ANOVA tests differences between group means and does not define a concentration threshold. Trap: Choosing the time‑kill assay because it measures antibacterial activity, although it tracks killing over time rather than the lowest concentration that prevents growth.

qs.q: If the OD600 at 8 µg/mL is 0.40, what is the percent inhibition relative to the control?
o: Correct
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
qs.x: Percent inhibition = [(1.00 – 0.40)/1.00] × 100 = 60%. Trap: Some students may mistakenly use the OD600 of 0.70 (for 4 µg/mL) or miscalculate the subtraction.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: The AMP completely inhibits growth at 32 µg/mL.
Not the best answer
The MIC is 32 µg/mL.
Not the best answer
The AMP shows a 2.5‑log reduction at 8 µg/mL after 6 hours.
Not the best answer
The OD600 at 0 µg/mL is 0.85.
Correct
qs.x: Correct: The table lists the OD600 at 0 µg/mL as 1.00, not 0.85 (0.85 is the value at 2 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: A) the table shows 100% inhibition and OD600 of 0.00 at 32 µg/mL. B) the passage gives the MIC as 32 µg/mL, the lowest tested concentration with complete inhibition. C) the table and passage both report a 2.5‑log CFU reduction at 8 µg/mL at 6 h. Trap: Confusing the OD600 of the 2 µg/mL well (0.85) with the untreated control value (1.00).

qs.q: Which follow‑up experiment would best test whether the in vitro activity of the AMP is likely to translate into therapeutic benefit?
o: Repeating the same 24‑hour OD600 assay in the same medium and strain.
Not the best answer
Measuring OD600 in wells that contain no bacteria.
Not the best answer
Testing the AMP in an animal model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.
Correct
Testing only concentrations below 2 µg/mL.
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: An animal infection model tests efficacy in a living host, which is the logical step after in vitro activity is shown. Why the others are wrong: A) repeating the same in vitro assay adds replication but no new information on efficacy in a host. B) wells without bacteria only provide a blank reading and say nothing about activity. D) the lowest concentrations had the least inhibition, so they add little about therapeutic potential. Trap: Choosing more in vitro replication because it feels rigorous, though it does not address efficacy in an infection.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: When people explain behavior, they weigh dispositional causes, which lie in the person, against situational causes, which lie in the circumstances. The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to favor dispositional explanations for other people's behavior even when the situation is obvious. The actor-observer asymmetry adds that people explain their own behavior more situationally than they explain the same behavior in someone else. One proposed reason is a difference in perspective: an actor looks outward and sees the situation, while an observer looks at the actor.

Researchers tested 240 undergraduates. Each read a short scenario in which a student arrived 20 minutes late to a study group, with no explanation given. In the self condition, participants imagined that they themselves had arrived late. In the other condition, they read about a classmate. Half of the participants in each condition were also told that the campus shuttle had broken down that morning. Participants then rated, from 1 to 7, how much the lateness was caused by the person's character and how much by the circumstances (Table 1).

The researchers noted that imagining oneself in a scenario is not the same as actually being late, and that a participant who imagines being late may picture a reason without meaning to. To check this, they asked a separate group of 40 participants to describe what they had pictured; 32 reported imagining a specific cause, most often traffic or oversleeping. The researchers argued that this is itself part of the asymmetry: an actor supplies reasons that an observer never sees.

In a second study, participants in the other condition watched a 30-second video filmed from the late student's point of view, showing the empty shuttle stop and the walk to campus. Their character rating fell to 3.2. A third group watched the same scene filmed from across the street, showing the student walking; their character rating was 4.9.

qs.q: Which comparison best demonstrates the actor-observer asymmetry?
o: Other with and without shuttle information
Both are other-ratings.
Self versus other, no shuttle news
Correct: 2.6 against 5.1 for character.
The two video groups
Both watched someone else.
Self with and without shuttle information
Both are self-ratings.
qs.x: Correct: The asymmetry is the difference between explaining one's own behavior and the same behavior in another person. With the same information, participants rated character as the cause at 2.6 for themselves and 5.1 for a classmate. Why the others are wrong: The other comparisons vary information or camera angle within one perspective rather than comparing self with other. Trap: Choosing a comparison that varies something else while holding perspective constant.

qs.q: What do the camera angle results suggest?
o: Video evidence always reduces blame
The across-the-street video did not.
The actor-observer effect disappears with video
It persisted at 4.9.
People ignore video evidence entirely
Ratings changed with angle.
The actor's viewpoint shifts attribution
Correct: 3.2 versus 4.9.
qs.x: Correct: Both groups saw the same event; only the camera position differed. Seeing what the actor saw lowered character attributions to 3.2, while watching the actor from outside left them at 4.9. This supports the perspective explanation for the asymmetry. Why the others are wrong: One video did not reduce blame; ratings did respond to the videos; the effect remained in the outside-view group. Trap: Treating all video evidence as equally informative.

qs.q: Why does giving the shuttle information reduce character ratings more in the other condition?
o: Actors always ignore new information
Their ratings also shifted.
Observers care more about accuracy than actors
Motivation was not measured.
Observers lacked what actors already knew
Correct: it moved from 5.1 to 4.0.
The shuttle information was false
Nothing suggests it was false.
qs.x: Correct: Someone imagining their own lateness already has reasons in mind, so added information changes little (2.6 to 2.1). An observer starts without those reasons, so supplying one produces a larger change (5.1 to 4.0). Why the others are wrong: No measure of motivation is given; actor ratings shifted too; the information was presented as true. Trap: Explaining a group difference by a difference in motives rather than in information.

qs.q: Even when told about the shuttle, observers rated character at 4.0, above the actors' 2.1. Which conclusion does this best support?
o: The information reduces but keeps the bias
Correct: a gap persists.
Situational information has no effect on observers
Ratings fell by 1.1.
Actors ignore their own character entirely
They rated it at 2.1, not 1.
Observers are unable to consider situations
They adjusted their ratings.
qs.x: Correct: The observers' character ratings dropped when they learned about the shuttle, yet they remained well above the actors'. Knowing the situation helps, but the tendency to explain another person's behavior by their character is not erased. Why the others are wrong: The information clearly had an effect; observers did adjust; actors did not rate character at the minimum. Trap: Reading a partial change as no change or as a complete one.

qs.q: Which situation would most likely reduce the fundamental attribution error in everyday life?
o: Watching the person for a longer time
More observation keeps the observer's view.
Being told the person is usually reliable
That is dispositional information.
Judging someone from a different culture
Unfamiliarity tends to increase the error.
Having been in the same situation
Correct: it supplies the actor's view.
qs.x: Correct: The error comes largely from not seeing the constraints the other person faces. Having faced the same constraints supplies that missing information, much as the actor-perspective video did. Why the others are wrong: Reputation is still information about the person; longer observation does not change the vantage point; unfamiliarity makes situational constraints harder to recognize. Trap: Assuming more observation automatically corrects a bias in perspective.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Distillation separates liquids by exploiting differences in boiling point. Heating a mixture produces a vapor richer in the more volatile component, and condensing that vapor gives a distillate enriched in it. The enrichment achieved in one such cycle is set by the ratio of the components' vapor pressures at the boiling temperature.

One cycle is often not enough. Simple distillation, which condenses the vapor directly, works when the boiling points differ by roughly 25 degrees or more. When they are closer, the vapor is only slightly enriched and the distillate remains a mixture.

Fractional distillation addresses this by inserting a packed column between the flask and the condenser. Vapor rising through the packing repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates, and each cycle enriches it further, so a column of sufficient length can separate components differing by only a few degrees. The number of effective cycles is described as the column's theoretical plates.
A mixture of two liquids was distilled by both methods, and the composition of the first fraction collected was measured (Table 1).

The two methods diverge as the boiling points converge. Simple distillation gives a usable separation at a 44-degree difference and fails at 12 degrees, where the first fraction is only slightly enriched over the starting mixture, while fractional distillation exceeds 90% purity in every case.

The hexane and cyclohexane pair shows why the column matters. A single vaporization enriches the vapor from 50% to 58%, so about eight percentage points per cycle, and reaching 91% requires several such cycles, which the packing supplies within one apparatus.

Two limits should be kept in mind. These purities are for the first fraction, and later fractions are progressively poorer as the flask is depleted of the volatile component, so the yield at a stated purity is lower than the purity alone suggests. And a pair that forms an azeotrope cannot be separated beyond the azeotropic composition by either method, however many plates the column has.

qs.q: Why does fractional distillation succeed where simple distillation fails?
o: The column raises the boiling point of the mixture
Boiling point is set by the liquids.
The packing provides repeated vaporization cycles
Correct: each cycle enriches further.
The mixture is heated more slowly in a column
Rate is not what creates the separation.
The vapor is condensed at a lower temperature there
Condenser temperature is not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: Each condensation and re-evaporation within the packing enriches the vapor by the same factor as the first vaporization, so a column multiplies a small single-cycle enrichment into a large overall one. Why the others are wrong: Boiling point is a property of the liquids, condenser temperature only liquefies the vapor, and heating rate does not change the enrichment per cycle. Trap: Attributing the improvement to the temperature rather than to the number of cycles.

qs.q: What does the 58% figure for hexane indicate?
o: Cyclohexane is the more volatile component
Hexane boils lower and is enriched.
The simple apparatus was assembled wrongly
It performed as expected for one cycle.
One vaporization enriches only slightly
Correct: from 50% to 58%.
Hexane and cyclohexane cannot be separated
Fractional distillation reached 91%.
qs.x: Correct: Starting from an equal mixture, a single vaporization produces a vapor that is 58% hexane, an enrichment of eight points, which is why many cycles are needed to approach purity. Why the others are wrong: The pair was separated by column, the simple apparatus worked correctly, and hexane is the more volatile of the two. Trap: Reading a poor result as a failure of the method rather than as the size of one cycle's effect.

qs.q: What determines the enrichment achieved in a single cycle?
o: The volume of the distillation flask being used
Volume affects scale, not enrichment.
The length of the condenser attached
The condenser only liquefies vapor.
The total mass of the mixture distilled
Mass does not change composition.
The ratio of the components' vapor pressures
Correct: at the boiling temperature.
qs.x: Correct: The vapor above a mixture is richer in the component with the higher vapor pressure, and the ratio of those pressures fixes how much richer, which is the enrichment of one cycle. Why the others are wrong: Flask volume, condenser length and total mass affect the scale and rate of the operation rather than the composition of the vapor. Trap: Looking to the apparatus for a quantity set by the liquids themselves.

qs.q: By how many percentage points does the column improve the benzene fraction?
o: That is the improvement for acetone.
That is the improvement for methanol.
Correct: 96% against 71%.
That is the improvement for hexane.
qs.x: Correct: Benzene reaches 71% by simple distillation and 96% with a column, an improvement of 25 points. Why the others are wrong: 5, 10 and 33 points are the improvements for the other three pairs. Trap: Taking the pair with the largest improvement rather than the one asked about.

qs.q: Why does an azeotrope defeat both methods?
o: Columns cannot be made long enough
Length would not help at all.
Its vapor has the same composition as the liquid
Correct: no enrichment occurs.
Azeotropes have no measurable boiling point at all
They boil at a fixed temperature.
The components decompose on heating then
Decomposition is a separate problem.
qs.x: Correct: At the azeotropic composition the vapor and the liquid have the same proportions, so a vaporization cycle produces no enrichment and adding plates achieves nothing. Why the others are wrong: An azeotrope boils at a definite temperature, decomposition is unrelated, and the problem is not one of insufficient column length. Trap: Treating a thermodynamic limit as an engineering one.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Sociologists distinguish material culture, the physical objects a group makes and uses, from nonmaterial culture, its beliefs, norms and values. Culture changes unevenly: William Ogburn argued that material culture often changes faster than the norms that govern its use, leaving a culture lag during which a technology is in wide use before shared rules for it exist. Norms themselves vary in strength. Folkways are everyday customs whose violation brings mild disapproval; mores carry moral weight and their violation brings serious sanction; taboos are prohibitions so strong that the act is almost unthinkable.

A society's dominant culture coexists with subcultures, which differ from it without rejecting it, and countercultures, which oppose it. Judging another culture by the standards of one's own is ethnocentrism; understanding practices on their own terms is cultural relativism.

Researchers surveyed 4,000 adults in one country about the use of personal recording devices in public, a technology adopted rapidly over the previous decade. Respondents rated how wrong each act is on a 1 to 7 scale and reported whether they would say something to the person (Table 1).

The researchers noted two limits of the survey. First, what people say they would do is not what they do: self-reported willingness to speak up is usually higher than observed behavior, so the figures in the last two columns should be read as attitudes rather than as predictions. Second, the sample was drawn from an online panel, which underrepresents adults without regular internet access, a group that is older and less urban on average.

Respondents aged 18 to 29 rated recording a stranger's conversation at 3.4, while those over 60 rated it at 4.9. In follow-up interviews, many respondents of all ages said they were unsure what the rules were and that no clear etiquette had developed. Researchers in a second country, where recording in public has been regulated for 20 years, found far less disagreement across age groups on the same items.

qs.q: Which act is best described as violating a taboo?
o: Recording a street performance
It is rated 1.4 and rarely challenged.
Recording a friend without telling them
It draws moderate disapproval.
Recording inside a locker room
Correct: nearly universal condemnation.
Recording a conversation on a train
Opinion is divided.
qs.x: Correct: The locker room item drew a wrongness rating of 6.8, with 61% willing to confront the person and 92% supporting a legal prohibition. Near-unanimous condemnation and legal backing mark the strongest category of norm. Why the others are wrong: The street performance is barely disapproved, and the other two items draw mixed, moderate reactions typical of contested norms. Trap: Ranking acts by how unpleasant they sound rather than by the strength of the social reaction.

qs.q: Which finding best illustrates culture lag?
o: Widespread use with no agreed etiquette
Correct: the technology outpaced the norms.
Near-unanimous condemnation of locker-room recording
That norm is settled.
A low rating for recording a street performance
That is also settled.
Support for prohibiting locker-room recording
A clear rule already exists.
qs.x: Correct: Culture lag is the gap between a change in material culture and the norms that follow it. Rapid adoption of recording devices, combined with respondents of every age saying they did not know the rules, is exactly that gap. Why the others are wrong: Items with near-unanimous agreement show norms that have already settled, which is the opposite of lag. Trap: Choosing the item with the strongest opinion when lag is marked by the absence of agreement.

qs.q: What does the age difference on the train item most likely reflect?
o: The question was unclear to older adults
Both groups answered it.
Different generations learned different norms
Correct: socialization differs by cohort.
Older adults cannot operate recording devices
Skill was not measured.
Younger adults are less moral in general
They agreed on the locker room item.
qs.x: Correct: People are socialized in the era they grow up in. Those who came of age with recording devices in constant use absorbed more permissive expectations, giving 3.4 against 4.9. The gap is largest on precisely the item where no settled rule exists. Why the others are wrong: Device skill was not measured; both groups condemned the locker-room item strongly; both groups answered the same question. Trap: Reading a difference in norms as a difference in character.

qs.q: What does the comparison with the second country suggest?
o: Age has no effect on attitudes anywhere
Age mattered in the first country.
Laws always follow public opinion
Here the law preceded the consensus.
Recording is less common there
Prevalence was not reported.
Formal rules can reduce disagreement
Correct: less variation where regulation is long-standing.
qs.x: Correct: Where recording in public has been regulated for two decades, age groups agreed far more closely. A clear formal rule gives everyone the same reference point, which narrows the gap that culture lag opens. Why the others are wrong: Nothing is reported about how often people record there; age mattered in the surveyed country; this example shows regulation preceding agreement rather than following it. Trap: Assuming law always codifies an existing consensus.

qs.q: A traveler calls the second country's rules "an overreaction" without learning why they were adopted. Which concept does this illustrate?
o: Culture lag
That concerns norms trailing technology.
Counterculture
That is a group opposing the dominant culture.
Cultural relativism
That means understanding practices on their own terms.
Ethnocentrism
Correct: judging by one's own standards.
qs.x: Correct: Evaluating another society's practice by the standards of one's own, without examining its context, is ethnocentrism. Cultural relativism would involve asking what problem those rules were meant to solve. Why the others are wrong: Relativism is the opposite stance, culture lag concerns the pace of normative change, and a counterculture is a group rather than a judgment. Trap: Choosing a term that names the situation instead of the attitude described.

h: Respondents who said a law should prohibit it (%)
r: Recording a stranger's conversation on a train
Recording a friend without telling them

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Enzymes from organisms that live at different temperatures often catalyze the same reaction with the same active-site residues, yet they differ in speed and in heat tolerance. One explanation is that a protein must be flexible enough to move through the conformational changes of its catalytic cycle but rigid enough to stay folded. A protein from a heat-loving organism may be well suited to high temperatures yet sluggish at room temperature, because the same interactions that hold it together also restrict its motion.

To test this idea, researchers purified adenylate kinase, which catalyzes 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP, from a bacterium that grows best at 37 °C (Enzyme M) and from a related species isolated from a hot spring that grows best at 70 °C (Enzyme T). The two proteins share 74% sequence identity, and every residue that contacts the substrates is conserved. Turnover number (kcat) was measured at several temperatures with saturating substrate (Table 1). Each value is the mean of three runs that differed by less than 5%.

The researchers also measured the melting temperature (Tm), the temperature at which half of the protein is unfolded, using circular dichroism. Enzyme M had a Tm of 47 °C and Enzyme T had a Tm of 82 °C. Inspection of the Enzyme T crystal structure showed that Glu142, a surface residue far from the active site, forms an ion pair with Arg87. A mutant of Enzyme T in which Glu142 was replaced by glutamine (E142Q) had a Tm of 71 °C. At 40 °C, the kcat of E142Q was 5.8 s⁻¹.

Heat tolerance has practical uses. Enzymes from heat-loving organisms are used in laboratory methods that cycle between high temperatures, such as the polymerase chain reaction, and in industrial processes that run hot to keep reactants dissolved and to limit microbial growth. Engineers who want an enzyme that is both stable and fast at moderate temperatures often start by adding or removing surface ion pairs and then testing how the changes affect Tm and kcat separately.

In a final experiment, Enzyme M was held at 60 °C for 10 minutes in the presence of substrate. Its activity was then measured after the solution was cooled to 30 °C. The rate was 4% of the rate of an unheated sample. When fresh, unheated Enzyme M was added to the heated solution, the rate returned to the expected value.

qs.q: Which explanation of the kcat values of the two enzymes at 20–30 °C is most consistent with the passage?
o: Enzyme T is too rigid to cycle quickly at low temperature
Correct: the stabilizing interactions that resist unfolding also slow conformational change.
Enzyme T makes the reaction less favorable overall
An enzyme cannot change ΔG of the reaction.
Enzyme T is partly unfolded when the temperature is low
Its Tm is 82 °C, so it is folded at 20–30 °C.
Enzyme T is missing some of the residues that bind substrate
Every substrate-contacting residue is conserved.
qs.x: Correct: Enzyme T is folded and has the same active site, yet it turns over about eight times more slowly than Enzyme M at 20–30 °C. The passage proposes that the interactions that keep a heat-tolerant protein folded also restrict the motions needed for catalysis, so it is sluggish at low temperature. Why the others are wrong: A Tm of 82 °C means Enzyme T is folded well below that temperature; the substrate-contacting residues are conserved; a catalyst changes the rate, not the free energy change. Trap: Assuming a slow enzyme must be damaged or missing part of its active site.

qs.q: To estimate the activation energy of Enzyme T from Table 1, which plot should the researchers make?
o: kcat against T, which has a slope of Eₐ/R
kcat is not linear in T.
1/kcat against 1/T, which has a slope equal to Eₐ/R
This is not the Arrhenius form.
ln kcat against T in kelvin, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
The x-axis must be 1/T.
ln kcat against 1/T, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
Correct: the linear form of the Arrhenius equation.
qs.x: Correct: Taking the natural log of k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) gives ln k = ln A − (Eₐ/R)(1/T), so a plot of ln k against 1/T (in kelvin) is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R. Only the points below the Tm should be used. Why the others are wrong: The rate constant rises exponentially, not linearly, with temperature; ln k is linear in 1/T, not in T; a double-reciprocal plot belongs to Michaelis–Menten analysis, not to the Arrhenius equation. Trap: Mixing up the Arrhenius plot with a Lineweaver–Burk plot.

qs.q: What do the results for the E142Q mutant most strongly suggest?
o: The mutation shifts the equilibrium toward ATP and AMP
Enzymes and mutations do not change Keq.
The Glu142–Arg87 ion pair stabilizes the folded enzyme
Correct: Tm fell by 11 °C while kcat stayed the same.
Glu142 is required for the chemical step of catalysis
kcat at 40 °C was unchanged.
Glutamine side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds
Glutamine's amide is a good hydrogen bond donor and acceptor.
qs.x: Correct: Replacing the charged Glu with the neutral Gln removes the salt bridge to Arg87. The Tm dropped from 82 °C to 71 °C, but kcat at 40 °C (5.8 s⁻¹) was essentially the same as the wild type (5.9 s⁻¹). The residue therefore contributes to stability, not to catalysis. Why the others are wrong: An unchanged kcat rules out a catalytic role, and Glu142 is far from the active site; glutamine hydrogen bonds well but carries no charge; no enzyme or mutation alters the equilibrium constant. Trap: Assuming any residue whose mutation matters must be in the active site.

qs.q: Which observation shows that the loss of Enzyme M activity at 60 °C is due to the enzyme rather than the substrate?
o: Raising substrate levels after heating restored the rate
This would point to substrate loss, and it was not observed.
Enzyme M activity at 50 °C is lower than at 40 °C
This does not separate enzyme loss from substrate loss.
Fresh enzyme added after heating restored the rate
Correct: the substrate was still usable.
Enzyme M is faster than Enzyme T at 30 °C
This compares enzymes, not substrate stability.
qs.x: Correct: If heat had destroyed the substrate, adding new enzyme would not help. Because fresh enzyme restored the expected rate in the same heated solution, the substrate survived and the original enzyme had been inactivated, consistent with unfolding above its Tm of 47 °C. Why the others are wrong: Comparing the two enzymes at 30 °C says nothing about heat damage; a lower rate at 50 °C is the finding being explained, not evidence for a cause; restoring activity by adding substrate would implicate the substrate. Trap: Choosing a result that restates the observation instead of one that tests the explanation.

qs.q: If kcat were measured at 75 °C, how would E142Q most likely compare with wild-type Enzyme T?
o: Higher, because glutamine is less charged than glutamate
Charge loss lowered stability.
The same, because the active site is unchanged
A folded active site is needed for activity.
Higher, because kcat rises with temperature for both
This holds only while the protein stays folded.
Lower, because most E142Q molecules would be unfolded
Correct: 75 °C is above its Tm of 71 °C.
qs.x: Correct: At 75 °C, more than half of E142Q is unfolded because its Tm is 71 °C, while wild-type Enzyme T, whose Tm is 82 °C, is mostly folded and still speeding up, as its rise from 20 to 35 s⁻¹ between 60 and 70 °C shows. The mutant should therefore be slower. Why the others are wrong: The Arrhenius trend holds only for folded enzyme; an identical active site is useless once the protein unfolds; removing the charge lowered stability rather than raising activity. Trap: Applying the Arrhenius trend past the melting temperature.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Stereotype threat is the performance decrement that appears when a person is at risk of confirming a negative stereotype about a group they belong to. The proposed mechanism is not reduced ability or effort but competition for working memory: monitoring one's own performance, suppressing anxious thoughts and worrying about what a poor score would mean all consume the same limited resource the task requires.

The mechanism generates a testable prediction. If threat acts through working memory, then a measure of load taken during the task should rise under threatening conditions and should move inversely with performance, and interventions that reduce threat should lower load as well as raising scores. If load stayed constant while scores moved, the account would be in trouble.

Two interventions are commonly used. Self-affirmation has the person write briefly about a value that matters to them before the task, which is held to reduce the stake the task carries for the self. Explicitly describing the stereotype as unfounded removes the inference a poor score would license.

Students completed the same difficult quantitative test under one of four randomly assigned framings. A concurrent secondary task indexed working memory load, scored so that higher values mean more load (Table 1).

The two columns move inversely across all four conditions, from 62 and 7.8 in the threatening condition to 74 and 5.1 in the puzzle framing, with the two interventions landing in between on both measures. That is the pattern the working memory account predicts.

The correspondence is suggestive but not decisive. Load and score are both outcomes measured at the same time, so a third factor, such as how engaging each framing felt, could move them together, and a mediation claim requires showing that the load change accounts for the score change statistically. The secondary task also competes with the test for resources, so the measurement may itself alter what it measures, and the test was difficult by design, which is the condition under which threat effects are largest and therefore not a general estimate.

qs.q: Which result supports the working memory account?
o: Self-affirmation raised the measured load index
It lowered load, to 5.6.
Scores exceeded 60 points in all of the four conditions
That is true but uninformative.
Load moved inversely with score across the conditions
Correct: the predicted relationship.
Four different framings were tested in the study
The number of conditions is not a result.
qs.x: Correct: The account predicts that threat consumes working memory, so load should rise as scores fall, and the table shows exactly that from 7.8 and 62 under threat to 5.1 and 74 under the puzzle framing. Why the others are wrong: Affirmation reduced load, the common floor above 60 bears on nothing, and the number of conditions is a design feature. Trap: Selecting a true statement about the table that does not test the hypothesis.

qs.q: Why does the puzzle framing help?
o: Anxiety is unaffected by how a task is framed
Framing changed load substantially.
The time limit for the test has been removed
Timing did not vary.
The questions themselves have been made easier
The test was identical.
No judgment of ability is implied by the task
Correct: nothing is at stake for the stereotype.
qs.x: Correct: Threat arises from the possibility of confirming a stereotype, and a task presented as a puzzle rather than as a measure of ability provides no inference about ability to be confirmed, so the monitoring that consumes working memory does not begin. Why the others are wrong: The items and the timing were constant, and framing clearly moved the load index. Trap: Attributing a framing effect to a change in task difficulty.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the account?
o: Scores rose after the self-affirmation task
That also fits the account.
Load was highest in the diagnostic framing
That is what the account predicts.
Students were already aware of the stereotype in question
Awareness is a precondition.
Load fell under the interventions while scores stayed low
Correct: the mediator moved without the outcome.
qs.x: Correct: If relieving load left performance unchanged, then load could not be the route by which threat lowers scores, which is the central claim, so that dissociation is the damaging result. Why the others are wrong: High load under threat and improved scores after affirmation are both predicted, and awareness of the stereotype is assumed by the account. Trap: Choosing the result that is most striking rather than the one that breaks the proposed link.

qs.q: What was randomly assigned in this experiment?
o: The framing each student received
