Correct: four framings were assigned.
The items that appeared on the test
The test was the same for all.
The working memory load measure used
One measure was used throughout.
The group membership of the students
That cannot be assigned.
qs.x: Correct: Students were randomly assigned to one of four framings, which is what licenses a causal claim about framing, while the test, the group memberships and the load measure were held constant. Why the others are wrong: Test content and the load measure did not vary, and group membership is a characteristic rather than a manipulation. Trap: Treating the variable the study is about as the variable that was assigned.

qs.q: Which practical implication follows most directly?
o: Avoid timed assessments wherever possible
Timing was not manipulated.
Present assessments as tools for learning
Correct: it removes the ability inference.
Separate students by group for testing
That makes group salient.
Reduce the difficulty of all assessments
Difficulty was not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: The effective manipulation here was describing the task as a puzzle rather than as a measure of ability, which maps onto presenting assessment as feedback for learning rather than as a verdict. Why the others are wrong: Separating by group heightens the salience that drives threat, and neither difficulty nor timing was the operative variable. Trap: Drawing an implication from a feature of the task that the experiment held constant.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antibiotic on the growth of *Staphylococcus aureus* in vitro. The experiment involved culturing the bacteria in a nutrient broth and adding the antibiotic at a single concentration (5 µg/mL). Samples were taken just before the antibiotic was added (Day 0) and at 1, 3, 5, and 7 days post-treatment. Bacterial counts were measured by serial dilution and plating, and the antibiotic concentration was confirmed by high-performance liquid chromatography. The goal was to describe the time-dependent bactericidal activity at that concentration; the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was not determined. The data collected provide insights into both the potency and the kinetics of bacterial killing, which are critical for informing dosing regimens in clinical settings. The researchers plan to use these findings to design subsequent in vivo studies and to evaluate potential resistance mechanisms.

qs.q: Based on the table, which day shows the highest bacterial count?
o: Day 0
Correct
Day 1
Not the best answer
Day 3
Not the best answer
Day 5
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: Day 0 has 1.2×10⁶ CFU/mL, the highest count, and no antibiotic is present yet (0 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: B) Day 1 is 8.5×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower than Day 0. C) Day 3 is 3.1×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower. D) Day 5 is 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, far lower. Trap: Picking a later day by assuming bacteria keep multiplying in broth over time, ignoring that counts fell after the antibiotic was added on Day 0.

qs.q: Which experimental control would best determine whether the observed bacterial killing is due to the antibiotic rather than other variables?
o: A culture with no antibiotic added
Correct
A culture with a known ineffective antibiotic
Not the best answer
A culture with vancomycin at the same concentration
Not the best answer
A culture with the antibiotic but no bacteria
Not the best answer
qs.x: A culture with no antibiotic serves as a negative control, showing bacterial growth in the absence of treatment. This allows comparison to antibiotic-treated cultures to attribute effects specifically to the drug. Trap: Option B is tempting because it introduces another antibiotic, but it does not isolate the effect of the novel drug.

qs.q: Calculate the percent reduction in bacterial count from Day 0 to Day 5.
o: Correct
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(1.2×10⁶ – 1.0×10⁴) / 1.2×10⁶] × 100 ≈ 99.2%. The calculation uses the baseline and Day 5 counts. Trap: Using the wrong time point or denominator; for example, the fall to Day 3 is only 74.2%, whereas the fall to Day 5 relative to the Day 0 count is 99.2%.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is best supported by the data in Table 1?
o: The antibiotic is bacteriostatic because bacterial counts never return to baseline.
Not the best answer
The MIC is 5 µg/mL since no growth is seen after Day 5.
Not the best answer
The antibiotic kills all bacteria within 3 days.
Not the best answer
No bacteria were recovered at Day 7, consistent with bactericidal activity at 5 µg/mL.
Correct
qs.x: CFU/mL fell from 1.2×10⁶ at Day 0 to 0 at Day 7 at a constant 5 µg/mL, consistent with bactericidal killing. Counts were still 3.1×10⁵ at Day 3, so killing was not complete within 3 days; a single concentration cannot define an MIC; and a progressive fall to zero is not bacteriostatic behavior. Trap: Option B is tempting because the concentration is constant, but an MIC requires testing multiple concentrations, and Day 5 still shows 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, so 'no growth after Day 5' is wrong.

qs.q: Table 1 tests only one antibiotic concentration (5 µg/mL). Which additional experiment would be needed to determine the MIC of the antibiotic?
o: Finding the lowest antibiotic concentration that prevents visible growth
Correct
Counting bacteria at more time points while keeping the concentration at 5 µg/mL
Not the best answer
Measuring bacterial counts at Day 7 only
Not the best answer
Adding vancomycin to the cultures treated with 5 µg/mL
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: The MIC is by definition the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires testing several concentrations. Why the others are wrong: B) more time points at one concentration describe kinetics, not the lowest inhibitory concentration. C) a Day 7 count at one concentration cannot compare concentrations. D) adding a second drug confounds the result and does not define the MIC of the novel drug. Trap: Treating the Day 7 count of zero at 5 µg/mL as the MIC, although only one concentration was tested.

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Solomon Asch studied conformity by asking participants to judge which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. The task was easy: people working alone were correct almost every time. In the group version, several confederates answered aloud before the participant and gave the same wrong answer on certain trials. About a third of participants' responses matched the wrong majority, and about three-quarters of participants conformed at least once.

Psychologists distinguish two reasons for conformity. Normative influence is the wish to be accepted, which produces public agreement without private belief. Informational influence is the belief that others know better, which changes private judgment as well. Ambiguous tasks favor informational influence, while clear tasks with a visible audience favor normative influence.

Researchers ran a modern replication with 160 participants in four conditions. In every condition, five confederates answered before the participant on 12 of 18 trials, giving a wrong answer on each of those 12. In the private condition, the participant wrote answers on a card that the others could not see. In the unanimous condition, all five confederates gave the same wrong answer. In the dissenter condition, the fourth confederate gave the correct answer. In the hard condition, the comparison lines differed by only 1 mm, making the judgment genuinely difficult (Table 1).

The researchers also recorded how long each participant took to answer on the critical trials. In the unanimous spoken condition, participants who went along with the majority took about 1.8 seconds longer than those who gave the correct answer, which the researchers read as a sign of conflict between what they saw and what they said.

In interviews afterward, most participants in the unanimous spoken condition said they had seen the correct answer but had not wanted to appear foolish. In the hard condition, most said they had not been sure and had assumed the others saw better.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates normative influence?
o: Hard versus easy judgment, both spoken
Difficulty differs, not the audience.
Spoken versus written, both unanimous
Correct: only the audience differs.
Unanimous versus dissenter, both spoken
Both are spoken.
Written versus the hard condition
Two things differ at once.
qs.x: Correct: Normative influence depends on being seen by the group. Holding everything else constant and removing the audience cut conformity from 31% to 8%, which measures the part driven by the wish to be accepted. Why the others are wrong: Comparing unanimity with a dissenter changes the group's agreement; changing difficulty changes how much people rely on others for information; the last comparison varies both. Trap: Picking a comparison in which more than one factor changes.

qs.q: Why is conformity highest in the hard condition?
o: Uncertainty makes other answers useful
Correct: informational influence.
The task had no correct answer
One line still matched.
Participants wanted acceptance more there
The audience was the same as in the unanimous condition.
The group was larger in that condition
All conditions used five confederates.
qs.x: Correct: When the lines differ by 1 mm, participants cannot be confident, so they treat the majority's answer as evidence. Their interviews confirm this: they assumed the others saw better. Why the others are wrong: Group size and audience were held constant; a correct answer existed. Trap: Explaining every rise in conformity by social pressure.

qs.q: Why does a single dissenter reduce conformity so sharply?
o: The dissenter makes the task ambiguous
The easy task stayed easy.
The dissenter makes the group smaller
Group size was unchanged.
Unanimity is what creates the pressure
Correct: 31% fell to 7%.
The dissenter gives the participant new information about the lines
The lines were easy to judge.
qs.x: Correct: Asch found that breaking unanimity matters more than how many people agree. One ally shows that disagreeing is possible, and the fear of standing alone drops. Why the others are wrong: There were still five confederates; the easy task needed no extra information; the task remained unambiguous. Trap: Assuming conformity depends simply on how many people hold the majority view.

qs.q: What do the interview responses add to the numerical results?
o: They prove that participants were lying
Reports are not proof.
They replace the need for the written condition
Self-report is weaker evidence.
They show the task was impossible
Most answers were correct.
They suggest which kind of influence operated
Correct: public agreement versus private belief.
qs.x: Correct: Participants in the easy spoken condition said they had seen the right answer but did not want to look foolish, which fits normative influence, while those in the hard condition said they assumed the others saw better, which fits informational influence. The behavioral conditions test the same distinction more directly. Why the others are wrong: Self-reports are evidence, not proof of lying; the written condition provides stronger evidence than self-report; most answers were correct, so the task was manageable. Trap: Treating self-report as either worthless or decisive.

qs.q: A student concludes from the 31% figure that most people conform. What is the best correction?
o: Only one person conformed in that condition
Most conformed at least once.
The figure counts trials, not people
Correct: 27% never conformed at all.
The figure should be 46%
That is the hard condition.
Conformity never occurs on easy tasks
It occurred on 31% of critical trials.
qs.x: Correct: The 31% is the proportion of critical responses that matched the wrong majority, averaged across participants. A separate figure shows that 27% of participants never conformed, so the statistic does not mean that most people conform on most trials. Why the others are wrong: 46% belongs to the hard condition; conformity did occur; many participants conformed at least once. Trap: Reading a per-trial percentage as a per-person one.

h: Participants' wrong answers on the 12 critical trials (%)

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Le Châtelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting in the direction that partly opposes it. Ammonia is made industrially by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. The equilibrium constant Kp depends only on temperature; pressure and catalysts do not change it. Because the reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants and lowers Kp.

The reaction also has four moles of gas on the left and two on the right, so compressing the mixture shifts it toward ammonia. The reaction is slow at low temperature, however, because breaking the triple bond of N₂ has a high activation energy. An iron catalyst lowers that barrier and speeds both the forward and the reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position does not change.
An engineering team measured the percentage of ammonia present at equilibrium under several conditions (Table 1). In each run the starting mixture was one part N₂ to three parts H₂ by moles.

The team also considered what sets the starting ratio. Using one part N₂ to three parts H₂ matches the stoichiometry of the reaction, which gives the highest conversion of both gases; an excess of either one would raise the conversion of the other but leave the excess gas unreacted and circulating through the plant. Hydrogen for the process is usually obtained from methane and steam, a step that is itself energy-intensive, so plants are designed around the cost of hydrogen as much as around the equilibrium yield. Roughly 1% of the world's energy use goes into this one reaction, which supplies the nitrogen in most agricultural fertilizer.

Industrial plants typically run at about 400 °C and 200 atm. The team also noted that ammonia is removed continuously by cooling it to a liquid while the unreacted gases are recycled through the reactor.

qs.q: Why does the ammonia percentage fall as temperature rises?
o: The forward reaction releases heat
Correct: added heat shifts it back toward reactants.
The catalyst stops working when hot
These values are equilibrium amounts.
Ammonia decomposes into different products
It reverts to N₂ and H₂.
Higher temperature lowers the pressure
Pressure was held constant in each row.
qs.x: Correct: In an exothermic reaction, heat behaves like a product. Adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, so Kp and the equilibrium percentage of ammonia both fall, from 81% at 200 °C to 5% at 600 °C. Why the others are wrong: The equilibrium position does not depend on the catalyst; each comparison holds pressure fixed; the reverse reaction gives back the original reactants. Trap: Expecting more ammonia at higher temperature because the reaction goes faster.

qs.q: Why does raising the pressure increase the yield?
o: Pressure converts the gases into liquids
The reaction occurs in the gas phase.
The product side has fewer gas moles
Correct: 4 moles become 2.
Pressure lowers the activation energy
That is the catalyst's role.
Pressure raises the value of Kp
Kp depends only on temperature.
qs.x: Correct: Compressing the mixture raises the partial pressures of all species. The system shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the ammonia side, so the percentage rises from 25% to 47% as pressure goes from 100 to 400 atm. Why the others are wrong: Kp is fixed at a given temperature; catalysts lower activation energy; the gases are not liquefied in the reactor. Trap: Assuming a greater yield means a larger equilibrium constant.

qs.q: Why does industry use 400 °C rather than 200 °C, where the yield is far higher?
o: The catalyst does not work at 200 °C
It cut the time to four hours there.
Kp is larger at 400 °C
Kp is larger at 200 °C.
Ammonia is unstable at 200 °C
The equilibrium percentage is highest there.
Equilibrium takes months at 200 °C
Correct: yield without speed is useless.
qs.x: Correct: Thermodynamics favors low temperature, but kinetics does not. Even with a catalyst, reaching equilibrium takes four hours at 200 °C and only 20 minutes at 400 °C. The higher temperature trades some yield for a rate the plant can use. Why the others are wrong: Kp is larger at the lower temperature; the catalyst works there; ammonia's equilibrium share is highest at 200 °C. Trap: Choosing conditions from the equilibrium table alone.

qs.q: Why does removing ammonia as a liquid increase the total amount produced?
o: Liquid ammonia catalyzes the reaction
It has left the gas phase.
Removing ammonia raises Kp
Kp is unchanged at fixed temperature.
The system shifts to replace it
Correct: equilibrium is re-established.
Removing ammonia raises the temperature
Cooling is used to liquefy it.
qs.x: Correct: Taking a product out lowers its partial pressure, so the reaction quotient falls below Kp and the forward reaction proceeds until equilibrium is restored. Repeating this converts far more of the starting gases than a single equilibrium would allow. Why the others are wrong: Kp is a constant at a given temperature; the liquid is removed from the reaction; the gas is cooled, not heated. Trap: Treating a one-time equilibrium percentage as the maximum obtainable yield.

qs.q: How would the catalyst change the time to equilibrium and the yield at 400 °C and 200 atm?
o: Less time and a lower yield
The equilibrium position does not move.
Less time and a higher yield
Yield is set by the equilibrium constant.
Less time, same yield
Correct: it speeds both directions equally.
The same time and a higher yield
A catalyst's role is to speed the approach.
qs.x: Correct: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so it speeds both. Equilibrium arrives sooner but its position, and therefore the percentage of ammonia, is unchanged. Why the others are wrong: Any change in yield would require a change in Kp, which depends only on temperature. Trap: Assuming a catalyst produces more product rather than producing it sooner.

h: Time to reach equilibrium, no catalyst
Time to reach equilibrium, with catalyst

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination are distinct. A stereotype is a belief about the attributes of a group, prejudice is an evaluative attitude toward the group, and discrimination is behavior that treats people differently on the basis of group membership. A person can hold a stereotype without endorsing it, and can behave in a discriminatory way without reporting a hostile attitude.

That last possibility motivated implicit measures. A reaction-time association task infers the strength of a learned association from how quickly a person pairs group labels with evaluative words, on the premise that such associations operate without deliberate control and so escape both self-presentation and introspective limits. Explicit measures, by contrast, ask directly, and are subject to both.

The principle of correspondence predicts how each should behave. Deliberate, considered actions should be predicted better by explicit attitudes, because the person has time to apply what they endorse. Spontaneous, hard-to-monitor behaviors should be predicted better by implicit associations.

Researchers measured explicit attitudes with a questionnaire, implicit associations with a reaction-time task, and four outcomes in 800 adults, then computed the correlation of each outcome with each measure (Table 1).

The pattern is a crossover rather than a contest. The two deliberate, verbal outcomes correlate with the explicit measure at 0.61 and 0.52 and with the implicit score near 0.15, while the two spontaneous nonverbal outcomes reverse that, which is what correspondence predicts and which neither measure would produce on its own.

Several things the table does not settle matter. All of these are correlations in a single cross-sectional sample, so nothing here shows that changing an association would change a behavior; only manipulating the association could. The table also gives no information about the test-retest reliability of the implicit measure, a standing criticism of it, and a measure that is unstable over weeks cannot support claims about enduring individual differences even when it predicts behavior on the day of testing.

qs.q: What pattern do the correlations in Table 1 show?
o: The two measures are interchangeable indices of the same attitude
Their correlations diverge sharply.
Explicit self-report measures are without predictive value
They reach 0.61 here.
The implicit score predicts every outcome better than the explicit measure
It predicts the verbal outcomes worse.
Each measure predicts the kind of behavior that matches it
Correct: deliberate with explicit, spontaneous with implicit.
qs.x: Correct: Deliberate verbal outcomes correlate with the explicit measure near 0.5 to 0.6 and with the implicit score near 0.15, while spontaneous nonverbal outcomes reverse the pattern, a crossover that matches the correspondence principle. Why the others are wrong: The implicit score is the weaker predictor for the verbal outcomes, the divergence rules out interchangeability, and the explicit measure is the stronger predictor twice. Trap: Treating the question as asking which measure is better overall.

qs.q: Which of the outcomes measured is best described as discrimination?
o: The score on the reaction-time association task
That is a measure, not behavior.
The chosen seating distance in a waiting room
Correct: it is behavior toward a person.
Self-reported willingness to befriend someone
That is a reported attitude.
Agreement with an item describing a group's attributes
That is a stereotype endorsement.
qs.x: Correct: Discrimination is differential behavior toward people on the basis of group membership, and physically placing oneself further away is such a behavior, whereas the other three are self-reports or a laboratory index. Why the others are wrong: Reported willingness is an attitude, the association score is a measure of a presumed association, and endorsing attributes is stereotyping. Trap: Classifying by how negative the content sounds rather than by whether it is behavior.

qs.q: Which standing criticism of implicit measures do these data leave untouched?
o: Whether the measure is stable when a person is retested
Correct: no repeated testing was done.
Whether it relates to nonverbal behavior specifically
Seating and eye contact address this.
Whether the measure predicts any kind of behavior at all
Two correlations near 0.4 address this.
Whether it diverges from what people report explicitly
The crossover addresses this.
qs.x: Correct: Test-retest reliability requires measuring the same people twice, and this study measured each participant once, so the criticism that implicit scores fluctuate from session to session is neither supported nor answered here. Why the others are wrong: Predictive validity, divergence from explicit measures and relevance to nonverbal behavior are each addressed by at least one column of the table. Trap: Picking a criticism the data in fact speak to because it is the most familiar one.

qs.q: Which correlation in Table 1 is the largest in absolute value?
o: Implicit with the hiring recommendation.
Implicit with seating distance.
Explicit with the hiring recommendation.
Correct: explicit attitude with willingness to befriend.
qs.x: Correct: The largest value in the table is 0.61, the correlation between the explicit measure and self-reported willingness to befriend, which is unsurprising because both are verbal self-reports made in the same session. Why the others are wrong: 0.52 is the next largest, 0.43 is the strongest implicit correlation, and 0.19 is one of the weakest. Trap: Choosing the largest implicit correlation because the implicit measure is the novel one.

qs.q: Which change to the design would permit a causal claim?
o: Add a third and a fourth nonverbal behavioral outcome
More outcomes, still correlational.
Increase the sample from the 800 adults tested to 2,000 or more
That sharpens estimates only.
Experimentally alter the associations and then measure behavior
Correct: manipulation is required.
Measure explicit attitudes twice rather than once
That addresses reliability.
qs.x: Correct: Every number in the table is a correlation within one sample, so a causal claim requires manipulating the proposed cause, for instance by training a counterstereotypical association and then observing whether the behavior shifts. Why the others are wrong: A larger sample narrows confidence intervals, additional outcomes remain observational, and repeated measurement addresses reliability rather than causation. Trap: Mistaking a more precise correlation for evidence of cause.

r: Hiring recommendation on a rated form
Seating distance chosen in a waiting room
Duration of eye contact during conversation

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Obedience research asks what makes an ordinary person carry out instructions that harm someone else. In the standard paradigm a participant is told to deliver increasing electric shocks to another person who is in fact a confederate and receives none, and the measure is the fraction who continue to the maximum level on the generator.

Two accounts compete. A dispositional account locates obedience in the person, so the people who continue would be unusually callous. A situational account locates it in the features of the setting: the physical presence of a legitimate authority, the distance of the victim, the absence of visible dissent, and a graded sequence of requests in which each step is barely worse than the one before. The experimental strategy is therefore to hold the task constant and vary one situational feature at a time.
Participants were drawn from the same community sample and randomly assigned across five variations, each identical to the baseline procedure except in the feature named (Table 1).

Every manipulation moved the rate, and the largest single drop, to 10%, came from watching two other apparently ordinary participants refuse. Making the victim visible cut obedience by 25 points, and removing either the authority's presence or the authority's legitimacy produced similar rates near 20%, which suggests that presence and legitimacy contribute in comparable measure.

What the design can and cannot show is worth separating. Random assignment across variations licenses causal claims about the situational features. The design says nothing, however, about which individuals obey, because personality was not measured; the finding is that the rate is movable, not that dispositions are irrelevant. The procedure also depends on participants believing the shocks were real, and it deliberately imposed severe distress, which is why review boards would not approve it today and why replications use milder analogues.

qs.q: Which variation produced the largest reduction in obedience?
o: Instructions come from an ordinary person rather than an authority
That gives 20%.
Two confederates refuse to continue
Correct: the rate falls to 10%.
The authority gives instructions by telephone
That gives 21%.
The victim is seated in the same room as the participant
That gives 40%.
qs.x: Correct: The dissenting-confederates condition yields 10%, the lowest in the table, a 55-point drop from baseline, indicating that visible refusal by peers is the most powerful of the features varied. Why the others are wrong: Victim proximity leaves 40%, and the two conditions that remove the authority's presence or legitimacy both leave about 20%. Trap: Choosing the condition that sounds most dramatic rather than reading the column.

qs.q: What do the five variations taken together support?
o: The people who continue are unusually cruel individuals
No disposition was measured.
Obedience to authority cannot be studied experimentally
These are experiments.
Obedience is fixed by stable features of personality
Personality was never varied.
Situational features substantially determine the rate
Correct: each manipulation moved it.
qs.x: Correct: Holding the task constant and varying one feature at a time moved obedience from 65% to as low as 10%, which establishes that the rate depends heavily on the circumstances rather than on who happened to be recruited. Why the others are wrong: Personality was neither manipulated nor measured, so claims about cruel individuals are unsupported, and the table is itself the product of experiments. Trap: Concluding that dispositions do not matter when the study simply did not measure them.

qs.q: Why is the condition with an ordinary person giving instructions informative?
o: It separates legitimacy from the instruction itself
Correct: the orders are the same.
It proves that the authority's presence is entirely irrelevant
Removing presence also lowered the rate.
It provides a measure of how distressed the victim appeared
The victim's behavior was held constant.
It demonstrates that no one obeys instructions from anybody
One in five still continued.
qs.x: Correct: The same instructions are given by someone with no claim to authority, so the 20% rate shows that it is the authority's legitimacy, rather than the content of the orders, that carries most of the baseline obedience. Why the others are wrong: A fifth of participants still complied, the telephone condition shows presence matters too, and the victim's scripted behavior did not change. Trap: Reading a reduction as abolition.

qs.q: Which concept best explains why a present, legitimate authority raises obedience?
o: Participants had not understood the task instructions
The task was explained clearly.
The authority is physically compelling compliance
No force was used in the procedure.
Responsibility is shifted to the authority
Correct: the participant becomes an instrument.
Participants find delivering shocks intrinsically rewarding
Participants showed distress.
qs.x: Correct: In the presence of an authority who accepts responsibility for the outcome, participants come to see themselves as carrying out another person's plan rather than as the agent of the harm, which lowers the felt cost of continuing. Why the others are wrong: Participants were visibly distressed rather than gratified, no physical coercion occurred, and the instructions were understood. Trap: Looking for a motive to harm when the mechanism is a reassignment of responsibility.

qs.q: What would these data not establish?
o: That visible dissent by peers reduces obedience sharply
The rate falls to 10%.
That victim proximity reduces the rate of obedience
The table shows a 25-point drop.
That the legitimacy of the authority affects compliance
The no-authority condition shows it.
Which individuals are most likely to comply
Correct: no person-level variable was measured.
qs.x: Correct: Every variation manipulated the situation, and no characteristic of the participants was measured, so the study cannot say which kinds of people obey even though it establishes a great deal about which circumstances produce obedience. Why the others are wrong: Proximity, dissent and legitimacy were each manipulated with random assignment and each moved the rate. Trap: Assuming a well-designed experiment answers every question one might ask of its topic.

h: Share continuing to the maximum shock
r: Baseline, authority present, victim in another room
Victim seated in the same room
Instructions given by an ordinary person, no authority

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: The presence of others changes performance, and the direction depends on the task. Social facilitation is the improvement seen on simple or well-learned tasks when others are present; impairment appears on complex or novel tasks. Zajonc's account is that the presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant. On a well-practiced task the dominant response is the correct one, so performance improves; on a novel task the dominant responses are errors, so performance worsens.

Social loafing is a different phenomenon that is easily confused with it. Loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when contributions are pooled and no one's output can be identified, and its remedy is making individual contributions visible, which is close to the opposite of removing an audience.

Participants completed two tasks either alone in a cubicle or at a desk observed by two silent confederates, with task and audience condition crossed so that each cell had a separate group of participants. Scores are percent correct (Table 1).

The crossover is the result. An audience adds 9 points to typing and removes 15 points from the logic puzzle, so the effect of being watched reverses with the nature of the task, which no account positing a single direction of effect can produce.

Arousal was not measured, and that is the gap. The arousal account predicts the crossover, but so does an account in which an audience consumes attention that complex tasks require and simple ones do not, and these data cannot distinguish them. Recording heart rate or skin conductance would show whether arousal rose, and manipulating how much attention the audience demanded, for instance by having observers face away, would separate the two. The between-groups design also means that differences between the people assigned to each cell contribute to the variance, and a within-subject design would be more sensitive if practice effects could be controlled.

qs.q: Why does an audience help typing and hurt the logic puzzle?
o: Arousal strengthens whichever response is dominant
Correct: dominant responses differ by task.
Arousal improves performance on any task at all
The puzzle score fell by 15 points.
An audience distracts only while people are typing
Typing improved with an audience.
Logic puzzles require no attention to solve
They require a great deal.
qs.x: Correct: Raised arousal favors the dominant response, which is correct typing for a practiced skill and an error for an unfamiliar puzzle, so the same increase in arousal moves the two scores in opposite directions. Why the others are wrong: Puzzles are attention-demanding, arousal did not help in both cases, and the typing score rose rather than fell. Trap: Looking for a single direction of effect when the account predicts a reversal.

qs.q: How does social loafing differ from social facilitation?
o: It occurs only when a task is simple
Loafing is not task-specific in that way.
It concerns pooled effort that cannot be identified
Correct: identifiability, not observation.
It requires an audience to be watching closely
Watching is what reduces loafing.
It describes an improvement in the group's performance
It describes reduced individual effort.
qs.x: Correct: Loafing arises when individual contributions are merged and unidentifiable, so effort falls; the remedy is making each person's output visible, which is nearly the opposite of removing observers. Why the others are wrong: Loafing is not confined to simple tasks, it involves reduced rather than improved output, and close observation reduces it. Trap: Grouping the two phenomena because both involve other people.

qs.q: Which measurement would best distinguish the arousal account from an attention account?
o: The time each participant spent on the task
That is an effort measure.
The number of observers present in the room
That varies the manipulation.
Physiological arousal recorded during each task
Correct: it tests the proposed mediator.
Participants' ratings of how much they liked the task
That indexes preference.
qs.x: Correct: The arousal account specifies an intervening physiological state, so recording heart rate or skin conductance tests whether that state actually rose, while an attention account predicts the same behavioral crossover without it. Why the others are wrong: Adding observers strengthens the manipulation without identifying the mechanism, and time on task and task liking are not the mediator either account proposes. Trap: Strengthening the manipulation instead of measuring the mediator.

qs.q: How could the puzzle result be reduced in a workplace?
o: Add more observers to the room during the task
That strengthens the effect.
Require that the task be done in public first
That is the impairing condition.
Increase the time pressure on the task as well
That raises arousal further.
Allow practice before anyone is observed
Correct: practice makes the correct response dominant.
qs.x: Correct: Impairment occurs because errors are dominant on an unfamiliar task, so practicing until the correct response is dominant converts the audience effect from a cost into a benefit. Why the others are wrong: Public performance of a novel task, added time pressure and additional observers all intensify the impairment. Trap: Treating the effect as something to be endured rather than as something practice removes.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the logic puzzle was novel?
o: Novel tasks cannot be scored for their accuracy at all
This one was scored.
Novelty removes arousal from the situation
Novelty does not remove arousal.
Novelty makes incorrect responses the dominant ones
Correct: that is what arousal amplifies.
Novel tasks are easier than practiced tasks
They are harder.
qs.x: Correct: The account turns on which response is dominant, and on an unfamiliar task the most readily available responses are wrong, which is why raised arousal lowers the score. Why the others are wrong: The puzzle was scored, novel tasks are harder rather than easier, and novelty does not eliminate arousal. Trap: Treating novelty as a feature of the measure rather than of the response hierarchy.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the cytotoxic effects of a novel chemotherapeutic agent on a human breast cancer cell line. Cells were exposed to varying concentrations of the drug (0, 10, 20, 40, and 80 µM) for 48 hours, after which cell viability was assessed using an MTT assay. The results, expressed as a percentage of the untreated control, are summarized in Table 1. The standard deviation for each concentration reflects the variability observed across three independent experiments. The data suggest a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration (80 µM) reducing viability to 20 % of the control. These findings support further investigation of the drug’s therapeutic potential and warrant additional studies to elucidate its mechanism of action.

qs.q: What is the cell viability at a drug concentration of 20 µM?
o: Not the best answer
Correct
Not the best answer
Not the best answer
qs.x: The table shows that at 20 µM the viability is 70 % of the untreated control. Trap: Option A (45 %) corresponds to the 40 µM concentration, which could mislead readers who overlook the concentration‑viability pairing.

qs.q: Which control would best distinguish an effect of the drug from an effect of the solvent used to dissolve it?
o: A vehicle control containing the solvent used to dissolve the drug.
Correct
A positive control using a known cytotoxic agent.
Not the best answer
A negative control with no cells.
Not the best answer
A time‑zero control measuring viability immediately after drug addition.
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: A) A vehicle control receives the solvent alone, so any change in viability beyond it is due to the drug. Why the others are wrong: B) A positive control checks that the assay can detect cytotoxicity but does not separate drug from solvent. C) A no-cell blank corrects background absorbance. D) A time-zero control sets the starting viability, not the solvent effect. Trap: Choosing a positive control because it validates the assay, even though only a vehicle-only control isolates the solvent effect.

qs.q: What is the percent decrease in viability from the control to the 80 µM concentration?
o: Not the best answer
Not the best answer
Correct
Not the best answer
qs.x: The control is 100 %. At 80 µM viability is 20 %, so the decrease is 100 % – 20 % = 80 %. Trap: Option B (50 %) might be chosen by students who mistakenly calculate the difference between 70 % (20 µM) and 20 % (80 µM) instead of comparing to the control.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is FALSE?
o: The viability decreases as drug concentration increases.
Not the best answer
The standard deviation increases with higher drug concentrations.
Not the best answer
The 10 µM concentration shows a lower viability than the 20 µM concentration.
Correct
The 0 µM concentration serves as the control and is set to 100 % viability.
Not the best answer
qs.x: Viability falls with dose (100, 85, 70, 45, 20 %) and the SD rises monotonically (2, 3, 4, 5, 6), so A, B and D are true. C is false because 10 µM (85 %) has higher, not lower, viability than 20 µM (70 %). Trap: Option B looks suspicious because of the word 'increases', but the SD does increase at every step (2 to 6).

qs.q: Assuming viability falls linearly between the 20 µM and 40 µM points, at about what concentration would viability be 50% of control?
o: 25 µM
Not the best answer
30 µM
Not the best answer
36 µM
Correct
40 µM
Not the best answer
qs.x: Correct: C) Between 20 and 40 µM viability falls from 70% to 45%, or 1.25 percentage points per µM; dropping from 70% to 50% needs 16 µM, so about 36 µM. Why the others are wrong: A) 25 µM would give about 64%. B) 30 µM would give about 58%. D) 40 µM gives 45%, which is below 50%. Trap: Picking 40 µM because 45% is the closest tabulated value, without interpolating between the 20 and 40 µM points.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Social capital refers to the resources a person can draw on through social relationships. The distinction that matters for outcomes is between two kinds. Bonding capital links people who are alike, typically within a family, a congregation or a block, and supplies trust, mutual aid and informal insurance. Bridging capital links people across groups and supplies what a closed circle cannot: information from outside, contacts in other institutions, and routes into labor markets a neighborhood is not already connected to.

The two kinds are not substitutes, and a neighborhood can be high on one and low on the other. A tight community with no outside links is rich in support and poor in access, which predicts resilience without mobility; a neighborhood whose residents have many outside contacts but little internal cohesion may have access without the trust needed to act collectively.

Investigators followed 90 neighborhoods in one metropolitan area for five years. Bonding and bridging indices were built from resident surveys at baseline, neighborhoods were grouped by whether each index fell above or below the metropolitan median, and the change in the employment rate over the five years was recorded from administrative data (Table 1).

Bridging is what moves employment: the two high-bridging groups gain 2.9 and 4.1 points while the high-bonding, low-bridging group is flat at 0.4. Bonding is not useless, though, because adding it to high bridging raises the gain from 2.9 to 4.1, which is consistent with internal trust helping a neighborhood act on outside information.

Nothing was assigned here. Neighborhoods were classified on characteristics they already had, and the kind of place that develops outside ties is also likely to differ in transit access, in the age and education of its residents, and in how far it sits from areas where employment was growing anyway. A measure of the pathway would help: if bridging capital works through information, then counting job referrals received by residents would show the mechanism directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the employment column.

qs.q: Which kind of capital best predicts employment gains in Table 1?
o: Bridging capital, the ties that link across groups
Correct: both high-bridging groups gained most.
Neither index showed any relationship to employment
The spread is 5.2 points.
Both indices contributed in equal measure here
Bridging accounts for most of it.
Bonding capital on its own, without outside ties
That group was nearly flat.
qs.x: Correct: The two high-bridging groups gained 2.9 and 4.1 points while the high-bonding, low-bridging group gained only 0.4, so bridging is doing most of the work, with bonding adding to it when bridging is already present. Why the others are wrong: Bonding alone was nearly flat, the groups differ widely, and the two indices are not equal contributors. Trap: Splitting the difference when the table clearly favors one index.

qs.q: What does bonding capital typically supply?
o: Access to institutions outside the neighborhood
That is bridging capital.
Formal authority over local decisions
That is political office.
A household's own financial assets
That is individual wealth.
Support and mutual aid within a group
Correct: trust among people who are alike.
qs.x: Correct: Bonding ties connect similar people and provide trust, informal help and a kind of mutual insurance, which is why high-bonding neighborhoods are resilient even when their employment is not improving. Why the others are wrong: Outside access is what bridging ties supply, formal authority is a feature of institutions, and personal assets are not a form of social capital at all. Trap: Equating any beneficial resource with social capital.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects a causal reading of these results?
o: The follow-up period extended over five years
Five years is appropriate here.
Ninety neighborhoods were followed for the study
That is a reasonable number.
Neighborhoods were classified, not assigned, by type
Correct: selection, not assignment.
Employment change was taken from administrative tax records
Records are the stronger source.
qs.x: Correct: A neighborhood's position on the two indices reflects everything about its history and location, so places with high bridging capital may differ in transit, education and proximity to growing employment, any of which could produce the gradient. Why the others are wrong: Administrative records are a strength, and the sample size and follow-up period are adequate for the comparison. Trap: Looking for a flaw in the measurement when the problem is in the assignment.

qs.q: Which type of neighborhood lost employment over the five years?
o: Low bonding with high bridging capital
That group gained 2.9.
The neighborhoods low on both indices
Correct: a 1.1-point decline.
High bonding with low bridging capital
That group gained 0.4.
High on both of the two indices
That group gained 4.1.
qs.x: Correct: Only the neighborhoods low on both indices declined, by 1.1 points, which fits an account in which neither internal trust nor outside access was available to buffer a labor-market shock. Why the others are wrong: Each of the other three types gained, by 0.4, 2.9 and 4.1 points respectively. Trap: Reading the smallest gain as a loss.

qs.q: Which additional measure would best show the pathway by which bridging capital acts?
o: The average number of years residents had lived there
That indexes stability.
The median housing price within each neighborhood
That indexes affluence.
The total number of residents in each neighborhood
That is a size measure.
The number of job referrals residents received
Correct: it measures the information flow.
qs.x: Correct: The proposed mechanism is access to information and contacts from outside, so counting referrals received puts the intervening step on the table instead of inferring it from the employment outcome it is meant to explain. Why the others are wrong: Residential tenure, housing price and population size are neighborhood characteristics rather than measures of information reaching residents. Trap: Adding a reasonable control variable instead of measuring the mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Environmental justice research examines whether environmental hazards and benefits are distributed unevenly across groups. Two explanations are debated. In the siting explanation, polluting facilities are built in neighborhoods with less political power. In the move-in explanation, housing near existing facilities is cheaper, so lower-income households move there afterward. The two can be separated only by data that record the order of events.

Researchers linked the locations of 1,100 industrial facilities that report toxic releases to census data for the surrounding tracts across three decades. For each facility, they recorded the characteristics of its tract in the decade before it opened and in the two decades after. They also measured ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and, from a state health registry, the rate of childhood asthma emergency visits (Table 1).

To check that the comparison tracts were reasonable, the researchers matched each facility tract to a tract in the same metropolitan area with similar population density and distance from the city center, since both affect land cost and the kinds of businesses that locate there. They also repeated the analysis using only facilities that opened in the middle decade, so that a full decade of data was available on each side of the opening, and the pattern was unchanged. Facilities that had closed during the study period were analyzed separately; disparities in those tracts persisted after closure, although PM2.5 in them fell toward the level of the comparison tracts within a few years of closure.

The researchers noted that income and demographic composition in these tracts were already different from comparison tracts before siting and changed only modestly afterward. They also noted that tracts were not assigned at random, that asthma has other causes including indoor allergens and secondhand smoke, and that people who live in a tract today may have moved there recently.

qs.q: What do the before-siting figures most directly address?
o: Whether the facilities comply with regulations
Compliance was not studied.
Whether PM2.5 causes asthma
Air measurements are separate.
Whether residents support the facilities
Opinion was not surveyed.
Whether disparities came before the facilities
Correct: they test the move-in explanation.
qs.x: Correct: If disparities appeared only after siting, the move-in explanation would be supported. The data show that tracts chosen for facilities already had lower income, lower homeownership and a higher share of residents of color a decade before, which points to siting rather than later in-migration. Why the others are wrong: Causation of asthma, resident opinion and regulatory compliance are different questions. Trap: Treating any disparity as evidence for a particular explanation without the timing data.

qs.q: Why is the modest change after siting important?
o: It argues against later turnover
Correct: composition barely shifted.
It shows the facilities later closed
Closure was not reported.
It shows residents were unaffected
Exposure and asthma rates differ.
It proves the facilities cause poverty
Income was already low before siting.
qs.x: Correct: The move-in explanation predicts that a tract's composition changes substantially after a facility opens. Income went from 71% to 68% of the state median and the share of residents of color from 46% to 52%, changes too small to account for the gap, which existed beforehand. Why the others are wrong: The income gap preceded siting; exposure and health measures do differ; nothing is said about closures. Trap: Reading a small change as no effect on residents.

qs.q: What most limits the conclusion that facility emissions cause the higher asthma rate?
o: The study covered three decades
A long period strengthens it.
Tracts differ in other asthma risks
Correct: confounding by housing and smoke exposure.
PM2.5 was measured in both groups
That is a strength.
Asthma visits came from a health registry
Registry data are reasonably objective.
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods differ in housing quality, indoor allergens, secondhand smoke exposure and access to care, all of which affect asthma. Without accounting for these, the difference between 34 and 19 visits per 1,000 cannot be attributed to emissions alone. Why the others are wrong: Measuring exposure in both groups, using registry data and following three decades all improve the study. Trap: Choosing a design feature that strengthens the study when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: Which concept best describes the pattern the siting explanation proposes?
o: Voluntary residential mobility
That describes moving between neighborhoods.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: routine decisions produce unequal outcomes.
The sick role in affected families
That describes expectations for people who are ill.
Stereotype threat among residents
That concerns performance under a negative stereotype.
qs.x: Correct: Institutional discrimination refers to unequal outcomes produced by the ordinary policies and procedures of organizations, such as siting decisions that follow land cost and local political capacity, without requiring individual prejudice. Why the others are wrong: Stereotype threat concerns test performance; residential mobility is what the move-in explanation describes; the sick role concerns the social expectations of illness. Trap: Assuming unequal outcomes require someone's intent.

qs.q: Which additional measurement would best strengthen the link between emissions and asthma?
o: Total number of facilities in the state
A count does not link exposure to health.
Average income in the state as a whole
A statewide figure adds no comparison.
The number of workers each facility employs
Employment is a separate outcome.
Asthma rates before and after opening
Correct: a within-tract comparison.
qs.x: Correct: Comparing asthma rates in the same tracts before and after a facility opened holds constant the many fixed features of each neighborhood, so a rise that follows openings is much harder to explain by pre-existing differences. Why the others are wrong: Facility counts, statewide income and employment figures do not connect exposure to health within the same population. Trap: Adding data that describe the setting instead of testing the relationship.

h: Tracts that later received a facility, decade before siting
Tracts with a facility, two decades after
r: Median household income (% of state median)
Residents who are people of color (%)

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: The demographic transition describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. In stage 1, both are high and population grows slowly. In stage 2, death rates fall first, usually because of clean water, sanitation and vaccination, while birth rates stay high, so population grows rapidly. In stage 3, birth rates fall as child survival improves, women gain education and employment, and families move to cities where children cost more to raise. In stage 4, both rates are low and growth is slow. Some countries have entered a stage in which births fall below deaths and the population shrinks without immigration.

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. A TFR of about 2.1 is replacement level in countries with low child mortality. Even when fertility falls to replacement, a population keeps growing for decades because a large share of it is young and entering childbearing years, an effect called population momentum.

These measures have limits. The crude birth and death rates depend on a population's age structure, so a country with many older residents can show a high death rate even when people there live long lives: Country D's rate of 12 per 1,000 reflects its age structure rather than poor health. Comparing countries fairly often requires age-adjusted rates or measures such as life expectancy at birth. The TFR has its own limitation, because it describes the rates of one year rather than the completed families of any real group of women. If fertility is falling, the TFR of a given year underestimates how many children women who are young that year will eventually have.

Country A built its first national vaccination program 15 years ago, and its death rate has fallen from 20 per 1,000 over that period. Country D's population declined by 0.3% last year despite net immigration of 2 per 1,000.

qs.q: What is the rate of natural increase in Country A, per 1,000?
o: This divides them.
This is the death rate.
Correct: 38 − 12.
This adds the two rates.
qs.x: Correct: Natural increase is the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, here 38 − 12 = 26 per 1,000, or 2.6% per year, excluding migration. Why the others are wrong: The rates are not added or divided, and 12 is the death rate alone. Trap: Confusing natural increase with total population change, which also includes migration.

qs.q: Which country best fits stage 2 of the transition?
o: Country C
Both rates are low.
Country B
Its birth rate has already fallen substantially.
Country A
Correct: falling deaths with still-high births.
Country D
Deaths exceed births.
qs.x: Correct: Country A's death rate has dropped from 20 to 12 per 1,000 since vaccination began, while its birth rate remains at 38. That gap produces rapid growth and a very young population, 44% under 15. Why the others are wrong: Country B is mid-transition, Country C has completed it, and Country D is beyond it. Trap: Classifying a country by its growth rate alone rather than by which rate is changing.

qs.q: Why would Country B keep growing for decades even if its TFR fell to 2.1 next year?
o: Its young cohort has yet to have children
Correct: population momentum.
Replacement fertility causes population growth
It leads to a stable size eventually.
Fertility rates cannot fall that quickly
Several countries have done so.
Its death rate would rise immediately
Death rates change slowly.
qs.x: Correct: Thirty percent of Country B's population is under 15. As that cohort enters childbearing age, the number of births stays high even at replacement fertility, so the population continues to grow until the age structure evens out. Why the others are wrong: Replacement fertility eventually stabilizes a population; death rates respond slowly; rapid fertility declines have occurred. Trap: Assuming replacement fertility means an immediate end to growth.

qs.q: What is the most likely consequence of Country D's age structure?
o: A rapidly rising birth rate
The TFR is 1.3.
More retirees per working adult
Correct: 28% over 64 against 13% under 15.
A growing labor force over the next decade
Few young people are entering it.
A falling median age
The median age is rising.
qs.x: Correct: With more than twice as many people over 64 as under 15, the number of workers supporting each retiree falls, which strains pension and health systems. This is why some countries in this position encourage immigration or later retirement. Why the others are wrong: The small young cohort limits labor force growth; the TFR is well below replacement; the median age rises as the population ages. Trap: Expecting low fertility to correct itself quickly.

qs.q: Why can Country D's population shrink despite net immigration?
o: Immigration lowers the birth rate
Immigrants often raise it.
Its death rate is the highest shown
Country A also has 12.
Emigration is not counted in net immigration
Net figures include both directions.
Deaths exceed births by more than 2
Correct: −3 per 1,000 against +2.
qs.x: Correct: Natural change is 9 − 12 = −3 per 1,000. Adding net immigration of 2 per 1,000 leaves about −1 per 1,000, or roughly the 0.3% decline reported once rounding is considered. Why the others are wrong: Immigration tends to add people of childbearing age; Country A has the same death rate; a net figure already accounts for departures. Trap: Assuming any immigration is enough to prevent decline.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute in a liquid lowers its vapor pressure, raises its boiling point and lowers its freezing point. These are colligative properties: they depend on the number of dissolved particles, not on what the particles are. The changes are ΔTb = iKb·m and ΔTf = iKf·m, where m is molality, Kb and Kf are constants of the solvent, and i is the van 't Hoff factor, the number of particles each formula unit produces in solution. For water, Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol and Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol.
Osmotic pressure follows Π = iMRT, where M is molarity. Because it can be large even for dilute solutions, it is the colligative property used to measure the molar mass of proteins.
Students measured freezing points of aqueous solutions, each prepared at 0.100 mol of solute per kilogram of water (Table 1).

Colligative properties are at work in several familiar situations. Salt spread on an icy road lowers the freezing point of the water film, so ice melts at temperatures below 0 °C. Antifreeze in a car both lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the coolant. In the body, the osmotic pressure set by plasma proteins pulls fluid back into capillaries at their venous end, and a low plasma protein level allows fluid to accumulate in the tissues as edema. Each of these depends on the number of dissolved particles rather than on their chemical identity, which is why the van 't Hoff factor matters so much for ionic solutes.

The students noted that the apparent values of i for the salts fall short of the whole numbers predicted from their formulas. In concentrated solutions, oppositely charged ions spend part of their time close together as ion pairs and behave as fewer particles. At 0.0010 mol/kg, the apparent i for NaCl rose to 1.97.

qs.q: Why does 0.100 mol/kg NaCl lower the freezing point more than the same amount of glucose?
o: Sodium chloride has a larger molar mass
Molar mass does not enter the equation.
Glucose evaporates from the solution
Glucose is nonvolatile.
Ionic solutes bind water more tightly
Binding strength is not what the law describes.
Each formula unit gives two particles
Correct: colligative effects count particles.
qs.x: Correct: NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so a 0.100 molal solution contains close to 0.200 mol of particles per kilogram. Glucose stays as one particle, so its freezing point depression is roughly half as large. Why the others are wrong: Colligative properties do not depend on the identity or mass of the particles; the equations count particles rather than interactions; glucose does not evaporate. Trap: Comparing masses when the law counts particles.

qs.q: What freezing point would 0.100 mol/kg of a solute with i = 3.00 produce?
o: This uses i = 1.
Freezing point is depressed.
This uses 1.00 mol/kg.
qs.x: Correct: ΔTf = iKf·m = 3.00 × 1.86 × 0.100 = 0.558 °C, and because the freezing point is lowered, the solution freezes at −0.558 °C. Why the others are wrong: Using i = 1 ignores dissociation; 5.58 uses a tenfold higher concentration; the freezing point goes down, not up. Trap: Reporting the size of the change as if it were the temperature.

qs.q: Why is the apparent i for MgCl₂ 2.70 rather than 3.00?
o: The measurement was taken too early
The same pattern appears for NaCl.
The formula produces only two ions
It gives Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻.
Some ions remain paired in solution
Correct: paired ions act as one particle.
MgCl₂ does not dissolve completely
It is soluble in water.
qs.x: Correct: In solution, Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ attract each other, and some spend part of the time associated. A paired cation and anion lower the freezing point as a single particle, so the effective number of particles is below three. The effect is stronger for Mg²⁺ because of its higher charge. Why the others are wrong: MgCl₂ is soluble; the formula gives three ions; the deviation is systematic across the salts. Trap: Assuming complete dissociation always means the full whole-number value.

qs.q: What does the rise of NaCl's apparent i to 1.97 at 0.0010 mol/kg show?
o: Dilution increases the number of ions
The number per kilogram falls.
Ion pairing weakens as the solution is diluted
Correct: ions meet less often.
The constant Kf changes with concentration
It is a property of the solvent.
Sodium chloride dissociates more at low temperature
Temperature is not the variable.
qs.x: Correct: In a dilute solution, ions are farther apart and spend less time paired, so the measured behavior approaches the ideal value of 2. Colligative equations describe ideal solutions, which real solutions approach as they are diluted. Why the others are wrong: Dilution lowers the number of particles per kilogram; Kf depends on the solvent; the comparison varies concentration. Trap: Reading a higher apparent i as more solute dissolving.

qs.q: Why is osmotic pressure the preferred colligative property for finding a protein's molar mass?
o: Proteins cannot be dissolved in water
Many are soluble.
Osmotic pressure does not depend on particle number
It does, through iM.
Dilute protein still gives usable pressure
Correct: the other changes are too small.
Proteins lower the freezing point most of all
Their molar mass makes molality tiny.
qs.x: Correct: A protein's large molar mass means even a few grams per liter give a very low molality, so the freezing point change would be thousandths of a degree and hard to measure. Osmotic pressure for the same solution is large enough to read on a simple column of liquid. Why the others are wrong: Proteins dissolve; osmotic pressure depends on particle concentration; a tiny molality produces a tiny freezing point change. Trap: Assuming a large molecule produces a large colligative effect.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers investigated the antibacterial activity of a novel amphipathic peptide, designated AP‑42, against *Escherichia coli* cultured under controlled laboratory conditions. The study employed a factorial design with two independent variables: peptide concentration (0, 5, 10, 20, 40 µg/mL) and medium pH (5.5, 7.0, 8.5). For each treatment combination, bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD600) over a 24‑hour period, and the maximum specific growth rate (μmax) was calculated from the exponential phase. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a dose‑dependent inhibition of growth at neutral and alkaline pH, whereas acidic pH attenuates the peptide’s efficacy. The authors concluded that AP‑42 exhibits potent antibacterial activity, particularly at pH 7.0 and 8.5, and suggested its potential as a therapeutic agent for infections in body sites with neutral to slightly alkaline pH. The data also raise questions about the peptide’s mechanism of action and its stability across pH ranges.

qs.q: Which peptide concentration at pH 7.0 produced the lowest μmax?
o: 5 µg/mL
5 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL; growth falls as concentration rises.
10 µg/mL
10 µg/mL still allowed more growth than the highest concentration.
20 µg/mL
20 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL.
40 µg/mL
Correct
qs.x: At pH 7.0 the μmax values decrease with increasing peptide concentration. The lowest μmax (0.15 h⁻¹) occurs at the highest concentration tested, 40 µg/mL. Trap: Option C (20 µg/mL) is tempting because it also shows a marked reduction, but it is not the lowest.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
o: Randomized controlled trial
No participants were randomized to treatment and control arms in a clinical sense; two factors were varied in combination.
Factorial design
Correct
Cohort study
A cohort study follows a group over time without manipulating variables.
Case‑control study
A case-control study compares groups chosen by outcome, which isn't what was done here.
qs.x: The investigators varied two independent variables (peptide concentration and pH) simultaneously and measured the outcome for each combination, which is the hallmark of a factorial design. Trap: Option A is plausible because the study involved controlled conditions, but it is not a randomized trial.

qs.q: If the μmax at 10 µg/mL and pH 7.0 is 0.45 h⁻¹, what is the percent reduction in μmax compared to the control (0 µg/mL) at the same pH, given the control μmax is 1.20 h⁻¹?
o: 25% would leave a μmax of 0.90 h⁻¹, not 0.45.
37.5% is the fraction remaining (0.45 ÷ 1.20), not the reduction.
50% would leave 0.60 h⁻¹, not 0.45.
Correct
qs.x: Reduction = (1.20 – 0.45)/1.20 = 0.75/1.20 = 0.625 = 62.5%. Trap: Option C (50%) is a common mis‑calculation if the difference is divided by the treated value instead of the control.

qs.q: Which statement is most likely incorrect regarding the peptide’s activity?
o: Activity is enhanced at higher pH
This is consistent with the data: the peptide works better at higher pH.
Activity is independent of concentration
Correct
Activity is reduced at acidic pH
This is consistent with the data: acidic pH reduces activity.
Activity is dose‑dependent
This is consistent with the data: more peptide means more inhibition.
qs.x: The data show a clear dose‑dependent inhibition; activity is not independent of concentration. Trap: Option A may seem plausible because the peptide performs best at neutral/alkaline pH, but the statement is true, not false.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best help elucidate the mechanism of action of AP‑42?
o: Determine the peptide’s secondary structure by circular dichroism
Circular dichroism shows the peptide's shape, not what it does to bacteria.
Measure the peptide’s half‑life in serum
Serum half-life is a pharmacokinetic question, not a mechanism question.
Assess the peptide’s effect on bacterial membrane potential
Correct
Evaluate the peptide’s toxicity in mammalian cell lines
Toxicity to mammalian cells is about safety, not how the peptide kills bacteria.
qs.x: Measuring changes in membrane potential directly probes whether the peptide disrupts bacterial membranes, a common antibacterial mechanism for amphipathic peptides. Trap: Option A is useful for structural characterization but does not reveal functional mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Social reproduction describes how advantage is transmitted across generations through schooling, networks, and credentials. Tracking, differential parental involvement, and unequal school resources are proposed channels, and interventions that change one channel may leave others intact.
Investigators followed 3,000 students from entry to graduation across schools with different practices (Table 1).

qs.q: Which practice combination worked best?
o: Open enrollment without staffing
It gave 31% and 64%.
Open enrollment with tutoring
Correct: 44% and 83%.
Open enrollment alone
It gave 38% and 71%.
Tracking by prior score
It gave 14% and 62%.
qs.x: Correct: Opening access and adding support produced both the highest advanced-course participation and the highest graduation rate. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining practice produced lower figures on both measures. Trap: Treating access alone as sufficient.

qs.q: What does the last row add?
o: Staffing is irrelevant
Removing it lowered both measures.
Open enrollment fails
It still beat tracking.
Tracking is preferable
Its figures were lowest.
Access needs resources
Correct: 31% without staffing.
qs.x: Correct: Open enrollment without added staffing produced smaller gains, showing that changing a rule without resources limits the effect. Why the others are wrong: Open enrollment still beat tracking, and staffing clearly mattered. Trap: Reading a weaker result as a failed policy.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
o: Three thousand students
That sample is adequate.
Four practices compared
Four cover the comparison.
Schools chose practices
Correct: no assignment.
Graduation was recorded
Records are objective.
qs.x: Correct: Because schools selected their own practices, school characteristics may explain the differences rather than the practices themselves. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are appropriate. Trap: Reading a multi-school comparison as a randomized trial.

qs.q: Which channel does tracking represent?
o: Network access
Networks were not measured.
School sorting
Correct: placement by prior score.
Credential inflation
Credentials were not studied.
Parental involvement
Parents were not measured.
qs.x: Correct: Tracking is a school practice that sorts students into different curricula, which is an institutional channel. Why the others are wrong: Involvement, networks, and credentials were not measured here. Trap: Naming a channel the study did not examine.

qs.q: Which added measure would test durability?
o: Number of advanced courses
That is participation.
Teacher ratings
That is a process measure.
Outcomes five years later
Correct: beyond graduation.
Course grades that year
That is contemporaneous.
qs.x: Correct: Following students after graduation shows whether the gains persist into later education or work. Why the others are wrong: Grades, course counts, and teacher ratings are measured during school. Trap: Confusing more detail with longer follow-up.

h: Share of low-income students in advanced courses

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Migration is analyzed in terms of push factors at the origin, which drive people to leave, and pull factors at the destination, which attract them. Push factors include conflict, crop failure and unemployment; pull factors include wages, safety and existing networks of earlier migrants. Intervening obstacles, such as distance, cost and legal barriers, determine which of those who want to move actually do.

Two refinements matter. Migration is selective: migrants are typically not a random sample of the origin population but are younger and, for longer moves, better educated, because the costs are paid up front and the returns accrue over a working life. And networks are self-reinforcing, since each earlier migrant lowers the cost of the next move by supplying information, housing and job contacts, which is why flows persist after the original push has eased.
Four origin-destination corridors were compared on the size of the flow and on three correlates measured in the same year (Table 1).

The wage ratio does not order the flows. Corridor Z has the highest ratio at 3.9 and the smallest flow at 2.1 per thousand, while Corridor Y has the lowest ratio at 1.8 and the second largest flow. What does track the flows is the combination of short distance and a high share of households with a prior migrant, which is the obstacles-and-networks account rather than a simple wage account.

Distance and network share are themselves closely related here, since corridors with short distances also have high prior-migrant shares, so the table cannot separate the two: a corridor that is near may send more people simply because moving is cheap, or because its long history of movement has built the networks. A corridor that was distant but had a high network share would distinguish them, and none of the four provides that combination.

The figures are also one year's snapshot of four corridors, so they describe a cross-section rather than a process, and the wage ratio is an average that says nothing about the wages available to the kind of worker who actually migrates.

qs.q: What does Corridor Z most clearly show?
o: Networks are unnecessary for migration to occur
Z has the smallest network share.
Wage ratios are measured with substantial error
Measurement is not the point.
Distance has no relation to migration flows
Z is the most distant and smallest.
A high wage gap need not produce a large flow
Correct: 3.9 with 2.1 per thousand.
qs.x: Correct: Corridor Z combines the largest wage ratio in the table with the smallest flow, which is the clearest demonstration that a wage incentive alone does not determine how many people move. Why the others are wrong: Nothing suggests mismeasurement, Z is consistent with distance mattering rather than not, and its low network share supports the network account. Trap: Reading a counterexample to one factor as evidence against every factor.

qs.q: Why is migration described as selective?
o: Migrants are younger and often better educated
Correct: costs are paid up front.
Destinations choose which applicants to admit
Legal selection is a separate matter.
Only those with networks are permitted to move
Networks lower cost, not permission.
Every member of a household moves together
Households often move in part.
qs.x: Correct: Because the costs of moving are borne immediately and the benefits accumulate over a working life, those with more years of work ahead and more transferable skills are overrepresented among migrants. Why the others are wrong: Admission policy is an obstacle rather than what selectivity means, networks reduce cost without granting permission, and partial household moves are common. Trap: Reading selectivity as selection by the destination.

qs.q: Why can this table not separate distance from networks?
o: Only four corridors appear in the comparison
More corridors of the same kind would not help.
The two move together across all four corridors
Correct: near corridors have dense networks.
Network share was reported by households
Self-report is a lesser concern.
Distance is reported in kilometres rather than hours
Units are not the obstacle.
qs.x: Correct: Every corridor that is close also has a high share of households with a prior migrant, so no contrast exists in which one varies while the other is held constant, and a distant corridor with dense networks is what the table lacks. Why the others are wrong: Units and self-report are minor issues, and adding corridors would not help unless they broke the pairing. Trap: Treating collinearity as a shortage of observations.

qs.q: Why do migration flows often persist after the original push factor eases?
o: Legal barriers fall as flows become established
Barriers often tighten instead.
Push factors never actually ease at the origin
Conflicts and crop failures do end.
Wage gaps widen automatically once a flow begins
Wages are not driven by the flow.
Each earlier migrant lowers the next move's cost
Correct: networks are self-reinforcing.
qs.x: Correct: Earlier migrants supply information, housing and job contacts, so the cost and risk of moving fall for those who follow, and the flow sustains itself once a network exists. Why the others are wrong: Flows do not raise wage gaps, push factors do ease, and legal barriers frequently tighten as flows grow. Trap: Looking for a continuing push when the explanation is a falling cost.

qs.q: Which corridor has the largest annual flow per 1,000 at the origin?
o: 2.1, Corridor Z
The smallest flow.
7.2, Corridor X
The second smallest.
11.9, Corridor Y
The second largest.
18.4, Corridor W
Correct: the largest in the column.
qs.x: Correct: Corridor W sends 18.4 migrants per thousand, the largest flow, and it combines the shortest practical distance with the highest prior-migrant share at 62%.
