Trap: Choosing the theory that names the expressions rather than the rule governing their display.

qs.q: What does this experiment not address?
o: Whether people in the four regions produce expressions alike
Correct: only judgment was measured.
Whether gestures are recognized better within their own region
The table shows 91%.
Whether tone of voice carries information across regions
Accuracy abroad was 68%.
Whether posture alone can convey an emotional state
Accuracy was 72% at home.
qs.x: Correct: Every participant was a judge of stimuli, so the study measures recognition, and it is silent on whether the same situations elicit the same expressions in the four regions, which is where display rules would be expected to act most strongly. Why the others are wrong: Within-region gesture recognition, cross-region tone of voice and posture-only accuracy are each reported in the table. Trap: Assuming a study of one side of a communicative act covers both.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure most strengthens the comparison across stimulus types?
o: Accuracy was the dependent measure in every one of the conditions
A common outcome is necessary but not sufficient.
Participants were drawn from four widely separated regions
That is the sampling, not the control.
All of the participants tested were adults
Age was constant but is not the key.
All participants saw the same stimuli with the same label list
Correct: chance level is held constant.
qs.x: Correct: Because every region saw an identical stimulus set and chose from a fixed list, the chance level and the response demands are the same for all four signal types, so differences in the drop column reflect the signals rather than differences in procedure. Why the others are wrong: Sampling four regions makes the comparison possible without controlling it, a common outcome measure is a prerequisite, and adult samples do not address the comparison across stimulus types. Trap: Naming a sampling decision when the question asks about experimental control.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Attraction is shaped by several well-documented factors. Proximity raises the chance of interaction and of repeated exposure; similarity in attitudes and values supports liking; reciprocity, the perception that liking is returned, strengthens it; and physical attractiveness influences first impressions more than later ones. The mere exposure effect is the finding that repeated encounters with a stimulus increase liking for it, even when the encounters are brief and the stimulus is not consciously noted.

Proximity ordinarily cannot be studied cleanly, because people choose where to live and the choice correlates with everything that also predicts friendship. A setting in which location is assigned by chance removes that problem, which is why housing lotteries are so useful.

Residents of a newly opened apartment building, whose units were assigned by lottery among applicants, were surveyed after one year. For each pair of residents the survey recorded whether each named the other as a friend, and residents also estimated how often they encountered each other in a typical week (Table 1).

The gradient follows the number of encounters closely, from 41% and 12 encounters for adjacent units down to 6% and 1 encounter for units with no shared route, which is what a mechanism based on repeated exposure and opportunity for interaction predicts.

The lottery is what makes this informative, since residents did not choose their neighbors or their position in the building, so the gradient cannot be explained by people who were already similar having selected adjacent units.

Two limits remain. Encounters were estimated by the residents themselves after the friendships had formed, so people may recall more encounters with those they came to like, which would produce the correspondence between the two columns without encounters having caused anything. The design also cannot separate repeated exposure from opportunity for extended conversation, since both rise together with proximity; a condition in which people passed each other often but could not easily talk, as in a busy corridor, would begin to separate them.

qs.q: Why does the lottery strengthen this study?
o: Four relationships between units were compared
That is the design, not the lottery.
Encounters were reported by the residents
That is a weakness rather than a strength.
Neither neighbors nor location was chosen
Correct: selection is removed.
The survey was administered after a full year
Timing is not what the lottery fixes.
qs.x: Correct: Because units were assigned by chance, residents who ended up adjacent are no more similar to one another than residents on different floors, so the friendship gradient cannot be attributed to like people having chosen to live near one another. Why the others are wrong: The one-year interval and the four-way comparison are separate features, and self-reported encounters are a limitation. Trap: Crediting randomization with fixing a measurement problem.

qs.q: Which mechanism do the encounter data most directly support?
o: Perceived reciprocity of liking
Reciprocity was not measured either.
Similarity of attitudes between residents
Attitudes were not measured.
Repeated exposure raising liking
Correct: encounters track friendship closely.
Physical attractiveness of neighbors
No appearance measure was taken.
qs.x: Correct: The only variable measured alongside friendship is the frequency of encounters, which rises from 1 to 12 per week in step with the friendship rate, so exposure is the mechanism these data speak to. Why the others are wrong: Similarity, reciprocity and attractiveness are all plausible influences that this study did not measure at all. Trap: Choosing a known cause of attraction that the study did not assess.

qs.q: Which finding would most complicate the proximity account?
o: Encounter frequency failed to predict friendship
Correct: the proposed route would be broken.
Adjacent residents reported the most friendships
That is the central result.
Few friendships formed across different stairwells
That also fits the account.
Residents sharing a stairwell formed some friendships
That is consistent with the account.
qs.x: Correct: Proximity is supposed to work by producing encounters, so if encounters bore no relation to friendship the gradient would have to be explained some other way, and the mechanism would be in doubt. Why the others are wrong: Stairwell friendships, the adjacency result and the scarcity of cross-stairwell friendships are all predicted by the account. Trap: Picking a result that supports the account because it is the most prominent one.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 isolates the effect of floor separation?
o: Adjacent doors against different stairwells
That varies everything at once.
Same floor four doors apart against the same stairwell
Correct: route length is similar, floor differs.
Same stairwell against different stairwells
That varies the shared route.
Adjacent doors against the units that are four doors apart
That varies distance on one floor.
qs.x: Correct: Units four doors apart on one floor and units on different floors sharing a stairwell involve comparable walking distance, so the contrast between 22% and 19% isolates what crossing a floor adds, which turns out to be very little. Why the others are wrong: The other three comparisons vary horizontal distance, shared route or both together. Trap: Choosing the comparison with the largest difference rather than the one holding distance constant.

qs.q: What is the mere exposure effect?
o: Liking based on physical appearance
That is attractiveness.
Liking that follows from shared attitudes
That is similarity.
Liking that follows from being liked in return
That is reciprocity.
Liking that grows from repeated encounters
Correct: familiarity itself increases liking.
qs.x: Correct: Mere exposure is the increase in liking produced by repeated encounters alone, independent of what is learned about the stimulus, which is why it operates even for brief and unremarked encounters. Why the others are wrong: Shared attitudes, returned liking and appearance are separate and well-documented influences on attraction. Trap: Attaching the term to whichever cause of liking se

h: Share naming the other a friend
r: Adjacent doors on the same floor

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Health insurance affects access through coverage breadth, cost sharing, and network adequacy. Underinsurance describes having coverage that still leaves high out-of-pocket costs, and coverage alone does not guarantee timely care.
A survey of 5,000 adults recorded coverage type and care experiences (Table 1).

qs.q: Which group best illustrates underinsurance?
o: The deductible group
Correct: covered yet 34% delay.
The uninsured group
They lack coverage.
The comprehensive group
Delay was 12%.
The narrow network group
Cost burden was 5%.
qs.x: Correct: Adults with high-deductible plans had coverage but still faced substantial out-of-pocket burden and frequent cost-related delay, which is the definition of underinsurance. Why the others are wrong: The uninsured are not insured at all, and the remaining groups show lower cost burden. Trap: Equating any access problem with underinsurance.

qs.q: Which barrier does the narrow network row highlight?
o: Health literacy
It was not measured.
Cost sharing
Out-of-pocket burden was low.
Lack of coverage
Coverage was present.
Network adequacy
Correct: supply of providers.
qs.x: Correct: With low cost burden but elevated delay, the limiting factor is the availability of participating providers. Why the others are wrong: Cost burden was low, coverage was present, and literacy was not measured. Trap: Attributing every access problem to cost.

qs.q: Which inference is unwarranted?
o: Delay varies by coverage
The table shows it.
Usual source varies by coverage
The table shows it.
Cost burden varies by coverage
The table shows it.
Coverage type caused delay
Correct: not assigned.
qs.x: Correct: People select or are sorted into coverage types by income, employment, and health, so a causal claim is not supported. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining statement is descriptive. Trap: Treating coverage categories as an assigned treatment.

qs.q: Which group least often had a usual source of care?
o: The high-deductible group
It is 68%.
The comprehensive group
It is 89%.
The uninsured group
Correct: 31%.
The narrow network group
It is 74%.
qs.x: Correct: Uninsured adults least often reported a usual source of care. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining group was higher. Trap: Reading the delay column.

qs.q: Which policy would the table most support?
o: Lower deductibles
Correct: addresses underinsurance.
Expand coverage counts only
High-deductible adults were covered.
Reduce provider networks
That worsens adequacy.
Publish spending data
Information is not access.
qs.x: Correct: Because covered adults with high deductibles still delayed care, reducing cost sharing addresses the gap the table documents. Why the others are wrong: Coverage counts alone miss underinsurance, narrower networks worsen access, and data publication does not change costs. Trap: Measuring success by coverage rates alone.

h: Share delaying care due to cost
Mean out-of-pocket spending as a share of income
Share with a usual source of care

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: In aqueous solution, glucose exists almost entirely as a six-membered ring. The C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, forming a cyclic hemiacetal whose C1 becomes a new stereocenter called the anomeric carbon. The two forms produced, α and β, differ only at that carbon: in α-D-glucopyranose the C1 hydroxyl is on the opposite side of the ring from the C6 group, and in β it is on the same side. The ring opens and closes continuously through the straight-chain aldehyde, so the two anomers interconvert, a process called mutarotation.

Because the anomers differ in shape, they rotate plane-polarized light differently. Freshly dissolved α-D-glucose has a specific rotation of +112°, pure β is +19°, and an equilibrium mixture settles at +52.7°.

A reducing sugar is one whose anomeric carbon is free to open to the aldehyde or ketone form, which can then be oxidized. Benedict's reagent, containing Cu²⁺, is reduced by such sugars and forms a brick-red precipitate. When the anomeric carbon is locked in a glycosidic bond, the sugar cannot open and gives no precipitate.
Students dissolved several sugars and measured optical rotation over time and the result of a Benedict's test (Table 1).

The hemiacetal carbon explains why glucose is a reducing sugar but is also only weakly reactive in the aldehyde form: at equilibrium, less than 0.01% of dissolved glucose is open-chain at any moment. That small fraction is enough for oxidation to proceed, because each molecule that reacts is replaced as the equilibrium re-establishes itself. The same slow exposure of the aldehyde lets glucose react with protein amino groups over time, forming the glycated hemoglobin measured as HbA1c in diabetes care.
Students also hydrolyzed sucrose with dilute acid. The rotation changed from +66.5° to −20° over 30 minutes, and the hydrolyzed solution gave a positive Benedict's test.

qs.q: Why do both pure anomers of glucose reach +52.7°?
o: Light changes the structure of the sugar
The polarimeter does not alter the sugar.
Both anomers decompose to the same product
Glucose is stable in water.
The ring opens and closes repeatedly
Correct: mutarotation mixes the two.
The solvent rotates light by that amount
Water is not optically active.
qs.x: Correct: Each anomer opens to the straight-chain aldehyde and closes again, producing the other anomer. Given time, both samples reach the same equilibrium mixture, about two-thirds β and one-third α, with a rotation of +52.7°. Why the others are wrong: Measuring rotation does not change the molecule; glucose is not decomposing; the water itself does not rotate light. Trap: Treating a change in rotation as a chemical reaction rather than a shift between forms.

qs.q: Why is sucrose not a reducing sugar while maltose is?
o: Both anomeric carbons are in its glycosidic bond
Correct: no ring can open.
Sucrose has no hydroxyl groups
It has many.
Sucrose is too large for the reagent
Maltose is a disaccharide too.
Sucrose contains fructose, which cannot be oxidized
Free fructose gives a positive test.
qs.x: Correct: In sucrose, C1 of glucose is joined to C2 of fructose, so the anomeric carbon of each sugar is tied up. Neither ring can open to an aldehyde or ketone, and no oxidation occurs. In maltose only one anomeric carbon is in the bond, leaving the other free. Why the others are wrong: Free fructose does reduce Benedict's reagent after isomerizing; size is not the obstacle; sucrose has many hydroxyls. Trap: Assuming a disaccharide cannot be a reducing sugar.

qs.q: Why does maltose's rotation change only slightly over six hours?
o: Acid is needed for any mutarotation
Glucose mutarotated without acid.
Only one anomeric carbon is free
Correct: one end is fixed.
Maltose does not mutarotate at all
Its rotation changed by 8°.
Both of its rings open freely
One anomeric carbon is in the bond.
qs.x: Correct: Maltose has one free anomeric carbon, which equilibrates between α and β, and one locked in the α1→4 bond. Only part of the molecule can change, so the rotation shifts by a small amount rather than the 60° seen with glucose. Why the others are wrong: It does mutarotate; one ring is locked; glucose mutarotated in plain water. Trap: Expecting a yes-or-no answer where the structure allows a partial change.

qs.q: Why does the rotation of hydrolyzed sucrose become negative?
o: Glucose becomes its mirror image
D-glucose is not converted to L-glucose.
Hydrolysis destroys all optical activity
The value is not zero.
Acid itself rotates light
Dilute acid is not optically active.
Fructose rotates light to the left
Correct: it outweighs glucose's positive value.
qs.x: Correct: Hydrolysis gives equal amounts of D-glucose (+52.7°) and D-fructose (−92°). Their sum is negative, so the solution's rotation passes through zero and ends near −20°. This is the origin of the name "invert sugar." Why the others are wrong: The products are still chiral; hydrolysis does not change configuration at every center; dilute acid does not rotate light. Trap: Assuming that mixing two sugars must give a positive rotation because glucose is positive.

qs.q: Why does methyl α-D-glucoside give a constant rotation and a negative test?
o: It is not a carbohydrate
It is a glucose derivative.
Its anomeric carbon is an acetal
Correct: the ring cannot open.
It has no stereocenters
It has several.
Methanol prevents oxidation of any sugar
The methyl group is bonded, not free.
qs.x: Correct: Replacing the anomeric hydroxyl with a methoxy group converts the hemiacetal to an acetal, which is stable in neutral water. The ring cannot open, so the compound neither mutarotates nor reduces Benedict's reagent. Why the others are wrong: It is a glucose derivative with several stereocenters, and the methyl group is attached rather than present as free methanol. Trap: Overlooking that hemiacetals open while acetals do not.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: An ester can be split into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol by hydrolysis, and the mechanism and outcome differ according to the catalyst. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is a reversible equilibrium that gives the carboxylic acid and the alcohol. Base-promoted hydrolysis, or saponification, gives the carboxylate salt and is effectively irreversible.

The difference in reversibility has a thermodynamic explanation. Under base, the carboxylic acid formed is immediately deprotonated to its carboxylate, which is not electrophilic and cannot be attacked by the alcohol, so the reaction cannot run backwards. Under acid, both products remain capable of recombining, and the position of equilibrium depends on the concentrations present.

A practical consequence is that acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is driven by using a large excess of water, while saponification needs only a stoichiometric amount of hydroxide, since nothing pulls the reaction back. The base is consumed rather than catalytic, which is why the term catalysis is inaccurate for it.
Methyl benzoate was hydrolyzed under both conditions, with the extent of reaction measured after four hours (Table 1).

The two conditions respond to stoichiometry quite differently. Under acid, reducing the water from a large excess to five equivalents lowers conversion from 87% to 52% because the equilibrium shifts back, while under base the conversion tracks the hydroxide supplied almost exactly, 96% with one equivalent and 49% with half.

The base result is the signature of an irreversible reaction consuming its reagent. Half an equivalent of hydroxide hydrolyzes about half the ester and then stops, which is what a reaction that cannot reverse and cannot regenerate its reagent must do.

Two further points apply. Recovering the free acid from a saponification requires acidifying the carboxylate afterwards, so the base route involves an extra step even though its conversion is higher. And the rates here are for a methyl ester; a bulkier alkoxy group slows attack at the carbonyl considerably, so these extents of reaction at four hours do not transfer to a tertiary ester.

qs.q: Why does half an equivalent of hydroxide stop at about half conversion?
o: Hydroxide is consumed, not regenerated
Correct: it is a reagent here.
The ester decomposes after four hours
No decomposition is indicated.
The reaction reaches equilibrium at 49%
Saponification does not reverse.
Hydroxide becomes less reactive over time
Its reactivity does not change.
qs.x: Correct: Each ester molecule hydrolyzed consumes one hydroxide, and the carboxylate product cannot give it back, so the reaction stops when the hydroxide runs out rather than at an equilibrium position. Why the others are wrong: The reaction is effectively irreversible, hydroxide's reactivity is unchanged, and nothing indicates decomposition. Trap: Reading a stoichiometric limit as an equilibrium.

qs.q: Why is saponification effectively irreversible?
o: The alcohol evaporates from the mixture
Evaporation is not the mechanism.
Hydroxide is a much stronger nucleophile than water
Strength does not prevent reversal.
The products are insoluble in the solvent
Sodium benzoate is water soluble.
The carboxylate cannot be attacked by the alcohol
Correct: it is not electrophilic.
qs.x: Correct: Deprotonation of the acid gives a carboxylate whose negative charge removes the electrophilic character needed for the alcohol to attack, so the reverse reaction has no pathway. Why the others are wrong: Evaporation is not involved, nucleophile strength affects the forward rate, and the carboxylate salt is soluble. Trap: Explaining irreversibility by the removal of a product rather than by its unreactivity.

qs.q: Why does acid-catalyzed hydrolysis need excess water?
o: It shifts a reversible equilibrium forward
Correct: water is a reactant.
Water removes the alcohol as it forms
The alcohol stays in solution.
Water acts as the real catalyst in that route
The acid is the catalyst.
The acid is diluted by the extra water
Dilution would slow the reaction.
qs.x: Correct: Because the reaction is a genuine equilibrium, a large excess of one reactant pushes the position of equilibrium toward the products, which is why conversion falls from 87% to 52% when the water is limited. Why the others are wrong: The acid is the catalyst, dilution does not drive the equilibrium, and the alcohol is not removed. Trap: Assigning the role of catalyst to the reactant used in excess.

qs.q: How much does limiting the water cost in conversion under acid?
o: 3 points
That compares nothing directly.
35 points
Correct: 87% against 52%.
44 points
That compares the two hydroxide rows.
47 points
That compares 96% with 49%.
qs.x: Correct: Conversion falls from 87% with excess water to 52% with five equivalents, a loss of 35 points. Why the others are wrong: 47 points is the difference between the two hydroxide rows and the other values match no stated comparison. Trap: Comparing rows across the two different conditions.

qs.q: Why does the base route involve an extra step?
o: The ester must be purified beforehand
Both routes start from the same ester.
The product precipitates and needs filtering
Filtering is not an extra chemical step.
The carboxylate must be acidified afterwards
Correct: to obtain the free acid.
The hydroxide must be removed by distillation
It is neutralized, not distilled.
qs.x: Correct: Saponification yields the carboxylate salt, so recovering the carboxylic acid itself requires a subsequent acidification that the acid-catalyzed route does not need. Why the others are wrong: Hydroxide is neutralized rather than distilled, the starting material is the same for both, and filtration is a workup detail rather than the chemical step at issue. Trap: Comparing two routes on conversion alone without counting the steps each requires.

r: 1 M sulfuric acid, water as solvent

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: When a body segment rotates about a joint, the relevant quantity is torque: τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point where the force acts and θ is the angle between r and the force. A muscle that inserts close to a joint has a small r, so it must generate a large force to produce a given torque, but a small shortening of the muscle produces a large movement at the end of the limb. Rotational equilibrium requires the sum of torques about any axis to be zero.

Researchers studied elbow flexion in 12 adults. The forearm was held horizontal while the participant supported a weight in the hand. The biceps tendon inserts about 4.0 cm from the elbow joint and pulls nearly vertically on the forearm in this position. The forearm plus hand has a mass of 1.6 kg with its center of mass 15 cm from the elbow, and the hand holds the weight 32 cm from the elbow. Muscle force was estimated from the measured torque, and electromyography (EMG) recorded the electrical activity of the biceps, in arbitrary units (Table 1). Take g = 10 m/s².
In a second trial, participants held the 2.0 kg mass with the elbow bent so that the forearm was 30° above horizontal. The torque from the loads fell to 7.6 N·m, and the EMG fell in proportion.

The researchers also asked what happens during a slow lowering of the weight, in which the muscle lengthens while still producing force. EMG in that phase was about 30% lower than when the same weight was held still, even though the torque the muscle had to resist was identical. Lengthening contractions are known to produce more force per unit of electrical activity, and they are also more likely to cause muscle soreness the following day.

The researchers noted that the biceps is not the only elbow flexor; the brachialis and brachioradialis also contribute, so the force attributed to the biceps is an overestimate of what that one muscle produces.

qs.q: What torque about the elbow does the 2.0 kg mass alone produce?
o: This uses 0.032 m.
This is the forearm's torque.
Correct: 20 N × 0.32 m.
This includes the forearm.
qs.x: Correct: The weight is 2.0 kg × 10 m/s² = 20 N, acting 0.32 m from the joint and perpendicular to the forearm, so τ = 20 × 0.32 = 6.4 N·m. Adding the forearm's own 2.4 N·m gives the 8.8 N·m in the table. Why the others are wrong: 2.4 N·m is the unloaded value, 8.8 N·m is the total, and 0.64 N·m comes from a misplaced decimal. Trap: Reading the table value as the load's torque alone.

qs.q: Why must the biceps force be so much larger than the weight held?
o: Its insertion is much closer to the joint
Correct: 4 cm against 32 cm.
Muscles are inefficient at converting energy
Efficiency does not set the force.
The biceps pulls at a shallow angle
It pulls nearly vertically here.
The forearm's mass dominates the load
The forearm contributes 2.4 N·m.
qs.x: Correct: Both the muscle and the load produce torque about the same axis. Because the muscle acts at 4 cm and the load at 32 cm, the muscle needs about eight times the force to balance it, which is why holding 20 N requires several hundred newtons of muscle force. Why the others are wrong: Energy efficiency is a separate matter; the forearm adds a minority of the torque; the muscle's pull is nearly perpendicular to the forearm. Trap: Comparing forces without comparing their distances from the joint.

qs.q: What explains the lower torque when the forearm is raised 30°?
o: The distances to the joint shorten
The bones do not change length.
Gravity weakens at that angle
Gravity is constant here.
The perpendicular component falls
Correct: torque scales with cos 30°.
The masses become lighter when raised
Mass does not change.
qs.x: Correct: Weight always acts straight down, so raising the forearm reduces the angle between the limb and the horizontal direction perpendicular to gravity. The torque becomes rF cos 30° ≈ 0.87 rF, which matches the fall from 8.8 to 7.6 N·m. Why the others are wrong: Mass, bone length and gravity are all unchanged. Trap: Looking for a change in the force or the distance when the angle is what changed.

qs.q: What does the EMG trend add to the force estimates?
o: It measures the torque directly
EMG records electrical activity.
It shows activation rising with load
Correct: 14 to 91 units.
It shows the muscle shortens as load rises
The arm was held still.
It identifies which muscle produces the force
Other flexors also contribute.
qs.x: Correct: EMG rises roughly in step with the estimated force, giving independent evidence that the biceps is working harder as the load increases rather than the force being a calculation artifact. Why the others are wrong: EMG is an electrical measure, not a torque meter; the position was held, so the muscle contracted isometrically; EMG from one muscle cannot apportion the force among several flexors. Trap: Treating a correlated measure as a direct measure.

qs.q: Why does the involvement of the brachialis make the estimate an overestimate for the biceps?
o: The brachialis has a longer moment arm
Its insertion is also close to the joint.
The biceps does not cross the elbow
It crosses both the elbow and the shoulder.
Several muscles share the torque
Correct: each supplies part of it.
The brachialis acts to extend the elbow
It is a flexor.
qs.x: Correct: The calculation attributes all the required flexion torque to the biceps. Because the brachialis and brachioradialis also flex the elbow, the true biceps force is lower than the figure in the table. Why the others are wrong: The brachialis is a flexor; its insertion is also near the joint; the biceps does cross the elbow. Trap: Accepting a single-muscle model without asking what else acts at the joint.

h: Total torque about the elbow from the loads (N·m)

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: Light changes direction when it passes between media in which it travels at different speeds. The index of refraction of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium, and the directions of the incident and refracted rays are related by n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

Two consequences matter for imaging. A ray entering a denser medium bends toward the normal, which is how a lens brings parallel rays to a focus, and the focal length of a lens depends on both its curvature and the difference in index between the lens and its surroundings. A lens in water focuses less strongly than the same lens in air.

Beyond a critical angle, a ray passing from a denser to a less dense medium is not refracted at all but totally reflected. The critical angle is given by sin θc = n₂ divided by n₁, so it exists only when the second medium is the less dense one.
A converging lens of fixed curvature was characterized in several surrounding media, and the critical angle at its surface was computed (Table 1).

Both effects follow from the index difference. As the surrounding index rises toward the lens's own 1.52, the focal length grows from 10.0 cm to 44.1 cm, and when the media match exactly the lens stops focusing altogether because no refraction occurs at its surfaces.

The critical angle behaves in the opposite direction. It rises from 41.1 degrees in air to 74.6 degrees in glycerol and vanishes in the matched oil, since total internal reflection requires the second medium to be less dense and there is no longer any difference to reflect from.

Two points qualify the table. The focal lengths assume rays close to the axis, and a real lens focuses rays far from the axis at a slightly different distance, an aberration that grows with aperture. And an index-matched lens still absorbs and scatters a little light, so it becomes nearly invisible rather than truly so.

qs.q: Why does the lens stop focusing in the matched oil?
o: No refraction occurs at its surfaces
Correct: the indices are equal.
The oil absorbs the light before it focuses
Absorption is slight.
The lens curvature changes in the oil
Curvature is fixed by the glass.
The focal length becomes negative there
It becomes undefined rather than negative.
qs.x: Correct: Bending at a surface depends on a difference in index between the two media, and with both at 1.52 a ray passes straight through, so the curved surfaces have no optical effect. Why the others are wrong: Absorption is minor, the curvature is a property of the glass, and the focus is absent rather than inverted. Trap: Looking for an effect of the medium other than the index difference that governs refraction.

qs.q: Why does the critical angle rise as the surrounding index rises?
o: The two indices become more similar
Correct: reflection requires a larger angle.
Light travels faster in denser media
It travels more slowly in them.
Total reflection needs a denser second medium
It needs a less dense one.
The lens becomes optically denser too
The lens index is unchanged at 1.52.
qs.x: Correct: The critical angle is set by the ratio of the two indices, so as the surrounding medium approaches the lens's index the ratio approaches one and the angle at which total reflection begins approaches 90 degrees. Why the others are wrong: Light slows in denser media, the lens index is fixed, and total reflection requires the second medium to be the less dense. Trap: Reversing the condition under which total internal reflection can occur.

qs.q: What does the index of refraction measure?
o: How much of the light a medium absorbs
Absorption is a separate property.
How much light slows in a medium
Correct: relative to vacuum.
The angle at which light enters
The angle is set by the geometry.
The curvature of a lens surface
Curvature is a geometric property.
qs.x: Correct: The index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium, which is why a higher index bends a ray more strongly at a boundary. Why the others are wrong: Absorption, curvature and the angle of incidence are all distinct quantities. Trap: Confusing an optical property of the material with a property of the lens or the ray.

qs.q: How many times longer is the focal length in glycerol than in air?
o: About 1.5
That compares glycerol with water.
About 2.9
That compares water with air.
About 3.4
That compares nothing in the table.
About 4.4
Correct: 44.1 cm against 10.0 cm.
qs.x: Correct: The focal length is 10.0 cm in air and 44.1 cm in glycerol, a factor of about 4.4. Why the others are wrong: 2.9 compares water with air, 1.5 compares glycerol with water, and 3.4 matches no pair. Trap: Comparing adjacent rows rather than the two named media.

qs.q: Why do the tabulated focal lengths hold only near the axis?
o: The index varies across the lens
The glass is uniform.
Off-axis rays are all absorbed inside the lens
They pass through it as well.
Focal length cannot be measured precisely
It is measured to a tenth of a centimetre.
Off-axis rays focus at a different distance
Correct: aberration grows with aperture.
qs.x: Correct: A spherical surface brings rays far from the axis to a focus nearer the lens than rays close to it, so a single focal length describes only the paraxial rays. Why the others are wrong: Off-axis rays are transmitted, the glass is uniform, and focal length is measurable precisely. Trap: Treating an aberration of a curved surface as an absorption or a material defect.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: A tendon stretched by a small amount behaves approximately like a spring, with the force rising in proportion to the extension, so the energy stored is one half times the stiffness times the extension squared. That stored energy is returned when the tendon recoils, which is why tendons contribute to the efficiency of running.

The return is not complete. Some of the stored energy is dissipated as heat within the tissue, and the fraction returned is called the resilience. A tendon with a resilience of 0.93 returns 93% of the energy put into it and loses the rest, which appears as a difference between the loading and unloading curves.

The spring approximation holds only for small extensions. Beyond a few percent of its length a tendon stiffens as collagen fibres align and then, at greater extensions, begins to fail, so neither the proportional relationship nor the energy expression applies in that region.
A tendon of 20 cm rest length was loaded cyclically, and the energy stored and returned was measured at several extensions (Table 1).

The spring description holds at the smaller extensions and then fails. Doubling the extension from 2 to 4 mm quadruples the stored energy, as the squared relationship requires, and the force doubles, but at 6 and 8 mm the force rises faster than proportionally and the stored energy exceeds the spring prediction.

Resilience falls in the same region. It holds at 0.93 for the first two extensions and then falls to 0.90 and 0.80, so the tendon both stiffens and dissipates more as it is stretched further, and the 8 mm cycle loses more than a joule as heat.

Two limits apply. The measurements come from a cyclic test at one rate, and tendon stiffness depends on how fast it is loaded, so a faster cycle would give higher forces at the same extension. And an isolated tendon lacks the muscle in series with it that shares the extension in life, so the extensions here do not correspond directly to joint angles.

qs.q: Which observation shows the spring approximation failing?
o: Resilience is 0.93 at small extensions
That is the spring region.
The tendon is 20 cm long at rest
Length is a fixed property.
Force rises faster than proportionally
Correct: beyond 4 mm.
Energy stored rises with extension
That is expected throughout.
qs.x: Correct: A spring requires force proportional to extension, which holds from 400 N at 2 mm to 800 N at 4 mm and then fails as 6 and 8 mm give 1,250 N and 1,800 N instead of 1,200 and 1,600. Why the others are wrong: Rising stored energy is expected, the constant resilience describes the region where the approximation works, and rest length is a fixed property. Trap: Looking at the energy column when the proportionality concerns the force.

qs.q: What does the fall in resilience represent?
o: A change in the tendon's rest length
Rest length was unchanged.
More energy dissipated as heat
Correct: less is returned.
An error in the force measurement
The forces are consistent.
A reduction in the energy stored
Stored energy rose throughout.
qs.x: Correct: Resilience is the fraction of stored energy returned on recoil, so a fall from 0.93 to 0.80 means a larger share is lost within the tissue as heat, more than a joule in the largest cycle. Why the others are wrong: Stored energy increased, rest length is fixed, and the force measurements are internally consistent. Trap: Reading a falling ratio as a falling numerator.

qs.q: Why do tendons improve the efficiency of running?
o: They reduce the force on the muscles
Force is transmitted through them.
They shorten the stride involuntarily
Stride length is not set by them.
They convert heat into movement
Heat is a loss, not a source.
Stored energy is returned on recoil
Correct: most of it comes back.
qs.x: Correct: Energy put into stretching a tendon during one part of the stride is largely returned as it recoils, so less work has to be done by muscle on the next step. Why the others are wrong: Tendons transmit force, stride length is not determined by them, and the heat produced is a loss. Trap: Treating the dissipated energy as something the tissue can recover.

qs.q: How much energy is lost as heat in the 8 mm cycle?
o: That is the loss at 2 mm.
That is the loss at 4 mm.
That is the loss at 6 mm.
Correct: 5.20 minus 4.16.
qs.x: Correct: The 8 mm cycle stores 5.20 J and returns 4.16 J, so 1.04 J is dissipated. Why the others are wrong: 0.03, 0.11 and 0.30 J are the losses at the smaller extensions. Trap: Taking the loss from a row other than the one named.

qs.q: Why do these extensions not correspond to joint angles?
o: Muscle in series shares the extension
Correct: the tendon is isolated here.
Tendons do not act across joints
They act across them in life.
Extension is unrelated to joint movement
It is related, but not directly.
Joint angles cannot be measured precisely
They are measured routinely.
qs.x: Correct: In the body a tendon works in series with muscle that also changes length, so a given joint rotation is shared between them and the tendon's own extension cannot be read off the joint angle. Why the others are wrong: Joint angles are measurable, tendons do act across joints, and the quantities are related through that sharing. Trap: Treating an isolated-tissue measurement as directly transferable to the intact limb.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Hemophilia A is caused by loss-of-function variants in F8, a gene on the X chromosome that encodes clotting factor VIII. Men with one variant allele and no normal copy have factor VIII activity below about 40% of normal and bleed excessively; activity below 1% causes spontaneous joint bleeding. About 45% of severe cases are caused by a single recurrent inversion in intron 22 of F8, which can be detected with a long-range PCR test.

Women with one variant allele are carriers. In each of their cells one X chromosome is randomly silenced early in development, so a carrier's liver cells form a mosaic in which some cells make factor VIII and others do not. Most carriers have about half the normal activity and no symptoms, but some have low enough activity to bleed after surgery or childbirth.

A clinic studied one family. Man I-1 had severe hemophilia A caused by the intron 22 inversion. His daughter II-2 married an unaffected man, II-3. They have two sons (III-1 and III-2) and three daughters (III-3, III-4 and III-5). III-5 had heavy bleeding after a tooth extraction. The clinic measured factor VIII activity and ran the inversion test on each family member (Table 1).

Knowing a woman's carrier status matters for planning. A carrier who is pregnant may choose prenatal testing, and her delivery can be managed to lower the risk of bleeding in an affected newborn, for example by avoiding instruments that can injure the baby's head. Carriers with low factor VIII levels can be treated with desmopressin or factor concentrate before surgery. For these reasons the clinic offered testing to every woman in the family, including those with no symptoms, and explained the results to each one in a separate genetic counseling visit.
In a survey of 300 women from other families whose carrier status was known from DNA testing, factor VIII activity ranged from 22% to 116% in carriers and from 55% to 180% in non-carriers.

qs.q: Why is II-2 certain to be a carrier even before testing?
o: Hemophilia A is inherited as a dominant trait
It is X-linked recessive.
She received her father's only X chromosome
Correct: fathers pass their X to every daughter.
Her mother must also have been a carrier
The mother's status does not matter here.
Her factor VIII level is near half of normal
She was certain to be a carrier before any test.
qs.x: Correct: A man has one X chromosome, and every daughter receives it, so I-1's daughter must carry his F8 inversion. Her test result (one copy, 47% activity) confirms this. Why the others are wrong: The disorder is X-linked recessive, not dominant; her mother's genotype is irrelevant because the variant came from her father; the question asks why she was certain before testing. Trap: Basing an obligate-carrier conclusion on a lab value instead of on the pattern of inheritance.

qs.q: What is the most likely reason that III-5 has bleeding symptoms?
o: Her normal X was silenced in most liver cells
Correct: skewed X inactivation.
Her normal F8 allele interferes with the variant protein
Dominant-negative action is not described.
She inherited the inversion from both parents
Her father II-3 has no inversion.
She has Turner syndrome and so has only one X chromosome
She shows one copy plus a normal allele.
qs.x: Correct: III-5 carries one inversion and one normal allele. Random X inactivation usually leaves about half of the cells making factor VIII, but by chance the normal X was silenced in most of her liver cells, so her activity is only 14%. Why the others are wrong: Her father lacks the inversion, so she cannot be homozygous; a normal allele does not interfere with anything; the test detected one variant copy, and nothing suggests a missing X. Trap: Assuming a symptomatic female must have two variant alleles.

qs.q: If II-2 and II-3 have another child, what is the probability that the child is a son with hemophilia A?
o: Correct: 1/2 chance of a son × 1/2 chance he inherits the variant X.
This multiplies by an extra 1/2.
This is the chance for a son, not for any child.
Only half of her sons are affected.
qs.x: Correct: The child is a son with probability 1/2, and a son inherits his mother's variant X with probability 1/2, so the chance of an affected son is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Why the others are wrong: 1/8 adds a factor that does not exist; 1/2 is the risk for a son already known to be male; not every son is affected, as III-2 shows. Trap: Answering for sons when the question asks about any child.

qs.q: Based on the survey, why is factor VIII activity alone an unreliable way to tell whether a woman is a carrier?
o: Activity cannot be measured in women
It was measured in every woman in Table 1.
Factor VIII activity is normal in every carrier
Many carriers had low values.
Carrier and non-carrier activity ranges overlap
Correct: values from 55% to 116% fit either group.
Carriers have higher activity than non-carriers
Carrier activity is lower on average.
qs.x: Correct: Carriers ranged from 22% to 116% and non-carriers from 55% to 180%, so a woman with activity between 55% and 116% could belong to either group. III-3 (61%, no inversion) and III-4 (52%, one copy) illustrate how close the values can be. A DNA test is needed for a firm answer. Why the others are wrong: Many carriers have reduced activity; carriers average lower, not higher; the table shows the test works in women. Trap: Treating a lab value with overlapping ranges as diagnostic.

qs.q: If III-1 received gene therapy that restored normal factor VIII production in his liver, what would be true of his future daughters?
o: Half of them would be carriers
Every daughter gets his single X.
They would not be carriers
Liver therapy does not change germ cells.
They would all have hemophilia A
They also receive a normal X from their mother.
They would still be carriers
Correct: his sperm still carry the inversion.
qs.x: Correct: The therapy changes his liver cells, not his germ cells. His sperm still carry the X with the inversion, and every daughter receives that X, so all of his daughters would be carriers. Why the others are wrong: Somatic gene therapy is not inherited; daughters always receive their father's X, so the fraction is all, not half; they would also receive an X from their mother, which is normal unless she is a carrier. Trap: Assuming a somatic cure is passed to children.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Differential centrifugation separates cell components by size and density. A tissue is homogenized in an isotonic buffer and then spun at progressively higher speeds. Each spin pellets the largest remaining particles, and the supernatant is carried to the next, faster spin. Nuclei pellet first, then mitochondria, then membrane fragments, and finally ribosomes, leaving the soluble cytosol in the last supernatant.

Because identifying an organelle by sight is slow, fractions are usually identified by marker enzymes. A marker is an enzyme found in one compartment and nowhere else, so its activity reports where that compartment ended up. Common markers include DNA polymerase for the nucleus, succinate dehydrogenase for the inner mitochondrial membrane, acid phosphatase for lysosomes, glucose-6-phosphatase for the endoplasmic reticulum and lactate dehydrogenase for the cytosol.
Researchers homogenized rat liver and performed four spins. The activity of each marker in each pellet is shown as a percentage of the activity in the original homogenate (Table 1).

Two numbers are reported for a fraction. Yield is the percentage of the whole homogenate's marker activity that appears in that fraction, which is what the table shows. Purification is the activity per milligram of protein in the fraction divided by the same ratio in the homogenate, which reports how much the compartment has been concentrated. A fraction can have a high yield and poor purification if it also carries a great deal of unrelated material, so both figures are usually given together. In this preparation, P2 had a yield of 81% for succinate dehydrogenase and a purification of about 5-fold, while S3 had a high yield for lactate dehydrogenase but a purification close to 1, because the cytosol is most of the homogenate to begin with.

In a second preparation, the homogenate was prepared in distilled water rather than isotonic buffer. Acid phosphatase activity in P2 fell to 11%, and most of it appeared in the final supernatant. Succinate dehydrogenase showed the same shift, while DNA polymerase remained in P1.

qs.q: What does the P3 fraction mainly contain?
o: Fragments of endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: glucose-6-phosphatase is at 78%.
Intact nuclei from the liver cells
DNA polymerase is at 2%.
Soluble cytosolic enzymes
Those remain in the supernatant.
Mitochondria and their membranes
Succinate dehydrogenase is at 5%.
qs.x: Correct: Glucose-6-phosphatase, the endoplasmic reticulum marker, is concentrated in P3 at 78%, while every other marker is low there. When the cell is homogenized, the ER breaks into small vesicles that need a very high speed to pellet. Why the others are wrong: Nuclei pelleted in P1, mitochondria in P2, and soluble enzymes stayed in S3. Trap: Identifying a fraction by the organelle you expect at that speed rather than by its marker.

qs.q: Why do lysosomes appear in the same fraction as mitochondria?
o: Acid phosphatase is also a mitochondrial enzyme
It is a lysosomal marker.
They are similar in size and density
Correct: both pellet at 10,000 × g.
The spin speeds were chosen incorrectly
The separation worked for other organelles.
Lysosomes are attached to mitochondria
No such attachment is described.
qs.x: Correct: Differential centrifugation separates by size and density, so organelles with similar sedimentation properties co-pellet. Lysosomes and mitochondria overlap enough that 62% of the lysosomal marker appears in P2 with 81% of the mitochondrial marker. Separating them requires a density gradient. Why the others are wrong: The two organelles are not physically linked; acid phosphatase is specific to lysosomes; the protocol worked as intended for the nuclei and ER. Trap: Expecting one method to resolve every compartment.

qs.q: Why did acid phosphatase move to the supernatant when water was used?
o: Lysosomes became denser in water
They would then pellet, not float.
Water dissolves the lysosomal enzymes' cofactors
No cofactor loss is described.
Lysosomes burst and released their contents
Correct: water is hypotonic.
Acid phosphatase is destroyed by water
Its activity was still measured.
qs.x: Correct: In distilled water, osmosis drives water into membrane-bound organelles until they burst. The released soluble enzyme stays in the supernatant through every spin. Why the others are wrong: Activity was measurable, so the enzyme survived; a denser organelle would pellet sooner; no cofactor effect is described. Trap: Reading a change in location as a change in the enzyme itself.

qs.q: Why must an isotonic buffer be used for fractionation?
o: To keep organelles from bursting
Correct: no net water movement.
To dissolve the plasma membrane
The goal is to preserve membranes.
To keep enzymes at their optimum pH
That is the buffer's pH, not its tonicity.
To make the homogenate denser than organelles
Organelles must be denser to pellet.
qs.x: Correct: An isotonic medium has the same solute concentration as the organelle interiors, so there is no net osmotic flow and membranes stay intact. The water experiment shows what happens otherwise. Why the others are wrong: pH is controlled separately from tonicity; dissolving membranes would defeat the purpose; organelles pellet because they are denser than the medium. Trap: Confusing the two jobs a homogenization medium does.

qs.q: Which fraction would best test whether a newly discovered enzyme is cytosolic?
o: P3, compared with glucose-6-phosphatase
That tests for the endoplasmic reticulum.
P2, compared with succinate dehydrogenase
That tests for a mitochondrial location.
P1, compared with DNA polymerase
That tests for a nuclear location.
S3, compared with lactate dehydrogenase
Correct: the cytosolic marker is there.
qs.x: Correct: A cytosolic enzyme should follow lactate dehydrogenase, which is 84% in the final supernatant. Finding the new enzyme concentrated there, and not in any pellet, would support a cytosolic location. Why the others are wrong: Each of the other comparisons tests a different compartment. Trap: Choosing a fraction because it is the cleanest rather than because it contains the right marker.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: A soap molecule has a long hydrocarbon chain and a charged carboxylate head, so neither water nor oil accommodates it well. Below a certain concentration such molecules sit at the air-water surface with their chains out of the water, which lowers the surface tension. Above it they aggregate in the bulk into micelles, with the chains inward and the heads facing the water.

The concentration at which micelles form is the critical micelle concentration, and several properties change abruptly at it. Surface tension stops falling because the surface is already saturated, while the capacity to carry oily material rises sharply because the micelle interiors provide a nonpolar environment.

The critical concentration depends on the chain. Each additional two carbons lowers it by roughly a factor of ten, since a longer chain is more costly to keep in water, and added salt lowers it further by screening the repulsion between the charged heads.
A series of soaps was characterized in water and in 0.10 M sodium chloride (Table 1).

Both effects appear and are roughly multiplicative. Each two-carbon extension lowers the critical concentration by a factor of about ten across the series, and the salt lowers each value by a further factor of about 1.5 to 2.7.

The salt effect grows with chain length. It is a factor of 1.5 for the shortest soap and 2.7 for the longest, which is consistent with screening mattering more when the aggregate is held together more strongly and the heads are packed more closely.

Two limits are worth noting. The critical concentration is not a sharp threshold but a narrow range over which aggregation becomes appreciable, so the tabulated values depend somewhat on which property was used to locate it. And these soaps precipitate as insoluble salts in water containing calcium or magnesium, which removes them from solution entirely and is why synthetic detergents with sulfonate heads replaced them for hard water.

qs.q: Why does surface tension stop falling above the critical concentration?
o: The surface is already saturated
Correct: added molecules form micelles.
Micelles raise the surface tension again
Tension plateaus rather than rising.
The soap begins to precipitate there
Precipitation needs calcium or magnesium.
Surface tension cannot fall below water's
It falls well below it.
qs.x: Correct: Once the air-water surface is covered, further soap has nowhere to go at the surface and aggregates in the bulk instead, so surface tension levels off while micelle concentration rises. Why the others are wrong: Tension plateaus rather than increasing, precipitation requires divalent ions, and surface tension is indeed lowered below that of pure water. Trap: Assuming a plateau must mean a reversal.

qs.q: Why does added salt lower the critical concentration?
o: It makes the hydrocarbon chains shorter
Chain length is fixed.
It increases the surface tension of water
Salt's effect on tension is small.
It precipitates the soap from solution
Sodium salts stay dissolved.
It screens repulsion between the heads
Correct: aggregation is easier.
qs.x: Correct: The charged heads of a micelle repel one another, and dissolved ions reduce that repulsion, so micelles form at a lower soap concentration than in pure water. Why the others are wrong: Chain length is a property of the molecule, salt's effect on water's surface tension is minor here, and sodium salts remain soluble. Trap: Attributing an electrostatic effect to a change in the molecule.

qs.q: What makes a micelle able to carry oily material?
o: It has a larger volume than a soap molecule
Size alone does not dissolve oil.
Its interior is a nonpolar environment
Correct: chains point inward.
It forms only above a threshold concentration
That is when, not how.
Its surface carries a negative charge
That keeps micelles dispersed.
qs.x: Correct: The hydrocarbon chains face inward, creating a small nonpolar region in the middle of an aqueous solution in which oily molecules can dissolve. Why the others are wrong: The charged surface keeps micelles from coalescing, size alone is not the mechanism, and the threshold describes when micelles appear. Trap: Choosing a true property of micelles that does not answer the question asked.

qs.q: By what factor does salt lower the critical concentration for the 14-carbon soap?
o: About 1.5
That is the factor for the 8-carbon soap.
About 1.7
That is the factor for the 10-carbon soap.
About 2.0
That is the factor for the 12-carbon soap.
About 2.7
Correct: 0.24 mM against 0.09 mM.
qs.x: Correct: The critical concentration falls from 0.24 mM in water to 0.09 mM in salt, a factor of about 2.7, the largest in the series. Why the others are wrong: 1.5, 1.7 and 2.0 are the factors for the shorter soaps. Trap: Taking the factor from a row other than the longest chain.

qs.q: Why do the tabulated values depend on the property measured?
o: Different properties give unrelated values
They give closely similar values.
Micelles form at every concentration
They are negligible below the range.
Aggregation begins over a narrow range
Correct: not at a sharp point.
Surface tension cannot be measured precisely
It is measured precisely.
qs.x: Correct: Micelle formation becomes appreciable across a short span of concentration rather than switching on at one value, so a figure derived from surface tension can differ slightly from one derived from solubilization. Why the others are wrong: The values agree closely, surface tension is measurable precisely, and micelles are negligible well below the range. Trap: Reading a small dependence on method as a disagreement between methods.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Microtubules are hollow polymers of α/β-tubulin dimers. A dimer binds GTP on its β subunit before it adds to the growing plus end, and the GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP shortly after incorporation. As long as the newest dimers still hold GTP, the end forms a stable cap and growth continues. If hydrolysis catches up with the tip and the cap is lost, the GDP-bound lattice peels apart and the microtubule shrinks rapidly. This switch from growth to shrinkage is called a catastrophe, and the alternation between the two states is called dynamic instability.

Researchers attached short, stable microtubule seeds to a glass surface and added purified tubulin with GTP or with GMPCPP, a GTP analog that is hydrolyzed about 10,000 times more slowly. They recorded individual microtubules by microscopy for 20 minutes and measured growth and shrinkage rates and the number of catastrophes per minute of growth. Some trials included paclitaxel (taxol) or nocodazole, two drugs used to study microtubules (Table 1).

The researchers also examined the ends of shrinking microtubules by electron microscopy. In the GTP and nocodazole samples, the protofilaments at shrinking ends curled outward like the peeled skin of a banana, which is the shape expected when GDP-tubulin is released from the lattice. In the taxol samples, the few shrinking ends seen had short, straight protofilaments. Because taxol binds the inside surface of the microtubule wall, they proposed that it holds the protofilaments together even after hydrolysis has occurred.

To link these effects to cell division, the researchers treated cultured human cells with each drug for 12 hours and counted the fraction of cells in mitosis (the mitotic index). Cells in mitosis were identified by condensed chromosomes. Untreated cells had a mitotic index of 4%; taxol-treated cells, 38%; and nocodazole-treated cells, 41%. In both drug groups, most mitotic cells had chromosomes that were condensed but not aligned at the metaphase plate.

qs.q: Why were no catastrophes observed with GMPCPP?
o: GMPCPP speeds hydrolysis at the tip
It is hydrolyzed far more slowly.
The cap is never lost without hydrolysis
Correct: the whole lattice stays GTP-like.
GMPCPP forms covalent bonds between dimers
Tubulin assembly is noncovalent.
GMPCPP blocks dimers from adding to the plus end
Growth was nearly normal.
qs.x: Correct: A catastrophe begins when hydrolysis reaches the tip and removes the GTP cap. Because GMPCPP is hydrolyzed about 10,000 times more slowly, the end keeps a stable cap throughout the experiment. Why the others are wrong: Growth with GMPCPP (1.1 µm/min) was close to that with GTP, so addition was not blocked; tubulin dimers associate noncovalently; GMPCPP slows hydrolysis rather than speeding it. Trap: Explaining the result by a change in growth when the data show growth was normal.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the effect of raising tubulin from 10 µM to 20 µM?
o: More tubulin speeds GTP hydrolysis in the lattice
That would cause more catastrophes.
More tubulin removes the need for bound GTP
Assembly still uses GTP-tubulin.
Faster addition keeps a longer GTP cap at the tip
Correct: fewer catastrophes.
More tubulin slows shrinkage after a catastrophe
Shrinkage stayed at 25 µm/min.
qs.x: Correct: Doubling tubulin roughly doubled the growth rate. When dimers add faster than their GTP is hydrolyzed, more GTP-tubulin accumulates at the tip, so the cap is harder to lose and catastrophes fall from 0.30 to 0.12 per minute. Why the others are wrong: Faster hydrolysis would raise, not lower, catastrophe frequency; the shrinkage rate did not change; GTP binding is still required. Trap: Overlooking the unchanged shrinkage rate in the table.

qs.q: Taxol and nocodazole have opposite effects in vitro. Why do both raise the mitotic index?
o: Spindles need microtubules that grow and shrink
Correct: both block chromosome alignment.
Both drugs stop DNA replication in S phase
That would lower the mitotic index.
Both drugs speed cells into mitosis
The cells are stuck, not speeded up.
Both drugs cause the spindle to fall apart completely
Taxol stabilizes microtubules.
qs.x: Correct: To capture and align chromosomes, spindle microtubules must keep growing and shrinking. Taxol nearly freezes them (shrinkage 4 µm/min, 0.02 catastrophes per minute) and nocodazole keeps them short (growth 0.4 µm/min), so in both cases chromosomes fail to align and cells pile up in mitosis. Why the others are wrong: Taxol does the opposite of depolymerizing; blocking S phase would keep cells out of mitosis; the unaligned chromosomes show arrest, not faster entry. Trap: Assuming that two drugs with the same outcome must work the same way.

qs.q: Which cell-cycle control is most likely holding the drug-treated cells in mitosis?
o: The DNA damage checkpoint at G2/M
Those cells would not enter mitosis.
The spindle assembly checkpoint
Correct: it waits for every kinetochore to attach.
The restriction point in G1
That acts before DNA replication.
The checkpoint that controls cytokinesis
Chromosomes have not yet aligned.
qs.x: Correct: Condensed chromosomes that have not aligned at the metaphase plate show that cells entered mitosis and stopped before anaphase. The spindle assembly checkpoint prevents anaphase until every kinetochore is properly attached to spindle microtubules. Why the others are wrong: The G1 restriction point and the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint act before mitosis begins; cytokinesis comes after anaphase. Trap: Picking a checkpoint by name without matching it to the stage the cells are in.

qs.q: A new compound, Z, is proposed to act like taxol. Which in vitro result would best support this?
o: Growth speeds up when tubulin is doubled
This happens without any drug.
The mitotic index of cultured cells rises
Both drug types do this.
Shrinkage slows and catastrophes become rare
Correct: this matches the taxol row.
Growth slows and catastrophes become frequent
This matches nocodazole.
qs.x: Correct: In Table 1, taxol's signature is a sharp drop in shrinkage rate (25 to 4 µm/min) and in catastrophe frequency (0.30 to 0.02 per minute). Seeing the same pattern with compound Z would support a taxol-like stabilizing action. Why the others are wrong: Slower growth with more catastrophes is the nocodazole pattern; a higher mitotic index cannot tell the two mechanisms apart; faster growth at higher tubulin is normal behavior. Trap: Choosing a result that is consistent with the claim but also with the opposite claim.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood Ca²⁺ by stimulating bone resorption, increasing renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, reducing renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulating the kidney to make calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which increases intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption. Low Ca²⁺ is detected by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells.
An endocrine service reviewed four patients with abnormal Ca²⁺ (Table 1). Reference ranges: Ca²⁺ 8.5–10.2 mg/dL, PTH 15–65 pg/mL, phosphate 2.5–4.5 mg/dL.

qs.q: Why is phosphate low in Patient A?
o: PTH reduces renal phosphate reabsorption
Correct: phosphaturia.
PTH stimulates phosphate absorption in the gut
Calcitriol raises gut phosphate absorption, not lower it.
High Ca²⁺ blocks phosphate release from bone
Bone resorption releases both.
The adenoma stores phosphate
Tumors do not store phosphate.
qs.x: Correct: PTH inhibits proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption, so excess PTH causes phosphate loss in urine. Why the others are wrong: Gut absorption would raise phosphate; adenomas do not store phosphate; bone resorption releases phosphate. Trap: Expecting Ca²⁺ and phosphate to move in the same direction.

qs.q: What explains high PTH with low Ca²⁺ in Patient B?
o: PTH-related peptide from a tumor
This raises Ca²⁺ and lowers PTH.
The parathyroid glands were removed
PTH would be low.
A parathyroid adenoma secretes excess PTH
An adenoma would cause high Ca²⁺.
Kidney failure lowers calcitriol
Correct: secondary hyperparathyroidism.
qs.x: Correct: In kidney disease, phosphate builds up and calcitriol falls, so Ca²⁺ drops and the parathyroids respond by secreting more PTH. Why the others are wrong: Adenomas cause hypercalcemia; removal lowers PTH; PTHrP suppresses PTH. Trap: Calling any high PTH an adenoma.

qs.q: Why is PTH low in Patient C?
o: The lung tumor has spread to and destroyed the parathyroids
There is no evidence of destruction.
PTHrP-driven Ca²⁺ suppresses the glands
Correct: normal feedback.
The patient has kidney failure
Kidney failure raises PTH.
PTHrP is measured as PTH
Assays distinguish them.
qs.x: Correct: PTH-related peptide acts on PTH receptors and raises Ca²⁺; the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptors detect the high Ca²⁺ and stop PTH secretion. Why the others are wrong: Glands are not destroyed; standard assays do not detect PTHrP as PTH; kidney failure raises PTH. Trap: Expecting PTH to rise whenever Ca²⁺ is high.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of Patient D's findings?
o: PTHrP from a tumor
Ca²⁺ would be high.
Vitamin D excess
This would raise Ca²⁺.
Surgical parathyroid damage
Correct: hypoparathyroidism.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
PTH would be high.
qs.x: Correct: Low PTH with low Ca²⁺ and high phosphate after neck surgery suggests the parathyroid glands were removed or damaged. Why the others are wrong: Vitamin D excess raises Ca²⁺; secondary hyperparathyroidism raises PTH; PTHrP raises Ca²⁺. Trap: Missing the clue in the notes column.

qs.q: Which treatment would best correct Patient D's Ca²⁺ in the long term?
o: Calcium plus calcitriol
Correct: bypasses the missing PTH step.
Calcium alone, at small doses
Absorption is poor without calcitriol.
A drug that blocks the calcium-sensing receptor
Few parathyroid cells are left to respond.
Removal of the remaining parathyroid tissue
This would worsen the deficiency.
qs.x: Correct: Without PTH, the kidney makes little calcitriol, so oral Ca²⁺ is poorly absorbed. Giving active vitamin D with Ca²⁺ restores intestinal uptake. Why the others are wrong: Calcium alone is poorly absorbed; receptor drugs need functional glands; removing tissue worsens the problem. Trap: Overlooking PTH's role in activating vitamin D.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Genes on the same chromosome are inherited together unless crossing over separates them. The chance of a crossover between two loci rises with the distance between them, so the frequency of recombinant offspring estimates that distance; one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to 1% recombinants. A testcross, in which an individual heterozygous at every locus is crossed with one homozygous recessive at every locus, reveals directly which gametes the heterozygous parent produced, because each offspring's phenotype reflects the allele combination it received from that parent.

In a three-point testcross, the two rarest classes arise from double crossovers. Comparing these with the two most common classes, which are the parental types, shows which gene lies in the middle: the gene whose allele has switched sides in the double-crossover class is the middle one.

Interference describes the finding that one crossover reduces the chance of another nearby. It is measured by the coefficient of coincidence, the number of double-crossover offspring observed divided by the number expected if the two intervals were independent. A coefficient of 1 means no interference; a coefficient near 0 means a crossover almost completely prevents a second one close by. In Drosophila, interference is strong over short distances and weakens as the intervals grow farther apart.

In Drosophila melanogaster, the recessive alleles b (black body), pr (purple eyes) and vg (vestigial wings) are all on chromosome 2. A female heterozygous for all three was crossed with a male homozygous recessive for all three, and 1,000 offspring were scored (Table 1).

The researchers crossed virgin females to avoid earlier matings, and scored offspring under light anesthesia within a day of emerging, because wing and body color can be judged most reliably then. They also noted that recombination frequencies above about 50% cannot be measured directly: genes that far apart assort as if they were on different chromosomes, and their true distance is found by adding shorter intervals between them. Mapping a chromosome therefore means stitching together many small crosses rather than measuring any pair directly.

qs.q: What is the recombination frequency between b and pr, as a percentage?
o: This is the pr–vg distance.
This omits the double crossovers.
This is the b–vg distance.
qs.x: Correct: Recombinants between b and pr are the classes in which those two genes have separated: 58, 54, 4 and 4, totaling 120 of 1,000, or 12.0%. Counting carefully matters: the pairs 58 + 54 come from single crossovers in that interval, and the double-crossover classes must be included as well. Why the others are wrong: 11.2 leaves out the double crossovers, 8.8 is the other interval, and 19.2 is the distance between the outer genes. Trap: Forgetting that double-crossover offspring are recombinant for both intervals.

qs.q: Which gene lies in the middle?
o: b
Its alleles stay with the parental arrangement.
pr
Correct: it switches sides in the double-crossover classes.
vg
Its alleles also stay with the parental arrangement.
The data cannot determine the order
The rare classes identify it.
qs.x: Correct: The parental classes are wild type for all three and mutant for all three. The rarest classes, "black, vestigial" and "purple only", differ from the parentals in the purple allele alone, so pr is the gene that changed position. The gene that appears to switch is the middle one. Why the others are wrong: Neither b nor vg changes relative to the parental combination; the rare classes do settle the order. Trap: Assuming the gene order matches the order in which the mutations are listed.

qs.q: Why are the two parental classes the most numerous?
o: The male parent contributes those combinations
He is homozygous recessive.
They result from double crossovers
Those give the rarest classes.
They carry dominant alleles that survive better
Survival differences are not described.
No crossover is needed to produce them
Correct: most meioses have none here.
qs.x: Correct: Linked genes travel together unless a crossover separates them. Because crossovers in a short interval are uncommon, most gametes carry the parental combination, giving 412 and 388 offspring. Why the others are wrong: Nothing suggests a survival difference; double crossovers produce the smallest classes; the homozygous recessive father contributes the same alleles to every offspring. Trap: Explaining class sizes by viability rather than by meiosis.

qs.q: Why is the testcross parent homozygous recessive at all three loci?
o: It contributes the same alleles each time
Correct: the phenotype reveals the other gamete.
It produces more offspring than other crosses
Fertility is not the reason.
It prevents crossing over in the female
Crossing over is unaffected.
It makes all offspring wild type
Many offspring show mutant traits.
qs.x: Correct: Because this parent can contribute only recessive alleles, each offspring's appearance is determined entirely by the gamete from the heterozygous parent, so the gametes can be counted directly from the phenotypes. Why the others are wrong: The cross does not change fertility or crossing over, and the offspring show many phenotypes. Trap: Thinking the testcross parent exists to supply variation.

qs.q: Why does the sum of the two interval distances exceed the b–vg recombination frequency?
o: The sample size was too small
The discrepancy is systematic, not random.
Recombination frequencies cannot be added
Adjacent intervals are additive in principle.
Double crossovers go uncounted
Correct: they go uncounted.
The middle gene was misidentified
The rare classes identify pr clearly.
qs.x: Correct: A double crossover swaps the middle gene but leaves b and vg in their original combination, so those offspring are scored as parental for the outer pair. The direct b–vg frequency therefore underestimates the true distance, and the sum of the two shorter intervals is the better estimate. Why the others are wrong: Adjacent map distances are added by design; the order is well supported; the effect appears regardless of sample size. Trap: Treating the longest measured interval as the most accurate.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: During fasting, falling glucose lowers insulin and raises glucagon. Glucagon acts on the liver through a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP. In the first day, glycogenolysis supplies most glucose; after that, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids becomes the main source. With prolonged fasting, the liver also makes ketone bodies from fatty acids, and the brain gradually uses them as fuel.
Healthy volunteers fasted for 5 days under medical supervision. Blood samples were collected each morning (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does glucose stay near 65 mg/dL rather than continuing to fall?
o: Muscle releases free glucose from its glycogen
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
Glycogen stores increase as the fast goes on
Glycogen is depleted in about a day.
Insulin secretion rises to protect the brain
Insulin falls.
Gluconeogenesis and ketone use spare glucose
Correct: production rises and demand falls.
qs.x: Correct: The liver makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids, while rising ketones let the brain use less glucose, so glucose levels off. Why the others are wrong: Glycogen falls; insulin drops; muscle cannot release free glucose. Trap: Assuming glycogen is the main source throughout a fast.

qs.q: Why do ketone bodies rise steeply by day 3?
o: Ketones are made from glycogen
Glycogen gives glucose.
High insulin stimulates fat breakdown
Insulin inhibits lipolysis.
Low insulin frees fatty acids
Correct: lipolysis and β-oxidation increase.
The brain releases ketone bodies into the blood
The liver makes ketones.
qs.x: Correct: Low insulin and high glucagon activate lipolysis; fatty acids reach the liver, where β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA that is converted into ketone bodies. Why the others are wrong: The brain uses but does not make ketones; ketones come from fat; insulin is low. Trap: Thinking the brain makes its own ketones.

qs.q: Which second messenger mediates glucagon's effects in the liver?
o: cGMP
This is used by nitric oxide signaling.
cAMP
Correct: glucagon receptors couple to Gs.
IP₃ alone
Gq signaling uses IP₃.
Insulin receptor substrate
This belongs to insulin signaling.
qs.x: Correct: Glucagon activates Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, which activates PKA. Why the others are wrong: cGMP is used by NO; IP₃ is a Gq messenger; IRS belongs to the insulin pathway. Trap: Mixing up the second messengers of different receptors.

qs.q: Why is the brain's use of ketone bodies important for survival during prolonged fasting?
o: It allows the brain to use fatty acids directly
Fatty acids do not cross into the brain well.
It increases insulin secretion
Insulin stays low.
It spares protein used for gluconeogenesis
Correct: less muscle is broken down.
It refills liver glycogen
Glycogen remains low.
qs.x: Correct: Less glucose demand means less gluconeogenesis from amino acids, which preserves muscle protein during a long fast. Why the others are wrong: Fatty acids are not a main brain fuel; insulin remains low; glycogen is not refilled. Trap: Forgetting the protein cost of gluconeogenesis.

qs.q: Which change would be expected in urinary nitrogen between day 1 and day 5?
o: It disappears completely by day 5
Some protein breakdown continues.
It falls as protein breakdown slows
Correct: protein sparing.
It rises steadily throughout the fast
Protein sparing lowers it later.
It does not change during fasting
Breakdown changes over time.
qs.x: Correct: Early in a fast, amino acids supply gluconeogenesis and urinary nitrogen is high; as ketones replace glucose in the brain, protein breakdown and nitrogen loss fall. Why the others are wrong: Nitrogen loss falls later; it does not reach zero; it does change. Trap: Assuming catabolism increases steadily the longer one fasts.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Sickle cell disease is caused by homozygosity for the HbS allele of the β-globin gene (HBB). Heterozygotes (HbAS) are largely healthy and are partly protected against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Researchers screened 1,000 randomly selected newborns at a regional hospital in a malaria-endemic area using hemoglobin electrophoresis.
