They found 640 HbAA, 330 HbAS and 30 HbSS newborns. The team compared these counts with the counts expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. They also screened 1,000 adults aged 20–40 years from the same region and found 590 HbAA, 404 HbAS and 6 HbSS individuals.

qs.q: What is the frequency of the HbS allele among the newborns?
o: This is the frequency of HbSS genotypes.
This counts only heterozygotes (330 / 2,000).
This is the frequency of newborns carrying any HbS allele.
qs.x: Correct: Each heterozygote carries one HbS allele and each HbSS newborn carries two: 330 + 60 = 390 alleles out of 2,000, so q = 0.195. Why the others are wrong: 0.165 omits homozygotes; 0.36 is a carrier-or-affected proportion; 0.03 is a genotype frequency. Trap: Confusing genotype frequency with allele frequency.

qs.q: Using q = 0.195, how many HbAS newborns would be expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
o: About 38
This is q² × 1,000, the expected HbSS count.
About 157
This is pq × 1,000, missing the factor of 2.
About 314
About 648
This is p² × 1,000, the expected HbAA count.
qs.x: Correct: 2pq = 2 × 0.805 × 0.195 ≈ 0.314, or about 314 newborns, close to the observed 330. Why the others are wrong: 38 and 648 are the other genotype expectations; 157 forgets the factor of two. Trap: Dropping the 2 in 2pq.

qs.q: Compared with newborns, adults have more HbAS and far fewer HbSS individuals. Which explanation best fits?
o: Selection against HbSS and for HbAS
Correct: heterozygote advantage and HbSS mortality shift adult counts.
Nonrandom mating among the adults who were screened
Mating affects offspring genotypes, not survival of the adults themselves.
Genetic drift: random changes in a small adult sample
Samples of 1,000 make large chance shifts unlikely.
New mutations converting HbAA to HbAS during childhood
Somatic changes do not alter inherited HBB genotype.
qs.x: Correct: Genotype frequencies change between birth and adulthood only if survival differs. HbSS children often die young without care, while HbAS children survive malaria better. This is balancing selection maintaining the allele. Why the others are wrong: Drift is unlikely with large samples; mutation does not convert genotypes in a lifetime; and mating patterns affect the next generation, not survival. Trap: Invoking nonrandom mating whenever genotype frequencies depart from expectation.

qs.q: Which feature of the study design limits conclusions about selection?
o: The adults were too young to have reached reproductive age
Adults aged 20–40 are of reproductive age.
Electrophoresis cannot separate hemoglobin A from S
Electrophoresis does separate HbA and HbS.
Different people were screened at birth and in adulthood
Correct: cross-sectional groups may differ for reasons besides survival.
Screening newborns at random introduces selection bias
Random selection reduces bias.
qs.x: Correct: Comparing two different cross-sectional samples assumes that adults born 20–40 years ago started with the same genotype frequencies as today's newborns, and that migration has not changed the population. A cohort followed from birth would be stronger. Why the others are wrong: Electrophoresis distinguishes HbA and HbS; random selection is a strength; and the adults are of reproductive age. Trap: Treating two snapshots as if they followed the same people.

qs.q: Why are HbAS individuals partly protected from severe falciparum malaria?
o: Heterozygotes produce antibodies against all Plasmodium species
Protection is not due to a special antibody response.
HbS binds the parasite directly and prevents it from entering cells
HbS does not block invasion directly.
HbAS red cells lack the receptors that all parasites need
Plasmodium falciparum can still invade HbAS cells.
Infected HbAS cells sickle and are cleared
Correct: early sickling and clearance limit parasite growth.
qs.x: Correct: Parasite metabolism lowers O₂ inside infected HbAS cells, promoting HbS polymerization and sickling. Sickled infected cells are removed by the spleen, limiting parasite growth. Why the others are wrong: HbS does not block invasion, the cells still have the required receptors, and no special antibody is made. Trap: Confusing sickle trait protection with Duffy-negative protection against P. vivax.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: A body at rest requires both zero net force and zero net torque. The second condition is what makes a lever analysis possible: taking torques about a chosen point, the sum of the clockwise torques equals the sum of the anticlockwise torques, and a point can be chosen so that an unknown force contributes no torque and drops out of the equation.

The lumbar spine is often analyzed this way. With the trunk bent forward, the weight of the upper body acts at a long distance from the lumbar pivot while the erector spinae muscles insert close to it, so the muscle must exert a force many times the weight it supports in order to balance the torques.

The compressive force on the disc is then the sum of the muscle force and the supported weight, which is why the compression is far larger than the weight involved. Reducing the moment arm of the load, by holding it close to the body, reduces both the required muscle force and the resulting compression.
A 70 kg person was analyzed lifting a 20 kg load at two trunk angles and two load positions (Table 1).

Both geometry and load matter, and geometry matters more. Bending with the load close raises the muscle force from 780 to 2,030 N, and extending the arms raises it further to 3,590 N without any change in the weight being lifted.

The no-load row isolates the trunk's own weight. Bending forward with nothing in the hands already requires 1,240 N of muscle force, so most of the compression in the loaded bent condition comes from supporting the upper body rather than the 20 kg load, whose weight is under 200 N.

Two limits apply. The analysis treats the erector spinae as a single muscle with one moment arm, while several muscles with different lines of action contribute, so the computed force is an aggregate. And it is a static analysis, and lifting involves acceleration, so a rapid lift produces forces above those tabulated for the same posture.

qs.q: Why is the compressive force so much larger than the weight lifted?
o: The load is held away from the body
That is true only in one row.
Compression includes the person's weight
It includes only the upper body.
The muscle has a short moment arm
Correct: it must pull hard to balance.
The disc is weaker than the muscle
Strength is not part of the calculation.
qs.x: Correct: Balancing the torque of a load acting far from the pivot with a muscle inserting close to it requires a large muscle force, and that force adds to the supported weight to compress the disc. Why the others are wrong: Tissue strength is not in the equation, the arm's-length case is one condition among four, and only the upper body's weight is supported. Trap: Explaining a mechanical result by the properties of the tissue.

qs.q: What does the no-load condition establish?
o: The load contributes nothing at all
It adds 790 N of muscle force.
The muscle moment arm changes with load
It is fixed by anatomy.
Bending forward is safe without a load
Safety is not assessed here.
Most compression comes from body weight
Correct: 1,240 N without any load.
qs.x: Correct: Bending to 60 degrees with empty hands already requires 1,240 N of muscle force against 2,030 N with the load, so supporting the trunk accounts for most of the demand. Why the others are wrong: The load does add substantially, no safety claim is made, and the muscle moment arm is anatomical. Trap: Reading a dominant contribution as the only contribution.

qs.q: Why is a pivot point chosen deliberately in such an analysis?
o: The pivot must be where the weight acts
The weight acts elsewhere.
An unknown force can be made to drop out
Correct: it exerts no torque there.
Torque is defined only about a joint
It can be taken about any point.
Only one pivot ever gives the correct answer
Any pivot gives the same answer.
qs.x: Correct: A force acting through the chosen point contributes no torque about it, so choosing the point where an unknown force acts removes that unknown from the torque equation. Why the others are wrong: Torque can be computed about any point, the pivot need not coincide with the weight, and all valid choices give the same result. Trap: Thinking the choice of pivot changes the physics rather than the algebra.

qs.q: How much extra muscle force does holding the load at arm's length require?
o: That is the load's effect when held close.
That is the effect of bending with the load close.
Correct: 3,590 against 2,030.
That compares arm's length with the no-load row.
qs.x: Correct: Muscle force rises from 2,030 N with the load held close to 3,590 N at arm's length, an increase of 1,560 N. Why the others are wrong: 790 N is the load's contribution when held close, 1,250 N is the effect of bending, and 2,350 N compares with the unloaded row. Trap: Comparing with a row that differs in more than the load position.

qs.q: Why does a rapid lift exceed these values?
o: Muscles are weaker at higher speeds
That concerns capacity, not demand.
The moment arms lengthen when moving
They change with posture, not speed.
Acceleration adds to the force required
Correct: the analysis is static.
Static analysis overestimates the forces
It underestimates them here.
qs.x: Correct: A static analysis balances torques for a body at rest, and accelerating the trunk and load requires additional force beyond that balance, so the same posture assumed quickly produces higher muscle and compressive forces. Why the others are wrong: Moment arms depend on posture, muscle capacity is a different question, and the static figures are an underestimate. Trap: Getting the direction of a static analysis's error backwards.

r: Bent 60 degrees, load held at arm's length

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: Sound intensity is power per unit area and spans an enormous range in hearing, so it is reported on a logarithmic scale. The sound level in decibels is 10 log of the ratio of the intensity to a reference intensity of 10⁻¹² watts per square metre, which is approximately the faintest audible sound at 1,000 hertz.

Two consequences of the logarithm matter. Each factor of ten in intensity adds 10 decibels, so 20 decibels represents a hundredfold intensity difference rather than a doubling, and a doubling of intensity adds about 3 decibels. Adding a second identical source therefore raises the level by 3 decibels, not by the level of that source.

Intensity also falls with distance from a point source. Power spreads over the surface of a sphere, so intensity falls as the inverse square of the distance, and each doubling of distance reduces the level by about 6 decibels.
A machine was measured at several distances in an open field, and a second identical machine was then switched on beside the first (Table 1).

Both rules appear. Each doubling of distance divides the intensity by four and lowers the level by 6 decibels, from 80 to 74 to 68, and adding the second machine doubles the intensity and raises the level by 3 decibels, from 80 to 83.

The second result is the counterintuitive one. Two machines each producing 80 decibels together produce 83 decibels rather than 160, because levels are logarithms of intensities and it is the intensities that add.

Two limits should be noted. The inverse square relationship assumes free spread in the open, and indoors reflections return energy so that the level falls more slowly with distance than the rule predicts. And the decibel scale as used here describes intensity rather than perceived loudness, which rises more slowly still, so a 10-decibel rise is usually judged as about a doubling of loudness rather than as a tenfold increase.

qs.q: Why do two 80-decibel machines produce 83 rather than 160 decibels?
o: The machines interfere destructively
No cancellation is assumed here.
Intensities add, not the levels
Correct: doubling adds 3 decibels.
Decibels cannot exceed 100 in air
Much higher levels occur.
One machine is further from the meter
Both were at one metre.
qs.x: Correct: The decibel level is a logarithm of intensity, so combining two equal sources doubles the intensity and adds 10 log 2, about 3 decibels, to the level. Why the others are wrong: No interference is assumed, both machines were at the same distance, and levels well above 100 decibels occur in practice. Trap: Adding logarithmic quantities as if they were the quantities they represent.

qs.q: Why does the level fall 6 decibels per doubling of distance?
o: Sound travels more slowly further away
Speed is essentially constant.
Intensity falls as the inverse square
Correct: a quarter is about 6 decibels.
The source becomes quieter with distance
The source output is unchanged.
Air absorbs the sound in proportion to the distance
Absorption is a smaller separate effect.
qs.x: Correct: Doubling the distance spreads the same power over four times the area, and 10 log of one quarter is about minus 6 decibels. Why the others are wrong: Absorption is a smaller additional effect, the source output is constant, and the speed of sound does not vary with distance here. Trap: Attributing geometric spreading to a property of the medium or the source.

qs.q: What does the reference intensity represent?
o: The intensity of an ordinary conversation
That is far higher.
The intensity produced by one machine
The machine is far louder.
The threshold at which damage begins
Damage occurs at much higher levels.
Approximately the faintest audible sound
Correct: at 1,000 hertz.
qs.x: Correct: The reference of 10⁻¹² watts per square metre is set near the threshold of hearing at 1,000 hertz, so 0 decibels corresponds to a barely audible sound. Why the others are wrong: Conversation, the damage threshold and the machine are all much more intense. Trap: Treating the zero of a scale as a typical rather than a threshold value.

qs.q: By what factor does the intensity rise from 4 m to 1 m with one machine?
o: About 2
That is the effect of the second machine.
About 4
That is one doubling of distance.
About 12
That matches no pair in the table.
About 16
Correct: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ against 6.3 × 10⁻⁶.
qs.x: Correct: Moving from 4 m to 1 m is two halvings of distance, so the intensity rises by a factor of four twice, about 16, which the tabulated values confirm. Why the others are wrong: Four corresponds to one halving, two to the added machine, and 12 to no comparison. Trap: Applying the inverse square rule once where the distance changed by a factor of four.

qs.q: Why does the rule fail indoors?
o: Reflections return energy to the listener
Correct: spread is not free.
Sound is absorbed completely by the walls
Walls reflect much of it.
Intensity rises with distance indoors
It still falls, but more slowly.
The decibel scale does not apply indoors
The scale applies anywhere.
qs.x: Correct: The inverse square relationship assumes energy spreads unimpeded over a sphere, and indoors reflected sound adds to the direct sound so the level falls more slowly than 6 decibels per doubling. Why the others are wrong: Walls reflect rather than fully absorb, the level still falls, and the scale is not restricted to open air. Trap: Overcorrecting a rule's failure into a reversal of its direction.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid tube, Poiseuille's law gives Q = πΔPr⁴ ÷ (8ηL), where Q is flow, ΔP the pressure difference, r the radius, η the viscosity and L the length. The fourth-power dependence on radius means small changes in vessel diameter have large effects on flow. Resistance is R = 8ηL ÷ (πr⁴), and for a given pressure difference, flow is inversely proportional to resistance. Vessels in series add their resistances directly; vessels in parallel combine so that the total resistance is less than that of any one branch.

Researchers studied an isolated rabbit artery preparation perfused with a salt solution at a fixed pressure difference of 60 mmHg. Vessel radius was measured by microscopy, and flow was collected and weighed. Drugs were added to the bath to change the smooth muscle tone of the vessel wall (Table 1).

The vessel was then replaced by one of the same radius but twice the length, and flow at baseline fell to 80 µL/min. In a final trial, the single vessel was replaced by four parallel vessels, each with half the original radius, and total flow was 40 µL/min.

In the body, the arterioles contribute most of the resistance in the circulation, which is why small changes in their smooth muscle tone have large effects on blood pressure and on how blood is distributed among organs. The capillaries are narrower still, but there are so many of them in parallel that their combined resistance is modest, and their total cross-sectional area is far larger than that of the aorta, so blood moves through them slowly enough for exchange to occur.

The researchers noted that blood is not a Newtonian fluid: its viscosity depends on the shear rate and on hematocrit, and in vessels narrower than about 300 µm the red cells line up near the center, which lowers the effective viscosity.

qs.q: Why did a 16% fall in radius cut flow by half?
o: Flow depends on the fourth power of radius
Correct: 0.84⁴ ≈ 0.5.
The pressure difference fell with the radius
Pressure was held at 60 mmHg.
Norepinephrine also raised the viscosity
Viscosity stayed at 1.0.
The vessel became longer as it narrowed
Length was unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: Flow is proportional to r⁴, so multiplying the radius by 0.84 multiplies flow by 0.84⁴ ≈ 0.50, taking it from 160 to 79 µL/min. Why the others are wrong: Viscosity, pressure and length were all held constant in that comparison. Trap: Expecting flow to change in proportion to the radius.

qs.q: By Poiseuille's law, what flow would a tripling of viscosity alone predict?
o: 13 µL/min
This divides by 12.
53 µL/min
Correct: 160 ÷ 3.
160 µL/min
Viscosity appears in the denominator.
480 µL/min
This multiplies instead of dividing.
qs.x: Correct: Flow is inversely proportional to viscosity, so tripling η divides flow by 3: 160 ÷ 3 ≈ 53 µL/min, which matches the measured value. Why the others are wrong: Higher viscosity lowers flow; flow cannot stay the same; dividing by 12 has no basis. Trap: Treating viscosity like radius, which acts in the opposite direction.

qs.q: Why did flow halve when the vessel length doubled?
o: Pressure is lost at the junctions
A single vessel was used.
The fluid cooled along the longer path
Temperature is not mentioned as varying.
Longer vessels have smaller radii
Radius was matched.
Resistance is proportional to length
Correct: twice the resistance halves the flow.
qs.x: Correct: In R = 8ηL ÷ (πr⁴), resistance rises in direct proportion to length. Doubling L doubles R, and at fixed pressure difference, flow falls by half, from 160 to 80 µL/min. Why the others are wrong: The replacement vessel had the same radius; there were no junctions; no temperature change is described. Trap: Assuming length matters as much as radius.

qs.q: Why did four parallel half-radius vessels carry less flow than the single vessel?
o: The pressure difference is divided among branches
Each branch sees the full difference.
Flow cannot be measured in parallel vessels
It was measured as 40 µL/min.
Each branch has 16 times the resistance
Correct: four of them still total four times.
Parallel vessels always raise resistance
Parallel paths lower it for identical vessels.
qs.x: Correct: Halving the radius multiplies one vessel's resistance by 2⁴ = 16. Four such vessels in parallel give 16 ÷ 4 = 4 times the original resistance, so flow falls to one-quarter, from 160 to 40 µL/min. Why the others are wrong: Adding parallel paths of the same size lowers resistance; each parallel branch experiences the same pressure difference; total flow was measured. Trap: Assuming that more vessels always means more flow.

qs.q: Why can Poiseuille's law only approximate flow in small arterioles in the body?
o: Blood flow in arterioles is always turbulent
It is usually laminar.
Arterioles are not cylindrical
They are approximately cylindrical.
Arterioles have no pressure difference across them
They have the largest drop.
Blood's viscosity is not constant
Correct: it is not Newtonian.
qs.x: Correct: The law assumes constant viscosity, but blood's viscosity depends on shear rate and hematocrit, and in small vessels the red cells concentrate centrally, lowering effective viscosity. Vessel walls are also elastic rather than rigid. Why the others are wrong: Arterioles produce the largest pressure drop in the circulation; flow there is normally laminar; their shape is roughly cylindrical. Trap: Applying an idealized equation without checking its assumptions.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: An incompressible fluid in steady flow carries the same volume per second past every cross-section of a tube, so the product of area and speed is constant: a narrowing raises the speed in inverse proportion to the area. Because area varies with the square of the radius, halving a radius quadruples the speed.

Bernoulli's relation then links speed to pressure. Along a streamline, the sum of the static pressure, the kinetic term and the height term is constant, so where the fluid speeds up the static pressure falls. A constriction therefore shows a higher speed and a lower pressure than the wide sections on either side.

This holds only while the flow remains smooth. Above a critical speed the flow becomes turbulent, energy is dissipated in eddies, and the pressure drop along the tube exceeds what Bernoulli's relation predicts, so the relation describes the ideal case and underestimates real losses.
Flow through a tube with a constriction was measured at several flow rates (Table 1).

The continuity relation holds throughout. The constriction has one quarter the area and the speed is four times greater at both flow rates, 63.7 against 15.9 and 509 against 127 cm per second, which is what conservation of volume requires.

The pressure behaves as predicted only at the lower rate. At 50 mL per second the constriction shows a small pressure drop consistent with the speed increase, while at 400 mL per second the flow turns turbulent and the pressure falls by 12.2 kPa, far more than the kinetic term accounts for.

Two points qualify this. The pressures are static pressures measured at the wall, and a reading taken facing the flow would include the kinetic term and behave quite differently. And blood is not strictly incompressible or Newtonian, and in vessels of small diameter its effective viscosity falls, so these relations describe large vessels better than capillaries.

qs.q: Why does the speed quadruple in the constriction?
o: Area varies with the square of the radius
Correct: a quarter the area.
The fluid is compressed as it enters
The fluid is incompressible.
Pressure simply pushes the fluid faster there
Pressure falls rather than driving it.
Viscosity is lower in narrow tubes
That is a separate blood effect.
qs.x: Correct: Halving the radius quarters the cross-sectional area, and carrying the same volume per second through a quarter of the area requires four times the speed. Why the others are wrong: The pressure drops rather than accelerating the fluid, the fluid is incompressible, and the viscosity effect is a separate matter concerning blood. Trap: Explaining a consequence of continuity by a pressure difference that follows from it.

qs.q: Why does the pressure drop exceed the prediction at the higher rate?
o: Turbulence dissipates energy in eddies
Correct: Bernoulli assumes smooth flow.
The fluid becomes compressible there
It remains incompressible.
The kinetic term grows with speed
It grows but accounts for less.
The radius decreases even further at high speed
The tube is rigid.
qs.x: Correct: Bernoulli's relation conserves energy along a streamline, and turbulent flow converts some of it into disordered motion and heat, so the measured pressure falls by more than the kinetic term alone requires. Why the others are wrong: The tube is rigid, the kinetic term is included in the prediction, and the fluid stays incompressible. Trap: Choosing the term the prediction already contains.

qs.q: What does the continuity relation express?
o: Energy is conserved along a streamline
That is Bernoulli's relation.
Equal volume passes every cross-section
Correct: conservation of volume.
Speed is the same along the tube
Speed varies with area.
Pressure is just the same all along the tube
Pressure varies with speed.
qs.x: Correct: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow the volume per second is the same everywhere, which is why area and speed vary inversely. Why the others are wrong: Pressure and speed both vary along the tube, and energy conservation along a streamline is the separate Bernoulli relation. Trap: Confusing the volume conservation statement with the energy one.

qs.q: What is the pressure drop across the constriction at 400 mL per second?
o: That is the drop at 50 mL per second.
That compares the two wide sections.
12.2 kPa
Correct: 99.4 minus 87.2.
That compares the two constrictions.
qs.x: Correct: The wide section reads 99.4 kPa and the constriction 87.2 kPa at that flow rate, a drop of 12.2 kPa. Why the others are wrong: 0.2 kPa is the drop at the lower rate, and the other values compare rows at different flow rates. Trap: Comparing sections across flow rates rather than within one.

qs.q: Why would a pressure reading facing the flow behave differently?
o: It could not be measured at all
Such readings are routinely taken.
It would be identical to the static value
It would be higher.
It would include the kinetic term
Correct: static pressure excludes it.
It would be unaffected by the speed
It depends directly on speed.
qs.x: Correct: A port facing upstream brings the fluid to rest against it, so the reading includes the kinetic energy converted to pressure and rises where the static pressure falls. Why the others are wrong: Such measurements are standard, the reading differs from the static value, and it depends strongly on speed. Trap: Treating all pressure measurements in a flowing fluid as equivalent.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Whether it floats therefore depends on the comparison of densities: a body less dense than the fluid floats with part of its volume above the surface, and the submerged fraction equals the ratio of the body's density to the fluid's.

Apparent weight follows from the same principle. A body weighed while submerged reads less than in air by exactly the buoyant force, so measuring both gives the displaced volume and hence the body's density without knowing its shape.

Human body composition is estimated this way. Fat is less dense than water and lean tissue is denser, so a person's whole-body density predicts the proportion of fat, provided the air in the lungs is accounted for, since trapped air lowers the measured density and inflates the estimate of fat.
Objects and a person were weighed in air and submerged in fresh water (Table 1).

The method works from the difference of two weights. The aluminium block loses 10.0 N when submerged, which corresponds to a displaced volume of about 1,020 cm³ and a density of 2.70 g per cubic centimetre, and the bone sample loses two thirds of its weight, giving 1.50.

The two lung conditions show the correction that matters. With the lungs emptied the person's density is 1.03 g per cubic centimetre and they sink slowly; with the lungs filled the apparent weight is negative, meaning the buoyant force exceeds their weight and they float, and the computed density of 0.96 is not a density of tissue at all.

Two limits are worth noting. Residual air remains in the lungs even after a maximal exhalation and must be measured separately or estimated, and an error there translates directly into an error in the fat estimate. And the relationship between whole-body density and fat proportion assumes fixed densities for fat and lean tissue, which vary with age and with bone mineral content.

qs.q: Why is the lungs-filled density not a tissue density?
o: Water enters the lungs during the test
The lungs hold air, not water.
Trapped air is counted as part of the body
Correct: it lowers the figure.
The scale cannot ever read negative weights
The negative value is meaningful.
Lung tissue is denser than other tissue
Its density is not the issue.
qs.x: Correct: The computation treats everything inside the body outline as body, so air in the lungs adds volume without mass and drives the computed density below that of any tissue. Why the others are wrong: A negative apparent weight is a real measurement of net upward force, the lungs hold air, and lung tissue density is not what produces the result. Trap: Taking a computed quantity as a property of the material when the measurement included something else.

qs.q: Why does weighing in air and in water give the density?
o: Water has a density of exactly one
That is a convenience, not the principle.
The weight lost equals the displaced fluid
Correct: that gives the volume.
Apparent weight is proportional to density
It depends on volume as well.
The scale is more accurate in water
Accuracy is unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: The difference between the two readings is the buoyant force, which equals the weight of the displaced fluid and therefore gives the volume, and mass divided by that volume is the density. Why the others are wrong: Scale accuracy is the same, water's convenient density simplifies arithmetic rather than supplying the principle, and apparent weight depends on both mass and volume. Trap: Choosing a convenient numerical fact instead of the physical relation.

qs.q: What determines the fraction of a floating body that is submerged?
o: The depth of the fluid beneath it
Depth is irrelevant to floating.
The shape of the body involved
Shape affects stability, not the fraction.
The ratio of the two densities
Correct: body to fluid.
The total mass of the body
Mass alone does not set it.
qs.x: Correct: A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid, so the submerged volume divided by the total volume equals the body's density divided by the fluid's. Why the others are wrong: Mass, shape and depth do not enter that ratio. Trap: Supposing a larger body floats differently from a small one of the same material.

qs.q: How much weight does the bone sample lose when submerged?
o: That is its apparent weight.
Correct: 6.0 minus 2.0.
That is its weight in air.
That is the aluminium block's loss.
qs.x: Correct: The bone sample weighs 6.0 N in air and 2.0 N submerged, so it loses 4.0 N to buoyancy. Why the others are wrong: 2.0 and 6.0 N are the two weights themselves and 10.0 N is the aluminium block's loss. Trap: Reporting one of the measured weights rather than their difference.

qs.q: Why does residual lung air limit the fat estimate?
o: Residual air can never really be measured at all
It is measured separately.
It affects only the lungs-filled reading
It affects both readings.
Residual air has the density of tissue
It has the density of air.
An error in it feeds straight into the result
Correct: it changes the volume.
qs.x: Correct: The computed density depends on the volume attributed to tissue, so a misestimate of the air still in the lungs after exhalation shifts that volume and propagates directly into the fat proportion derived from it. Why the others are wrong: Residual volume is measurable, air is far less dense than tissue, and residual air is present in both conditions. Trap: Assuming a correction applies only to the condition where the quantity is largest.

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: A patch of neuronal membrane behaves like a resistor and a capacitor in parallel. The lipid bilayer separates charge and acts as a capacitor; the ion channels provide a resistive path. When a steady current is injected, the membrane voltage does not jump but approaches its final value along an exponential curve, V(t) = V_final(1 − e^(−t/τ)), where the membrane time constant τ = RC. The voltage reaches about 63% of its final value after one time constant.

The final voltage change is set by Ohm's law, ΔV = IR, where R is the membrane resistance. Opening more channels lowers R, so the same current produces a smaller voltage change and the membrane responds faster. Myelin adds layers of membrane in series, which lowers capacitance per unit length and raises resistance across the wall.
Researchers injected 0.2 nA of current into cultured neurons through a microelectrode and recorded the voltage change at the injection site (Table 1).

These properties explain why a neuron does not respond instantly to its inputs. A brief synaptic current produces a voltage change that rises and decays over several milliseconds, so inputs arriving close together in time add up, a process called temporal summation. A membrane with a long time constant sums inputs over a longer window, which makes the cell more sensitive to steady input but slower to follow rapid changes. The researchers measured summation directly by injecting pairs of brief current pulses 5 ms apart and found that the second pulse produced a larger voltage change in the blocker condition than in the control.

The researchers also measured how far a voltage signal spread along a process from the injection point. The signal fell to 37% of its starting size after 0.6 mm in control neurons and after 1.1 mm in neurons whose membrane resistance had been doubled by a channel blocker.

qs.q: Why does the channel blocker double the voltage change?
o: Fewer open channels raise resistance
Correct: ΔV = IR with larger R.
The blocker increases membrane capacitance
Capacitance stayed at 400 pF.
The blocker shortens the time constant
It doubled to 40 ms.
The blocker increases the injected current
Current was fixed at 0.2 nA.
qs.x: Correct: Blocking channels removes parallel paths for ion flow, so resistance rises from 50 to 100 MΩ. With the same 0.2 nA injected, ΔV = IR doubles from 10 to 20 mV. Why the others are wrong: The current was set by the experimenter; capacitance depends on membrane area, which did not change; the time constant lengthened. Trap: Looking for a change in current when the resistance changed.

qs.q: What is the membrane resistance in the control condition, in megaohms?
o: This divides current by voltage.
This is the time constant.
Correct: 10 mV ÷ 0.2 nA.
This is off by a factor of ten.
qs.x: Correct: R = ΔV ÷ I = 10 × 10⁻³ V ÷ 0.2 × 10⁻⁹ A = 5 × 10⁷ Ω = 50 MΩ. Why the others are wrong: Dividing current by voltage gives conductance; 20 is the time constant in milliseconds; 500 misplaces a power of ten. Trap: Mixing units of millivolts and nanoamperes.

qs.q: Why does the larger neuron have the same time constant as the blocker condition?
o: Larger neurons always respond more slowly
Its τ equals the blocker condition's.
Lower resistance, higher capacitance
Correct: τ = RC is unchanged in product.
Its capacitance is unchanged by size
Capacitance rose fourfold.
Current spreads faster in large cells
Speed here is set by τ.
qs.x: Correct: The larger cell has four times the membrane area, so capacitance rises from 400 to 1,600 pF while resistance falls from 50 to 25 MΩ. The product RC is 25 MΩ × 1,600 pF = 40 ms, the same as 100 MΩ × 400 pF. Why the others are wrong: Its time constant matches another condition rather than being the slowest; capacitance scales with area; the time constant is what sets the response speed. Trap: Assuming the time constant depends on cell size alone.

qs.q: Why does a signal spread farther when membrane resistance is doubled?
o: The injected current was increased
Current was fixed.
Less current leaks across the membrane
Correct: more travels along the process.
The capacitance of the membrane falls
Capacitance was unchanged.
The internal resistance of the axon falls
The blocker acts on the membrane.
qs.x: Correct: Current injected at one point either travels along the inside of the process or leaks out across the membrane. Raising membrane resistance reduces the leak, so more current travels farther before the voltage decays, from 0.6 to 1.1 mm. Why the others are wrong: The internal resistance of the cytoplasm is unchanged; capacitance stayed constant; the current was fixed. Trap: Treating spread as a property of the cytoplasm alone.

qs.q: How does myelin speed conduction, in terms of these properties?
o: It raises capacitance so charge builds faster
Higher capacitance slows the voltage change.
It increases the current each channel passes
Channels are concentrated at the nodes, not altered.
It lowers the resistance of the axon's interior
Myelin wraps the outside.
It lowers capacitance and raises resistance
Correct: less charge stored, less leak.
qs.x: Correct: Wrapping many membrane layers in series reduces capacitance per unit length, so less charge is needed to change the voltage, and raises resistance across the wall, so less current leaks out. Both shorten the time constant and lengthen the distance a signal spreads, letting the depolarization reach the next node quickly. Why the others are wrong: Higher capacitance would slow the response; myelin is outside the axon; the channels themselves are unchanged. Trap: Assuming myelin works by making ions move faster.

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: Copper is an essential trace element, but dissolved Cu²⁺ above about 2 mg/L (roughly 3 × 10⁻⁵ M) in drinking water can cause nausea, and long exposure can damage the liver. Because copper enters tap water mainly from household pipes, inexpensive field tests are useful. One approach uses a galvanic cell whose voltage depends on the Cu²⁺ concentration.

A student group built a cell from a zinc strip in 1.0 M Zn(NO₃)₂ and a copper strip in the test solution. The two beakers were joined by a U-tube salt bridge filled with KNO₃ in agar, and the strips were connected to a high-resistance voltmeter so that almost no current flowed during readings. The relevant half-reactions are:

Under these conditions, the Nernst equation for the cell at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, where Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. The students first measured standard solutions to make a calibration curve (Table 1), then tested a sample of tap water from an old building and a second sample that had been concentrated 1000-fold by evaporation.

The group noted two limits of the method. First, the calibration assumes that the solutions are dilute enough for concentration to stand in for activity; in more concentrated solutions, ions interact and the measured voltage drifts from the prediction. Second, other dissolved metal ions that are easily reduced, such as Ag⁺, could also deposit on the copper strip and distort the reading. Neither was expected to matter for household water, but the group ran each sample in triplicate and discarded any run that drifted by more than 2 mV over one minute.

The concentrated tap-water sample gave a reading of 1.055 V. In a separate trial, the students removed the salt bridge and laid a glass rod across the two beakers; the voltmeter then read 0.000 V. Finally, they left one cell connected through a small resistor for 6 hours and noted that the voltage slowly fell, the copper strip gained mass, and the zinc strip lost mass.

qs.q: What is the approximate Cu²⁺ concentration of the concentrated tap-water sample?
o: This would read about 1.025 V.
Correct: 1.055 V lies between the 0.01 M and 0.1 M readings.
1.055 V is below the 0.10 M reading.
3 M
This would read above 1.10 V.
qs.x: Correct: Each tenfold change in [Cu²⁺] shifts the voltage by about 0.030 V. The reading of 1.055 V is about halfway between 1.040 V (0.010 M) and 1.071 V (0.10 M), so log[Cu²⁺] ≈ −1.5 and [Cu²⁺] ≈ 0.03 M. Undoing the 1000-fold concentration gives about 3 × 10⁻⁵ M in the tap water, right at the level of concern. Why the others are wrong: 0.003 M would read about 1.025 V; 0.3 M and 3 M would read at or above 1.085 V. Trap: Interpolating linearly in concentration instead of in log concentration.

qs.q: Why does each tenfold drop in [Cu²⁺] lower the voltage by about 30 mV rather than 59 mV?
o: Two electrons move per copper ion reduced
Correct: n = 2 halves the 0.0592 V term.
The salt bridge absorbs half of the potential
A salt bridge does not divide the voltage.
The zinc half-cell offsets half of the change
[Zn²⁺] was held constant at 1.0 M.
Only half of the Cu²⁺ ions reach the electrode
Concentration, not delivery, enters the equation.
qs.x: Correct: In the Nernst equation the log term is multiplied by 0.0592/n. Because n = 2 for Cu²⁺/Cu and Zn²⁺/Zn, a tenfold change in Q changes E by 0.0592/2 ≈ 0.030 V, as the calibration data show. Why the others are wrong: The zinc concentration was fixed, so it contributes no change; the equation depends on concentration, not on how many ions reach the metal; the salt bridge carries ions and does not split the voltage. Trap: Using the one-electron value of 59 mV per decade for every cell.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the 0.000 V reading with the glass rod?
o: The glass rod short-circuits the two half-cells
Glass is an insulator.
Charge can no longer be balanced by ion movement
Correct: the circuit is open without an ionic path.
Zn²⁺ ions are no longer able to reach the copper electrode
Zn²⁺ is not supposed to reach the copper.
Electrons can no longer travel through the bridge
Electrons travel through the external wire.
qs.x: Correct: As the cell runs, the zinc beaker gains positive ions and the copper beaker loses them. Ions moving through the salt bridge keep each beaker neutral. A glass rod carries no ions, so the circuit is incomplete and no potential difference can be measured. Why the others are wrong: Electrons move through the wire, never through the salt bridge; Zn²⁺ ions are not meant to cross to the copper side; glass does not conduct, so it cannot short the cell. Trap: Thinking the salt bridge carries electrons.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the voltage fell while the cell ran for 6 hours?
o: The zinc strip became smaller and less reactive
Electrode size does not appear in the Nernst equation.
The reaction became nonspontaneous after 1 hour
E stayed positive while it fell slowly.
Q rose as Cu²⁺ was used up and Zn²⁺ formed
Correct: a larger Q lowers E.
E° fell as copper metal plated onto the strip
E° is a fixed property of the half-reactions.
qs.x: Correct: The copper strip gained mass and the zinc strip lost mass, so Cu²⁺ was reduced and Zn was oxidized. [Cu²⁺] fell and [Zn²⁺] rose, raising Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]; by the Nernst equation, E decreases as Q increases and reaches zero only at equilibrium. Why the others are wrong: Standard potentials do not change during a run; electrode size does not set the voltage; a slowly falling but positive voltage shows the reaction is still spontaneous. Trap: Treating E° as if it were the voltage at any moment.

qs.q: Which change would make the cell's voltage respond more strongly to each tenfold change in [Cu²⁺]?
o: Raising [Zn²⁺] in the zinc beaker from 1.0 M to 2.0 M
This shifts every reading but keeps the slope.
Using a copper strip with twice the area
Electrode area does not enter the equation.
Using a longer salt bridge with more KNO₃
Bridge length does not change the Nernst slope.
Running the cell at a higher temperature
Correct: the slope 2.303RT/nF grows with T.
qs.x: Correct: The 0.0592 V term is 2.303RT/F evaluated at 298 K. Because it is proportional to absolute temperature, a warmer cell gives a slightly larger voltage change per decade of [Cu²⁺]. Why the others are wrong: Electrode area affects how much current can flow, not the equilibrium voltage; changing [Zn²⁺] shifts every reading by the same amount but leaves the change per decade unchanged; salt-bridge length affects resistance, not the Nernst slope. Trap: Confusing a shift of the whole calibration line with a change in its slope.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Self-esteem is a global evaluation of one's own worth. Self-concept is the broader set of beliefs a person holds about themselves, organized into domains such as academic ability, appearance, athletic competence and social acceptance. The two are related but not the same: self-concept supplies the content and self-esteem is an overall appraisal drawn from it.

How the appraisal is drawn is the interesting part. The weighting is not equal across domains. A person's global self-esteem depends most on the domains they consider important, so poor self-rated athletic ability lowers self-esteem in someone for whom sport matters and leaves it untouched in someone for whom it does not. This is why two people with identical domain profiles can differ in global self-esteem.

Social comparison supplies much of the domain content. A student's academic self-concept depends less on absolute attainment than on standing relative to the immediate comparison group, which is why the same student can hold a higher academic self-concept in an average school than in a selective one.

Investigators surveyed 1,100 adolescents, measuring global self-esteem, self-rated competence in four domains, and how important each domain was to the respondent, then computed the correlation of each domain with global self-esteem separately among those who rated it important and those who did not (Table 1).

The pattern is the same in all four domains: a domain is strongly related to global self-esteem among people who care about it and weakly related among those who do not, which is the weighting account in a single table.

Two limits are worth stating. Importance and competence were both reported by the respondent at the same sitting, so a person may call a domain important partly because they do well in it, which would produce the pattern without any weighting. And nothing in a cross-sectional survey shows direction, since low self-esteem could lead a person to dismiss domains in which they struggle, a protective move that would also produce the observed split.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the weighting account?
o: Domains correlate equally whatever their importance
Correct: weighting would do no work.
Self-esteem is lower on average in adolescence
That concerns the level, not the structure.
Appearance correlates most strongly of the four domains
That is a ranking, not a test.
Competence ratings are correlated across the domains
That concerns domain overlap.
qs.x: Correct: The account says importance determines how much a domain contributes, so finding the same correlation whether or not a domain is rated important would leave the weighting idea with nothing to explain. Why the others are wrong: Which domain ranks highest, the average level of self-esteem and correlations among domains are all separate questions. Trap: Choosing a prominent feature of the table rather than the result that tests the claim.

qs.q: How does self-concept differ from self-esteem?
o: It applies only to academic performance
It spans several domains.
It is entirely fixed in childhood and does not change
Both shift over the life course.
It cannot be measured by self-report
Both are measured by self-report.
It is the content rather than the overall appraisal
Correct: beliefs against evaluation.
qs.x: Correct: Self-concept is the organized set of beliefs about oneself across domains, while self-esteem is the single global evaluation of worth that is drawn from that content. Why the others are wrong: Neither is fixed in childhood, self-concept is not restricted to academics, and both are routinely measured by questionnaire. Trap: Treating the broader construct as a subtype of the narrower one.

qs.q: Why can the same student hold a higher academic self-concept in an average school?
o: Academic ability itself rises in that setting
Ability is what is being judged.
The comparison group sets the standard
Correct: standing is relative.
Self-concept does not depend on performance
It depends on relative performance.
Grading is more generous in average schools
Grading practice is not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: Academic self-concept is built from standing relative to the people a student sees daily, so the same attainment places a student higher in an average school and lower in a selective one. Why the others are wrong: Grading practice is a separate matter, ability is the thing judged rather than the cause, and performance does matter, in relative terms. Trap: Looking for a change in the student when the change is in the reference group.

qs.q: Which alternative explanation does this survey leave open?
o: Four domains is too few to study the self
More domains would show the same split.
Appearance clearly matters to most adolescents generally
That is consistent with the account.
People may call a domain important when they do well
Correct: importance may follow competence.
Global self-esteem is one overall evaluation
That is the construct's definition.
qs.x: Correct: Because importance and competence were reported together, a respondent may rate a domain important because they are competent in it, which would produce the same correlational split with no weighting of domains taking place. Why the others are wrong: The salience of appearance fits the account, the definition of self-esteem is not an alternative, and adding domains would not change the logic. Trap: Mistaking a feature of the construct for a rival explanation.

qs.q: Which domain shows the largest gap between the two columns?
o: 0.31, social acceptance
The smallest gap in the table.
0.36, appearance and academic ability
Both fall just short of the largest.
0.37, athletic competence
Correct: 0.41 against 0.04.
0.41, the athletic importance correlation
That is a correlation, not a gap.
qs.x: Correct: Athletic competence falls from 0.41 among those who rate it important to 0.04 among those who do not, a gap of 0.37, the largest in the table. Why the others are wrong: Appearance and academic ability both show gaps of 0.36, social acceptance the smallest at 0.31, and 0.41 is one of the correlations rather than a difference. Trap: Reading a single column instead of subtracting the two.

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: In electrolysis, an external power supply forces a nonspontaneous redox reaction. The charge passed is Q = It, and Faraday's laws relate charge to moles of electrons: moles of e⁻ = It ÷ F, with F = 96,485 C/mol. The mass deposited follows from the stoichiometry of the half-reaction.
Students electroplated copper from CuSO₄ solution onto a cathode at a constant 1.5 A (Table 1). The molar mass of copper is 63.5 g/mol.

qs.q: How many moles of electrons pass in 20 minutes?
o: This divides by 2 as well.
This multiplies by 2.
This omits Faraday's constant.
qs.x: Correct: moles e⁻ = Q ÷ F = 1,800 ÷ 96,485 ≈ 0.0187 mol. Why the others are wrong: Each applies an extra factor or omits F. Trap: Applying the 2-electron stoichiometry at the wrong step.

qs.q: What mass of copper should 1,800 C deposit?
o: This uses 900 C.
This omits the division by 2.
This is the molar mass.
qs.x: Correct: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles Cu = 0.0187 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.00933, and mass = 0.00933 × 63.5 ≈ 0.59 g, matching the data. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a step or uses the wrong charge. Trap: Forgetting that two electrons deposit one copper atom.

qs.q: Why is electrolysis nonspontaneous?
o: Its cell potential is negative
Correct: work must be supplied.
It has a negative ΔG
A negative ΔG means spontaneous.
Its cell potential is positive but small
Positive means spontaneous.
It requires no external energy
A power supply is needed.
qs.x: Correct: The forced reaction has E°cell < 0 and ΔG° > 0, so electrical work from an external source is required. Why the others are wrong: Positive E° and negative ΔG describe spontaneous reactions; external energy is required. Trap: Mixing up the signs of E° and ΔG.

qs.q: At which electrode is copper deposited?
o: The anode, where oxidation occurs
Oxidation does not deposit metal here.
Both electrodes equally
Deposition occurs at one.
Neither, since copper stays in solution
Mass is deposited.
The cathode, where reduction occurs
Correct: Cu²⁺ gains electrons.
qs.x: Correct: Reduction always occurs at the cathode, where Cu²⁺ gains two electrons and plates out as metal. Why the others are wrong: Oxidation occurs at the anode; deposition is at one electrode; mass was measured. Trap: Mixing up the electrodes between galvanic and electrolytic cells.

qs.q: To deposit silver (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) instead, how would the mass per coulomb compare?
o: Exactly the same moles per coulomb
Stoichiometry differs.
Fewer moles of metal per coulomb
One electron per atom needs less charge.
More moles of metal per coulomb
Correct: only one electron is needed.
No metal would be deposited
Silver plates readily.
qs.x: Correct: Because silver requires one electron per atom instead of two, the same charge deposits twice as many moles of metal. Why the others are wrong: Fewer electrons per atom means more atoms; stoichiometry differs; silver does plate. Trap: Comparing masses without accounting for electron stoichiometry and molar mass separately.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: When cells are placed in a solution, water moves by osmosis toward the side with higher concentration of impermeant solutes. Human red blood cells (RBCs) have an internal osmolarity of about 290 mOsm/L. A solution is isotonic when it causes no net change in cell volume, which depends on whether solutes can cross the membrane.

A student placed RBCs in five solutions and measured cell volume after 10 minutes and the percentage of cells that lysed (Table 1). Urea crosses the RBC membrane readily, while NaCl and sucrose do not.

qs.q: Why did cells lyse in 300 mM urea although its osmolarity is close to 290 mOsm/L?
o: Urea enters, and water follows it
Correct: a permeant solute is not effective osmotically.
Urea is hypertonic, so cells shrink and burst
Shrinking cells do not burst.
Urea dissolves the phospholipid bilayer
Urea does not dissolve membranes at this concentration.
Urea pumps Na⁺ into the cells actively
Urea is not a pump.
qs.x: Correct: Urea crosses the membrane until its concentration is equal on both sides. Inside, it adds to the cell's own impermeant solutes, so water enters and the cells swell and burst. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic. Why the others are wrong: Urea is not a detergent; shrinking cells crenate; urea does not pump ions. Trap: Equating isosmotic with isotonic.

qs.q: Which solution caused the cells to shrink the most?
o: 0.45% NaCl
Cells swelled in this solution.
0.9% NaCl
This is isotonic.
2.0% NaCl
Correct: relative volume fell to 0.62.
300 mM sucrose
Volume barely changed.
qs.x: Correct: 2.0% NaCl is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and volume falls to 0.62. Why the others are wrong: 0.45% NaCl is hypotonic; sucrose and 0.9% NaCl are near isotonic. Trap: Confusing hypotonic and hypertonic.

qs.q: Why did only 45% of cells lyse in 0.45% NaCl?
o: Cells differ in how much swelling they withstand
Correct: fragility varies among cells.
Half the cells were already isotonic to the solution
All cells began at about 290 mOsm/L.
NaCl at this concentration repairs membranes
Salt does not repair membranes.
Half the cells lack aquaporins and cannot swell
All cells swelled on average.
qs.x: Correct: Older and more spherical RBCs have less spare membrane and burst sooner, so lysis in a moderately hypotonic solution is partial. Why the others are wrong: Average volume rose; salt has no repair effect; cells started with the same osmolarity. Trap: Expecting an all-or-none response from a population.

qs.q: Which term describes 300 mM sucrose relative to RBCs?
o: Strongly hypotonic
Cells would swell.
Approximately isotonic
Correct: impermeant and near 290 mOsm/L.
Hypotonic, because sucrose enters cells
Sucrose does not cross the RBC membrane.
Strongly hypertonic
Cells would shrink.
qs.x: Correct: Sucrose cannot cross the membrane and has nearly the same osmolarity as cytoplasm, so volume barely changes. Why the others are wrong: Large volume changes would occur in strongly hypo- or hypertonic solutions; sucrose is impermeant. Trap: Treating every solute as permeant like urea.

qs.q: A patient receives a large volume of 5% dextrose in water (about 280 mOsm/L) intravenously. What happens to RBC volume after the glucose is taken up and metabolized?
o: It decreases, because water moves into the kidney tubules
This does not determine RBC volume.
It decreases, because glucose raises plasma osmolarity
Glucose is removed by metabolism.
It stays the same, because the solution was isosmotic
Isosmotic is not isotonic once glucose is used.
It increases, because free water is left
Correct: the solution becomes effectively hypotonic.
qs.x: Correct: Glucose is transported into cells and metabolized, leaving water that dilutes plasma and causes cells to swell. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not stay in plasma; isosmotic does not mean isotonic; renal handling does not set RBC volume directly. Trap: Judging tonicity by initial osmolarity alone.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out a specific action in a specific situation. It is not global self-worth; a person can hold high self-efficacy for public speaking and low self-efficacy for swimming. The distinction matters because self-efficacy predicts behavior in the domain it refers to, while global self-esteem predicts it weakly.

Four sources are proposed, and they are not interchangeable. Mastery experience, the direct experience of succeeding at a graded version of the task, is held to be the strongest, because it supplies evidence that is hard to discount. Vicarious experience works through observing a model, and depends on the observer judging the model to be similar to themselves. Verbal persuasion works through what a credible other says. The fourth source is the interpretation of physiological arousal: a racing heart read as fear lowers efficacy, while the same arousal read as readiness does not.

Eighty adults enrolled in a beginners' swimming course were randomly assigned to one of four confidence-building sessions held before their first attempt in deep water. Self-efficacy was rated on a ten-point scale immediately after the session, and completion of the deep-water swim was recorded (Table 1).

The ordering matches the theory's ranking, with mastery first and verbal persuasion last, and the two columns move together, which is what the construct predicts: efficacy ratings should track behavior in the same domain.

Three limits deserve note. The relaxation condition manipulated the level of arousal rather than its interpretation, so it does not test the fourth source as the theory states it; a condition reframing arousal as readiness would. Self-efficacy was also rated after the session but before the swim, so the ratings may partly reflect how encouraging each session felt rather than a stable belief. Finally, randomization was to session type, not to the outcome measure, and the instructor who recorded completions knew which session each participant had received.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 fits the theory's ranking of the four sources?
o: Graded mastery produced the highest rating and the highest completion rate
Correct: mastery is held to be strongest.
Verbal encouragement outperformed watching a similar peer succeed
It ranked last.
Relaxation training outperformed every one of the other approaches tested here
It ranked third.
The four approaches produced essentially identical results
They differ by 34 points.
qs.x: Correct: The theory ranks mastery experience first, and the mastery condition leads on both the efficacy rating of 7.9 and the completion rate of 78%, with verbal persuasion last on both as the theory also predicts. Why the others are wrong: Relaxation ranked third, encouragement ranked below modeling, and the conditions differ substantially rather than being equivalent. Trap: Checking only one of the two columns before deciding the ranking holds.

qs.q: Why does the modeling condition use a peer judged to be similar?
o: Similar peers are generally able to give much more accurate instruction
Modeling is observation, not instruction.
Observing a similar peer eliminates physiological arousal
Arousal is a separate source.
Peers who are similar swim faster than expert models do
Speed is not the variable.
Similarity makes the model's success feel relevant to the observer
Correct: it supports the inference.
qs.x: Correct: Vicarious experience works by inference, and the inference that a success is achievable for oneself is only warranted if the model is comparable, so similarity is what converts an observation into evidence about one's own capability. Why the others are wrong: Modeling involves watching rather than being taught, arousal is a distinct source, and swimming speed is irrelevant to the mechanism. Trap: Explaining a vicarious effect by the quality of the advice given.

qs.q: Why does the relaxation condition fail to test the fourth source as the theory states it?
o: Physiological arousal is unrelated to self-efficacy
The theory ties them together.
Arousal cannot be manipulated in a swimming course
Relaxation did change it.
The theory concerns how arousal is interpreted, not its level
Correct: the manipulation misses the construct.
Relaxation training requires more than one practice session to work
Dose is not the issue.
qs.x: Correct: The source is the interpretation of arousal, so the appropriate manipulation reframes a racing heart as readiness rather than fear, whereas lowering arousal tests a different claim and leaves the interpretive step untouched. Why the others are wrong: The number of sessions is not what the theory specifies, arousal was manipulated successfully, and the theory treats arousal as one of its four sources. Trap: Accepting a condition as a test of a construct because it mentions the same physiological variable.

qs.q: How does self-efficacy differ from self-esteem?
o: It is a stable personality trait that is fixed quite early in life
It is built from experience.
It refers to a specific task rather than to the self overall
Correct: the referent is narrower.
It is unrelated to what a person actually does
It predicted completion here.
It is a global evaluation of one's own worth
That describes self-esteem.
qs.x: Correct: Self-efficacy is a judgment about performing a particular action in a particular setting, which is why it predicts behavior in that domain, while self-esteem is a global appraisal of worth that predicts specific behaviors only weakly. Why the others are wrong: Self-efficacy is changed by experience rather than fixed, it tracked completion in this trial, and the global appraisal described is self-esteem. Trap: Treating the two as interchangeable because both are beliefs about the self.

qs.q: Which feature of this trial most limits the conclusion drawn from the completion column?
o: The instructor recording completions knew the assigned condition
Correct: unblinded outcome assessment.
Twenty of the adults were assigned to each of the four conditions
Equal groups help.
Self-efficacy was rated on a ten-point scale
The scale is adequate.
Participants were randomly assigned to the four sessions
Randomization is a strength.
qs.x: Correct: Completion of a deep-water swim involves judgment at the margin, and an instructor who knows which session a participant attended may encourage or evaluate differently, which can produce the group differences without any effect on belief. Why the others are wrong: Random assignment, a standard rating scale and equal group sizes all strengthen rather than weaken the design. Trap: Naming a design feature that protects the study instead of the one that leaves it open.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Erikson described development as a sequence of eight psychosocial stages, each posing a conflict whose resolution shapes what follows. The adolescent stage is identity versus role confusion, and it is followed in young adulthood by intimacy versus isolation, then generativity versus stagnation in midlife and integrity versus despair in late life. The sequencing claim is substantive: a person who has not formed a workable sense of who they are is held to be at a disadvantage in forming close relationships, because intimacy requires something to share.

Marcia operationalized the adolescent stage with two dimensions, exploration of alternatives and commitment to a choice, which cross to give four statuses. Achievement combines exploration with commitment. Moratorium is active exploration without commitment. Foreclosure is commitment without exploration, typically to a path adopted from family. Diffusion is neither.

Clinicians conducted semistructured interviews with 60 young adults aged 20 to 24 about career plans and values, and two raters classified each participant by status with disagreements resolved by discussion (Table 1).
The distribution is unremarkable for this age range, with moratorium and achievement most common, which is what a model placing identity work in the late teens and early twenties would expect.

What the design cannot do is test Erikson's sequencing claim, and that is its central limit. Status was measured once, in one age band, with no measure of the subsequent stage, so there is no way to ask whether identity achievement predicts later intimacy. Adding a measure of intimacy and following the same people forward would test it directly. Classification by interview also depends on the raters, and although two raters were used with disagreements resolved, agreement before discussion was not reported, so the reliability of the classification is unknown. The sample is small for estimating four proportions, and nothing here establishes that the four statuses are stable categories rather than positions a person moves through.

qs.q: Which status describes commitment without exploration?
o: Diffusion
That is neither dimension.
Foreclosure
Correct: a path is adopted without examining alternatives.
Moratorium
That is exploration without commitment.
Achievement
That combines both dimensions.
qs.x: Correct: Foreclosure is commitment reached without having explored alternatives, typically to a career or set of values taken over from family, and Table 1 records it as the only status with commitment but no exploration. Why the others are wrong: Moratorium is the reverse pattern, achievement has both, and diffusion has neither. Trap: Matching the status to how settled the person sounds rather than to the two dimensions.

qs.q: Which Eriksonian conflict follows identity versus role confusion?
o: Integrity versus despair
That is the final stage.
Industry versus inferiority
That precedes identity, in childhood.
Generativity versus stagnation
That is the midlife stage.
Intimacy versus isolation
Correct: it is the young-adult stage.
qs.x: Correct: Identity work in adolescence is followed in young adulthood by intimacy versus isolation, which is why the sequencing claim is that identity formation supports the capacity for close relationships. Why the others are wrong: Industry comes earlier in childhood, and generativity and integrity come later in midlife and old age. Trap: Choosing a later stage because it sounds more mature.

qs.q: Why can this study not test the sequencing claim?
o: Participants were young adults aged 20 to 24
That is the relevant age band.
No measure of the following stage was taken
Correct: intimacy was never assessed.
The interviews were semistructured in format
That is a reasonable method.
Only four identity statuses were used
Four is the standard scheme.
qs.x: Correct: The claim is that identity resolution affects the stage that follows, which requires measuring that later stage in the same people, and this study measured identity status alone at a single point in time. Why the others are wrong: The four-status scheme is standard, semistructured interviews are appropriate, and the age band is the one where identity work is expected. Trap: Naming a limitation of the method when the gap is a missing variable.

qs.q: Which status is the most common in this sample?
o: 17%, diffusion
The smallest share.
24%, foreclosure
The third largest.
28%, achievement
The second largest.
31%, moratorium
Correct: the largest share.
qs.x: Correct: Moratorium accounts for 31% of the sample, slightly ahead of achievement at 28%, which fits an age range in which many people are actively exploring without having settled. Why the others are wrong: Achievement is second at 28%, foreclosure third at 24%, and diffusion smallest at 17%. Trap: Choosing achievement because it is the status the model treats as the endpoint.

qs.q: What would most improve confidence in the classifications themselves?
o: Reporting rater agreement before discussion
Correct: it quantifies reliability.
Using three clinicians instead of two raters
More raters without a reliability figure.
Increasing the sample from 60 to 200 adults
That improves precision of proportions.
Resolving every disagreement by discussion
That is what was already done.
qs.x: Correct: Agreement reached by discussion tells you nothing about how reproducible the coding is, so the informative statistic is how often the two raters agreed independently, before they conferred. Why the others are wrong: Discussion is the existing procedure, a larger sample sharpens the proportions rather than the coding, and adding raters without reporting their agreement leaves the same gap. Trap: Adding effort to a procedure instead of reporting the statistic that evaluates it.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: Radioactive decay is first order: N = N₀(1/2)^(t/t½), where t½ is the half-life. In positron emission tomography (PET), ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is taken up by metabolically active cells. ¹⁸F decays by positron emission with t½ = 110 min; each positron annihilates with an electron, producing two 511-keV photons in opposite directions.
A radiopharmacy prepared doses and measured activity over time (Table 1).

qs.q: What activity remains 440 minutes after preparation?
o: 0 MBq
Activity decreases but does not reach zero.
12.5 MBq
This is five half-lives.
25 MBq
Correct: four half-lives of 110 minutes.
50 MBq
This is three half-lives.
qs.x: Correct: 440 min ÷ 110 min = 4 half-lives, so 400 × (1/2)⁴ = 25 MBq. Why the others are wrong: Each counts the wrong number of half-lives, or assumes complete decay. Trap: Mis-counting half-lives.

qs.q: Why must PET facilities be near a cyclotron?
o: The decay rate rises during transport
The rate falls as nuclei decay.
Cyclotrons are needed to detect the photons
Detection uses a scanner ring.
The short half-life limits transport time
Correct: activity falls quickly.
¹⁸F cannot be stored in any container
It can be stored briefly.
qs.x: Correct: With a 110-minute half-life, usable activity falls by half every two hours, so production must be close to use. Why the others are wrong: Detection uses the scanner; storage is possible; activity falls. Trap: Thinking decay rate increases with time.

qs.q: Why are two photons detected in opposite directions?
o: Annihilation conserves momentum
Correct: the pair must balance.
The detector creates a mirror image
The photons are real.
Positrons travel in two directions at once
One positron annihilates once.
The nucleus emits two photons directly
Photons come from annihilation.
qs.x: Correct: A positron and electron at rest have nearly zero net momentum, so the two 511-keV photons must leave in nearly opposite directions, which lets the scanner locate the event along a line. Why the others are wrong: The nucleus emits a positron; a positron has one path; the photons are physical. Trap: Attributing the photons to the nucleus.

qs.q: What particle is emitted in positron decay?
o: A neutron
Neutron emission is a different process.
A positive electron
Correct: the electron's antiparticle.
A helium nucleus
That is α decay.
A high-energy photon alone
That is γ emission.
qs.x: Correct: Positron (β⁺) decay emits a positron and a neutrino as a proton converts to a neutron. Why the others are wrong: Alpha, γ and neutron emission are different decay modes. Trap: Confusing β⁺ with β⁻ or γ decay.

qs.q: Why does FDG accumulate in tumors?
o: FDG decays faster inside tumors
Decay rate is independent of chemistry.
FDG binds tumor DNA specifically
FDG follows glucose transport.
Tumors have no blood supply
Tumors are usually vascularized.
Tumors take up more glucose
Correct: high metabolic rate.
qs.x: Correct: FDG enters cells through glucose transporters and is phosphorylated but not metabolized further, so it accumulates where glucose uptake is high, as in many tumors. Why the others are wrong: It is not DNA-binding; tumors have vessels; decay rates are fixed. Trap: Thinking radioactive decay depends on the environment.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: In the photoelectric effect, light striking a metal ejects electrons only if the photon energy hf exceeds the work function φ. The maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons is KE = hf − φ, independent of intensity; intensity controls how many electrons are ejected. Here h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.
Students shone monochromatic light on three metals and measured the stopping voltage, which equals the maximum electron kinetic energy in electron volts (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does zinc emit no electrons at either wavelength?
o: Zinc has no free electrons
Metals have conduction electrons.
The light intensity was too low
Intensity does not set the threshold.
Zinc reflects all ultraviolet light
The threshold, not reflection, explains it.
Both photon energies are below 4.3 eV
Correct: no ejection occurs.
qs.x: Correct: Photoemission requires hf > φ. At 4.13 eV and 2.48 eV, neither photon reaches zinc's 4.3-eV work function. Why the others are wrong: Metals have conduction electrons; intensity affects number, not threshold; the work function is the barrier. Trap: Expecting brighter light to overcome the threshold.

qs.q: What maximum kinetic energy would sodium electrons have at 250 nm (4.96 eV)?
o: This is the work function.
This ignores the work function.
This adds instead of subtracting.
qs.x: Correct: KE = hf − φ = 4.96 − 2.30 = 2.66 eV. Why the others are wrong: Each omits or misuses the work function. Trap: Adding the work function rather than subtracting it.

qs.q: Why does the photoelectric effect support a particle model of light?
o: Energy arrives in discrete quanta
Correct: a threshold frequency exists.
Light bends around obstacles
That is diffraction, a wave property.
Brighter light ejects faster electrons
Intensity does not change the maximum energy.
Light travels at a fixed speed
Both models accept this.
qs.x: Correct: A wave model predicts that enough intensity would eventually eject electrons at any frequency. The observed sharp frequency threshold and intensity-independent kinetic energy require photons of energy hf. Why the others are wrong: Diffraction supports waves; intensity does not change maximum energy; the speed of light is common to both. Trap: Choosing a wave property.

qs.q: What does increasing light intensity change?
o: The metal's work function
That is a property of the metal.
The threshold frequency
The threshold is fixed by φ.
The number of electrons ejected
Correct: more photons arrive.
The maximum kinetic energy of electrons
That depends on frequency.
qs.x: Correct: More photons per second eject more electrons, but each photon still carries the same energy. Why the others are wrong: Kinetic energy depends on frequency; φ and the threshold are material properties. Trap: Mixing up the effects of frequency and intensity.

qs.q: Which metal would make the most sensitive detector for visible light?
o: Sodium, since it is a liquid metal
Sodium is solid at room temperature.
Cesium, with the lowest work function
Correct: visible photons can eject electrons.
All three work equally in visible light
Zinc does not respond.
Zinc, with the highest work function
Visible light cannot eject electrons from zinc.
qs.x: Correct: Visible photons carry roughly 1.7–3.1 eV, so only a metal with a work function below that range, such as cesium at 2.1 eV, responds across much of the visible spectrum. Why the others are wrong: Zinc's threshold is too high; sodium is solid; responses differ. Trap: Ignoring the photon energy range of visible light.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, the electron energy is Eₙ = −13.6 eV ÷ n². A photon is emitted when the electron drops from a higher level to a lower one, with energy equal to the difference. The Balmer series involves transitions ending at n = 2 and gives visible lines.
Students observed a hydrogen discharge lamp through a spectrometer and recorded wavelengths (Table 1). Photon energy in eV equals 1,240 divided by wavelength in nanometers.

qs.q: What photon energy corresponds to the n = 3 to n = 2 transition?
o: This is the n = 2 energy.
This is the n = 1 to n = 3 difference.
This is the ionization energy from n = 1.
qs.x: Correct: E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV and E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV, so the emitted photon carries 1.89 eV. Why the others are wrong: Each uses a single level or the wrong pair. Trap: Using a level energy instead of a difference.

qs.q: Why are Lyman series lines (ending at n = 1) in the ultraviolet?
o: They involve two photons at once
Each transition emits one photon.
The electron gains energy in these transitions
Emission means energy is lost.
Their energy differences are smaller
Smaller differences give longer wavelengths.
Their energy differences are larger
Correct: shorter wavelength.
qs.x: Correct: The n = 1 level lies far below the others, so transitions to it release 10 eV or more, corresponding to ultraviolet wavelengths. Why the others are wrong: Smaller differences are infrared; one photon is emitted; emission releases energy. Trap: Reversing the relation between energy and wavelength.

qs.q: What wavelength corresponds to a 10.2-eV photon?
o: This confuses energy with wavelength.
122 nm
656 nm
This is the red Balmer line.
This omits the division.
qs.x: Correct: λ = 1,240 ÷ 10.2 ≈ 122 nm, the n = 2 to n = 1 Lyman-α line. Why the others are wrong: Each misuses the relation. Trap: Forgetting that energy and wavelength are inversely related.

qs.q: Why does hydrogen produce discrete lines rather than a continuous spectrum?
o: Electron energies are quantized
Correct: only certain differences exist.
The lamp filters out other colors
The spectrum is intrinsic.
Hydrogen has only one electron
One electron can still give many lines.
Photons can carry only visible energies
Photons span all energies.
