qs.x: Correct: Because only certain energy levels are allowed, only specific energy differences, and therefore specific wavelengths, can be emitted. Why the others are wrong: Line structure comes from quantization, not electron count; no filter is used; photon energies are not limited to visible light. Trap: Attributing discreteness to having a single electron.

qs.q: Why does the Bohr model fail for multi-electron atoms?
o: It assumes electrons have mass
Electrons do have mass.
It ignores electron repulsion
Correct: energies depend on more than n.
It predicts no spectral lines at all
It predicts lines for hydrogen well.
It assumes energy is quantized
Quantization is correct.
qs.x: Correct: With more than one electron, mutual repulsion and shielding make energies depend on the orbital's shape as well as n, which the simple Bohr model does not include. Why the others are wrong: Quantization holds; electrons have mass; the model works for hydrogen. Trap: Rejecting the parts of the model that are correct.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Boiling point reflects the strength of intermolecular forces. Hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O or F and a lone pair on an electronegative acceptor. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules, and London dispersion forces grow with molar mass and surface contact. Branching lowers boiling point by reducing contact area.
Students measured boiling points of compounds with similar molar masses (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does 1-propanol boil higher than acetone despite similar molar mass?
o: It has a larger dipole moment only
The key difference is hydrogen bonding.
Acetone is ionic
Acetone is a neutral polar molecule.
Its OH group hydrogen bonds
Correct: hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole-dipole forces.
It has more dispersion forces from branching
1-propanol is unbranched.
qs.x: Correct: 1-propanol has an O-H group that donates hydrogen bonds, which requires more energy to break than acetone's dipole-dipole attractions. Why the others are wrong: Dipole strength alone is not decisive; propanol is unbranched; acetone is molecular. Trap: Ranking forces by polarity without checking for an O-H or N-H donor.

qs.q: Why does 2-methyl-2-propanol boil lower than 1-propanol despite higher molar mass?
o: It cannot hydrogen bond at all
It has an OH group.
It is a gas at all temperatures
It boils at 82 °C.
Branching cuts surface contact
Correct: weaker dispersion forces.
It has a lower molar mass
Its molar mass is higher.
qs.x: Correct: The compact branched shape lowers the surface area available for dispersion forces and hinders hydrogen bonding, so the boiling point falls despite greater mass. Why the others are wrong: It does hydrogen bond; its mass is higher; it is a liquid at room temperature. Trap: Assuming boiling point always rises with molar mass.

qs.q: Which compound has only dispersion forces?
o: Acetone
It has a polar carbonyl group.
2-methyl-2-propanol
It hydrogen bonds.
1-propanol
It hydrogen bonds.
Butane
Correct: a nonpolar hydrocarbon.
qs.x: Correct: Butane's C-H and C-C bonds are essentially nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act. Why the others are wrong: The others have polar or hydrogen-bonding groups. Trap: Forgetting that dispersion forces exist in all molecules but dominate only in nonpolar ones.

qs.q: Why does dimethyl ether (46 g/mol) boil at −24 °C while ethanol (46 g/mol) boils at 78 °C?
o: Ethanol has a larger molar mass
Their masses are equal.
Only ethanol has an O-H
Correct: the ether has no O-H.
The ether is nonpolar
It has a bent polar C-O-C unit.
The ether has more carbon atoms
Both have two carbons.
qs.x: Correct: Both contain oxygen, but only ethanol has a hydrogen bonded to oxygen, so only ethanol can donate hydrogen bonds; the ether can only accept them. Why the others are wrong: The ether is polar; masses and carbon counts match. Trap: Assuming any oxygen-containing molecule hydrogen bonds strongly.

qs.q: Why is water's boiling point unusually high for its molar mass?
o: Each molecule makes several hydrogen bonds
Correct: two donors and two acceptor lone pairs.
Water forms covalent bonds between molecules
Hydrogen bonds are not covalent.
Water is a large molecule
It has a molar mass of 18 g/mol.
Water molecules are nonpolar
Water is highly polar.
qs.x: Correct: Each water molecule can donate two and accept two hydrogen bonds, producing an extensive network that requires much energy to disrupt. Why the others are wrong: Water is small and polar; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are not covalent. Trap: Explaining water's behavior by size rather than hydrogen bond count.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Drug absorption depends on polarity. Nonpolar drugs cross lipid membranes readily but dissolve poorly in plasma; very polar or charged drugs do the opposite. The octanol-water partition coefficient, log P, measures lipophilicity. Ionizable drugs cross membranes mainly in their uncharged form, so pH matters.
Researchers measured properties of four candidate drugs (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does drug Y cross the monolayer less well than drug X despite being more lipophilic?
o: It is permanently charged in water
No charge is described.
It is too polar to enter the membrane
Its log P is high.
It has a lower molar mass than X
Mass is not given.
It dissolves too poorly
Correct: very high log P hurts absorption.
qs.x: Correct: Permeability requires both membrane partitioning and aqueous solubility. With solubility of only 0.04 mg/mL, too little drug Y is dissolved to diffuse efficiently. Why the others are wrong: Y is lipophilic, not polar; no charge is stated; masses are not given. Trap: Assuming more lipophilic always means better absorbed.

qs.q: Why is drug W poorly permeable?
o: It has the highest log P
Its log P is the lowest.
It cannot dissolve in octanol or water
It dissolves well in water.
It is too polar
Correct: log P is negative.
It is too insoluble in water
Its solubility is highest.
qs.x: Correct: A negative log P means the drug prefers water strongly, so it partitions poorly into the hydrophobic interior of the membrane. Why the others are wrong: Its water solubility is high and its log P is lowest. Trap: Mixing up the two ends of the solubility problem.

qs.q: Which drugs are in the favorable middle range of lipophilicity?
o: W and Y
These are at the extremes.
X and Z
Correct: log P near 2 with good permeability.
W alone
It is too polar.
Y alone
Its solubility is too low.
qs.x: Correct: Drugs with log P roughly between 1 and 3 balance membrane partitioning against aqueous solubility; X and Z show the highest permeability. Why the others are wrong: W and Y are at the extremes. Trap: Choosing the highest log P as best.

qs.q: Aspirin is a weak acid with pKₐ 3.5. In the stomach at pH 2, what fraction is in the absorbable form?
o: Mostly uncharged and absorbable
Correct: pH below pKₐ favors the protonated form.
Entirely ionized regardless of pH
Ionization depends on pH.
Exactly half ionized
That occurs when pH equals pKₐ.
Mostly ionized and poorly absorbed
That occurs above the pKₐ.
qs.x: Correct: For a weak acid, a pH below the pKₐ keeps most molecules protonated and neutral, so they cross the gastric mucosa more readily. Why the others are wrong: Ionization dominates above the pKₐ; half ionization occurs at pH = pKₐ. Trap: Reversing the Henderson-Hasselbalch reasoning for acids.

qs.q: Why is log P measured with octanol and water?
o: Octanol dissolves only charged species
It dissolves neutral species better.
Octanol is more polar than water
Water is more polar.
Both phases are equally polar
They differ greatly.
Octanol mimics a membrane's interior
Correct: it is a nonpolar phase.
qs.x: Correct: Octanol approximates the hydrophobic but slightly hydrogen-bonding environment of a lipid bilayer, so the partition ratio predicts membrane behavior. Why the others are wrong: Water is far more polar; octanol favors neutral species; the phases differ. Trap: Reversing which phase is polar.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images with identical physical properties in achiral environments but different behavior in chiral environments such as enzyme active sites. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both and shows no net optical rotation. Diastereomers differ at some but not all stereocenters and have different physical properties.
A pharmacology laboratory measured properties of two enantiomers of a drug and the racemate (Table 1).

qs.q: Why do the two enantiomers differ so much in receptor binding?
o: The receptor site is chiral
Correct: one shape fits better.
One has more atoms than the other
They have identical formulas.
One enantiomer is more polar
Polarity is the same.
Their melting points differ
Melting points are identical.
qs.x: Correct: A protein binding site is made of chiral amino acids, so it interacts differently with mirror-image ligands, giving binding constants that differ by more than 200-fold here. Why the others are wrong: Melting points, polarity and formulas are identical. Trap: Looking for a difference in bulk physical properties.

qs.q: Why does the racemate melt at a lower temperature than either enantiomer?
o: One enantiomer decomposes on heating
Both are stable.
The racemate has a lower molar mass
Molar masses are equal.
The mixed crystal packs less efficiently
Correct: a different solid phase forms.
Mixtures always boil at lower temperatures too
The boiling point is unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: Enantiomers pack into separate, well-ordered crystals; the racemic solid has different packing and intermolecular contacts, which here lowers the melting point. Why the others are wrong: Both are stable; masses are equal; the boiling point did not change. Trap: Assuming a mixture lowers every transition temperature.

qs.q: Why does the racemate show zero optical rotation?
o: Light cannot pass through the mixture
Light passes through.
Equal and opposite rotations cancel
Correct: +32 and −32 sum to zero.
The mixture is achiral at the molecular level
Each molecule is still chiral.
Neither enantiomer rotates light
Each rotates by 32 degrees.
qs.x: Correct: A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers rotates plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, so the net rotation is zero even though every molecule is chiral. Why the others are wrong: Each enantiomer rotates light; light transmits; the molecules remain chiral. Trap: Concluding that zero rotation means no chiral molecules.

qs.q: Why are many drugs now sold as single enantiomers?
o: Racemates cannot be manufactured
They are easily made.
The inactive form may cause side effects
Correct: one enantiomer can be harmful.
Enantiomers have identical biological effects
Their effects differ.
Single enantiomers are always cheaper
Resolution adds cost.
qs.x: Correct: Because receptors and enzymes distinguish enantiomers, the unwanted form may be inactive or toxic, so purifying one enantiomer can improve safety and lower the dose. Why the others are wrong: Racemates are easy to make; single enantiomers often cost more; effects differ. Trap: Treating enantiomers as interchangeable.

qs.q: How could the enantiomers be separated?
o: Use a chiral resolving agent
Correct: diastereomers differ physically.
Distill the mixture carefully
Boiling points are identical.
Recrystallize from an achiral solvent
Solubilities match in achiral solvents.
Measure their optical rotation
Measurement does not separate them.
qs.x: Correct: Converting enantiomers into diastereomeric salts with a chiral acid or base gives species with different solubilities and melting points, which can be separated and then reconverted. Why the others are wrong: Distillation and achiral recrystallization cannot distinguish them; measurement is not separation. Trap: Choosing a technique that relies on properties that are identical.
